entries.text: onTick(dt) — one call per tick while running, with the seconds elapsed since the previous tick, clamped to about one tick (≈1/15 s at frame; one period on the calendar tiers, so a page returning from an hour hidden gets 60, not 3600). Three consecutive throws stop the Time, loudly, naming the node. running = true restarts it; a running that is constrained starts again the next time what the constraint reads changes. A clock is not a way to hear about a change. A Time gated on a condition, whose handler does its work and closes its own gate, is asking to be told that something crossed into a new state. Name the value in trackChanges and answer onChange (Node): it runs at the close of the settle that moved the value, not on the next frame, and it costs no clock. onTick(e: number)

entries.title: Keys
entries.text: The keyboard, as a member. Keys names one concept that a program can either ask or listen to: Keys.isDown("KeyA") is a call you make from any { } body; a Keys [ … ] member is how the keyboard calls you. It is the raw stream — it fires even while a text field has focus, so gate app-level shortcuts on app state where that matters. A focused view's own onKeyDown/onKeyUp handlers are the other half of the story, and usually the right one for keys that belong to a particular widget. Lifetime is the node's: subscribed at init, dropped when the node is discarded, nothing to clean up. Fan-out is by instance — a menu, a dialog, and a menubar each holding a Keys member all hear the keyboard at once. A page can run more than one program: a desktop runs one in each window's AppIsland. The keyboard goes to one of them at a time — the program holding the focused view, the program inside a focused island, or, with nothing focused, the outer program — and only that program's Keys members hear keys. A key held as the keyboard moves on gets its onKeyUp in the program that had it. App [ width = 240, height = 100, fill = white, textColor = black, n: number = 0, keys: Keys [ onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) { if (e.key == "ArrowUp") { app.n = app.n + 1 } else if (e.key == "ArrowDown") { app.n = app.n - 1 } } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 30, fontSize = 30, text = { n = ${n} } ] ]

entries.title: Keys.isDown
entries.text: Whether a key is physically down right now, by code ("ShiftLeft", "MetaLeft") — for modifier state at the moment of a gesture, which is not carried on a pointer event. How a table decides whether a click extends a range or toggles one member. onClick() { (parent as Table).rowClick(this.tableIndex(), this.item(), Keys.isDown("MetaLeft") Keys.isDown("ControlLeft"), Keys.isDown("ShiftLeft")) } It answers for the program whose body asks: a key counts as down in a program only if it went down while that program had the keyboard. The modifiers — Shift, Control, Option, Command — are the keyboard's state and read the same in every program. Polling a key also claims it: while the asking view is shown and its program has the keyboard, the browser's own use of the key stands down — Space and the arrows don't scroll the page, a letter doesn't open the browser's find. A key pressed with Command, Control or Option held, or typed into a text field, stays the browser's. A game reads its keys this way and needs nothing else. isDown(code: string): boolean

entries.title: Keys.held
entries.text: Every key currently down in the asking program, as code strings. held(): string[]

entries.title: Keys.navClaim
entries.text: Claims the navigation keys — arrows, Space, Home/End, Page — away from the browser's scroll defaults while an overlay is roving, and releases them when passed false. An open menu owns the arrow keys ; without the claim the page scrolls underneath it. Claim on open, release on close, always in pairs — a claim that outlives its overlay leaves the page unscrollable. While an overlay holds the claim, the keys it uses — Esc, Enter, the arrows — reach only the Keys members inside it, not the program's others. A claim made by an overlay that opened in a Window holds only while focus is in that window. navClaim(owner: object, on: boolean): void

entries.title: Keys.claimant
entries.text: The overlay the keys go to now: the latest claim that holds, or null. Esc closes this one. claimant(): any

entries.title: Keys.shortcutsInForce
entries.text: The shortcuts in force where focus is now — the nearest declaration of each key, walking from the focused view up through its program and on into the program that hosts it: records { id, key, label, enabled, origin, group }, origin being the declaring set's title and group the menu a menu bar's shortcut sits in (else the origin). What a panel of the available shortcuts lists (hold ⌘ in the desktop). shortcutsInForce(): any[]

entries.title: Keys.keyDown
entries.text: onKeyDown(e) — a key went down. e is a normalized KeyEvent: e.key ("ArrowUp", "Escape", "a"), e.code, and modifier flags — never a numeric code. onKeyDown(e: KeyEvent)

entries.title: Keys.keyUp
entries.text: onKeyUp(e) — a key came up, same payload. onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent)

entries.title: Keys.navClaim
entries.text: The navigation keys changed hands: true when something claimed them (an overlay opened and its arrows now rove it), false when the last claim released. It fires on the transition only, not per claim, so nested overlays that each claim do not chatter. This is how a focus ring stands down while a menu owns the arrows: the library's own ring subscribes to it, because during that time the menu's rover is the focus and a second indicator would be a lie. onNavClaim(e: boolean)

entries.title: Keys.commandHeld
entries.text: The command key (⌘ on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere) has been held alone for a moment: true; then false when it is let go, or another key joins it. Every program hears it, wherever the keyboard is — what a panel of the shortcuts in force (Keys.shortcutsInForce()) shows and hides on, as iPadOS shows its own while ⌘ is held. onCommandHeld(e: boolean)

entries.title: Focus
entries.text: The focus service, as a member. Like Keys, Focus names one concept a program can ask (Focus.focus(this), Focus.byKeyboard() — calls from any { } body) or listen to (a Focus [ … ] member). Listening is what a focus indicator does: the library's FocusRing follows focus with exactly these two handlers, tracking where focus went and the live silhouette of whatever holds it. Most apps never need it — focus rings, tab order, and activation are provided — but replacing the indicator is a supported thing to do, and this is how. watch: Focus [ onFocusChange(v: View) { classroot.target = v }, onGeometry(g: FocusGeometry) { classroot.tx = g.x; classroot.ty = g.y } ]

entries.title: Focus.focus
entries.text: Moves keyboard focus to a view — the only way to move it; assigning a control's focused does not. The call every control makes on pointer-down, so that the keyboard picks up where the pointer left off. Focusing a view that is not focusable is a no-op. onPointerDown() { Focus.focus(this) } focus(v: unknown): void

entries.title: Focus.blur
entries.text: Clears focus entirely, so nothing holds it. blur(): void

entries.title: Focus.next
entries.text: Moves focus to the next view in traversal order — what Tab does, callable directly when a control wants to advance focus itself (a field that moves on Enter). next(): void

entries.title: Focus.prev
entries.text: Moves focus to the previous view in traversal order — Shift-Tab's action. prev(): void

entries.title: Focus.byKeyboard
entries.text: Whether the current focus arrived by keyboard rather than by pointer — the web's :focus-visible rule, as a reactive read. This is what lets a clicked control show no focus edge while a tabbed one does, and what a focus indicator keys off to decide whether to appear at all. byKeyboard(): boolean

entries.title: Focus.getFocus
entries.text: The view that currently holds focus, or null. A tracked read: a constraint that reads it re-runs when focus moves (hint = { Focus.getFocus()?.tooltipLabel ?? "" }), and every view also carries its own focused fact. Also for saving focus before opening a modal and restoring it after. Restore on a later turn, not immediately: an in-flight keystroke must finish against the old focus, or the key that closed a dialog is delivered to the opener, which reopens it. getFocus(): any

entries.title: Focus.focusIn
entries.text: Moves focus into a view that holds focusable views — to what last had focus inside it, else its first stop — and answers whether anything took it. What an overlay that takes focus does on opening; a scope remembers where focus was, so reopening returns there. focusIn(v: unknown): boolean

entries.title: Focus.nextRegion
entries.text: Moves focus to the next (1) or previous (-1) region of the context around the one focus is in — what F6 and Shift-F6 do. A program's own command for cycling its windows calls it. nextRegion(dir: number): void

entries.title: Focus.holds
entries.text: Whether focus is on a view or anywhere inside it — a program hosted in an island inside it included. A Window answers whether it has the keyboard with it. holds(v: unknown): boolean

entries.title: Focus.focusChange
entries.text: onFocusChange(v) — focus moved to view v (or null when nothing is focused). onFocusChange(v: View)

entries.title: Focus.geometry
entries.text: onGeometry(g) — the focused control's live root-space silhouette: g.x, g.y, g.w, g.h, g.rad (its corner radius), g.view, and g.root (the app that owns it — an embedded app's ring ignores a target belonging to another). onGeometry(g: FocusGeometry)

entries.title: Tooltips
entries.text: The tooltip service, as a member: onTooltip(e) fires when a view carrying tooltipLabel = "…" wants its tooltip shown, and with null when it should hide. The service owns the platform conventions — the show delay, instant retarget while showing, hide on press — so a listener only renders. The library's Tooltip is the one listener most programs ever need, and it arrives automatically in any app whose views carry tips. Declare your own Tooltips [ … ] member only when you are replacing that rendition. tips: Tooltips [ onTooltip(e: TooltipEvent) { if (e == null) { classroot.shown = false; return } classroot.label = e.text classroot.shown = true } ]

entries.title: Tooltips.tooltip
entries.text: onTooltip(e) — show the tip described by e (e.text, plus the target's root-space box e.x/e.y/e.w/e.h and its owning app e.root), or hide when e is null. onTooltip(e: TooltipEvent)

entries.title: Stream
entries.text: The abstract base of the live-connection sources — EventStream (SSE) and Socket (WebSocket) extend it. Not instantiable: write the concrete transport. The one thing to know: there is no connect() or disconnect() — the declaration decides. A stream is connected exactly while active is true and url is non-empty; empty the url (or flip active) and it closes, change the url and it closes and reopens, remove the node and the connection dies with it. Nothing to unsubscribe, ever. Messages are transient: nothing accumulates unless a handler writes it somewhere — the runtime keeps only last. An app that streams JSON parses in the handler (JSON.parse(e.data)) and writes wherever it wants; accumulation is one line of app code, deliberately not a built-in policy. job: View [ output: string = "", progress: EventStream [ url = { /api/jobs/${classroot.jobId}/events }, active = { classroot.jobId != "" }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { classroot.output = classroot.output + e.data }, ], out: Text [ width = { parent.width }, text = { parent.output } ] ]

entries.title: Stream.url
entries.text: Where to connect — a literal or a { } constraint. Unlike DataSource.url, a change acts immediately: the old connection closes and a new one opens at the new address (there is no fetch() moment to wait for). "" means detached — the idiom for "no job yet" is deriving emptiness: url = { app.jobId != "" ? "/api/jobs/" + app.jobId + "/events" : "" }. string

entries.title: Stream.active
entries.text: The gate. false closes the connection (and cancels any pending retry); flipping back true reopens it. Constrain it to app state — active = { app.live } — rather than toggling imperatively. boolean

entries.title: Stream.retry
entries.text: Reconnect policy, visible in the declaration: seconds to wait before re-dialing after the connection is lost and the platform won't bring it back on its own — a Socket's unexpected close, an EventStream's terminal failure. 0 (the default) means no retry: the stream lands in status = "failed" and the app decides. A declared retry keeps trying while active is true, at a fixed interval — no invisible backoff, no give-up count. A structural failure (the factory itself refuses — headless extraction, a missing host service) never loops, whatever retry says. number

entries.title: Stream.status
entries.text: The connection lifecycle as one fact: "closed", "connecting", "open", "retrying", or "failed" (down, and will not reconnect). Read-only — computed for you; assigning it is a compile error. "retrying" covers both the platform's own recovery (SSE) and a declared retry waiting to re-dial. closed | connecting | open | retrying | failed

entries.title: Stream.error
entries.text: The last failure reason, "" when none; cleared when a connection opens. Read-only — the state side of onError (the event side). A status line is text = { feed.error != "" ? feed.error : feed.status }. string

entries.title: Stream.last
entries.text: The most recent message's data, reactive. Read-only. The zero-handler tier: a ticker that only shows the latest value needs no handler at all — text = { feed.last }. string

entries.title: Stream.open
entries.text: The boolean view of status == "open" — one fact, two spellings, never in disagreement. Read-only. The connection dot is visible = { feed.open }. boolean

entries.title: Stream.message
entries.text: onMessage(e: StreamMessage) — every message. e.data is always a string: parse it yourself if it is JSON, concatenate it if it is streamed text; the runtime never guesses. e.type is the SSE named event ("message" for unnamed messages and every socket frame); e.id is the SSE last-event-id ("" on sockets). onMessage(e: StreamMessage)

entries.title: Stream.open
entries.text: The connection is live — fires each time one opens, including reopens after a retry. Prefer deriving from open/status for anything a constraint can express; the handler is for work state cannot do (send a subscription frame, log). onOpen()

entries.title: Stream.close
entries.text: A connection that had opened went away — the app closed it (active, a url change, node removal at discard is silent), the server ended it, or it failed. Fires once per connection, before any retry dials the next one. onClose()

entries.title: Stream.error
entries.text: Something failed: a terminal connection loss, a refused transport, a send on a socket that is not open. The reason is in error when the handler runs. The platform's own in-flight retries (SSE) are not errors and stay quiet. onError()

entries.title: EventStream
entries.text: Server-Sent Events (text/event-stream) as a source: the server pushes, the app receives, an onMessage that concatenates is the whole consumer. See Stream for the shared surface (url/active/retry, the read-only status/open/error/last). Receive-only — there is no send. A stream that is the reply to a request — an AI model's answer arriving word by word from a POST — declares the request as a DataSource does: method, body, headers, credentials. It is one request, and its reply is read as it arrives; the stream closes when the reply ends (onClose), and a refusal fails it with the status and what the server said. A request is not sent again on its own — declare retry to ask again after a loss. A plain GET — none of the four — keeps the platform's EventSource machinery verbatim: it retries on its own (honoring the server's retry: hint) and resumes with Last-Event-ID, during which status reads "retrying" and no error is reported; retry/onError concern only terminal failure — the platform giving up. A declared stream holds a live connection for as long as it is active and its node lives — every open tab is one held server connection (browsers cap ~6 per host over HTTP/1.1, so a dev server's tabs can exhaust the pool). The lifecycle is the declaration: active = { app.jobId != "" } releases the connection the moment the condition goes false, and a discarded node closes its own — there is nothing to unsubscribe. output: string = "", progress: EventStream [ url = { /api/jobs/${app.jobId}/events }, active = { app.jobId != "" }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.output = app.output + e.data }, ] answer: string = "", asked: string = "", reply: EventStream [ url = "/api/chat", method = "POST", active = { app.asked != "" }, body = { { prompt: app.asked } }, headers = { { Authorization: "Bearer " + app.token } }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.answer = app.answer + e.data }, ]

entries.title: EventStream.listenTo
entries.text: The named SSE event types to deliver — listenTo = ["progress", "done"]. Required for any stream that labels messages with event: lines: the platform's EventSource physically cannot deliver a named event it was not asked to listen for, so an undeclared name is silently invisible — if onMessage sees nothing but the connection is open, this is the first thing to check. The name carries the contract: you hear what you listen to. Unnamed (default) messages always arrive; e.type says which kind each one is. array

entries.title: EventStream.method
entries.text: "GET" (the default), "POST", "PUT", "PATCH" or "DELETE" — the request whose reply is the stream. Anything but a plain GET is read as the reply to one request (above). "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "PATCH" | "DELETE"

entries.title: EventStream.headers
entries.text: The request's headers — a record, as a DataSource's. An empty value drops the header, so Authorization: app.token != "" ? "Bearer " + app.token : "" sends one only when signed in. Changing them asks again. object

entries.title: EventStream.body
entries.text: What the request sends, as a DataSource's: an object or array is JSON-encoded with a JSON Content-Type, a string is sent as it is. Ignored for a GET. object

entries.title: EventStream.credentials
entries.text: Whether the request carries the person's cookies and credentials — sameOrigin (the default), include, omit — as for a DataSource. omit | sameOrigin | include

entries.title: Socket
entries.text: WebSocket as a source: the Stream surface plus send(text) — send is a call you make, onMessage is it calling you. See Stream for url/active/retry and the read-only status/open/error/last. Unlike SSE the platform has no native reconnect, so a Socket that should survive a dropped connection must say so: retry = 2 re-dials two seconds after any close the app didn't ask for, for as long as active holds — the whole policy is that one number. Text frames only; a binary frame is dropped. live: Socket [ url = "wss://api.example.com/feed", retry = 2, onOpen() { this.send('{"subscribe":"prices"}') }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.tick(JSON.parse(e.data)) }, ]

entries.title: Socket.send
entries.text: Sends one text frame. Legal only while open — on a socket that is not open it sends nothing and reports through the error channel (error + onError), never a silent queue: if the app needs buffering-until-connected, that policy belongs in app state, visibly. Sending the opening frame belongs in onOpen (which also covers every reconnect); gate user-triggered sends on .open: live: Socket [ url = "wss://api.example.com/control", retry = 2, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.store.apply(JSON.parse(e.data)) } ], apply: Button [ label = "Apply", disabled = { !app.live.open }, onClick() { app.live.send(JSON.stringify({ t: "setpoint", value: app.target })) } ] What arrives lands in the data (app.store.apply), and every view reading it follows — the socket never touches a view. send(text: string): void

entries.title: State
entries.text: A named bundle of overrides that snaps on and off together. Its body is not ordinary children: a name = value entry is an override of the enclosing view's own attribute (checked against that view's schema, not the State's), applied while the state is on; an id: Type [ … ] entry is a conditional subtree that exists only while applied. Because attribute reads compose as a precedence stack, the base values return exactly when the state turns off — there is no manual undo to write, and no drift. card: View [ height = 72, fill = white, open: State [ applied = { expanded }, height = 184, fill = lightsteelblue, Text [ text = "shown only while open" ] ] ] Names inside it. An override is the view's value, computed on the view: this, a bare name and parent there mean what they would written on the view itself (height = { width / 2 } is half the view's own width), and the children it holds read the view the same way. Its own members — applied, its declarations, onApply/onRemove — are the State's: this is the State there, and parent the view (applied = { parent.expanded }). A State's own member is not in reach from an override, and a method written in a State is a compile error. Names inside it. An override is the view's value, computed on the view: this, a bare name and parent there mean what they would written on the view itself (height = { width / 2 } is half the view's own width), and the children it holds read the view the same way. Its own members — applied, its declarations, onApply/onRemove — are the State's: this is the State there, and parent the view (applied = { parent.expanded }). A State's own member is not in reach from an override, and a method written in a State is a compile error.

entries.title: State.applied
entries.text: Whether the state is on. Constrain it to a condition (applied = { expanded }) and the whole bundle snaps in and out as that flips — the base values restore themselves when it turns off. The declarative alternative to the apply() / remove() / toggle() verbs. boolean

entries.title: State.apply
entries.text: Turns the bundle on imperatively — the verb form of applied = true. Prefer constraining applied to a condition; reach for apply() only when the toggle is truly event-driven and has no natural boolean to constrain it to. apply(): void

entries.title: State.remove
entries.text: Turns the bundle off, restoring the base values via the precedence stack (no manual undo). The partner of apply(). remove(): void

entries.title: State.toggle
entries.text: Flips the bundle on/off from its current state — a one-call switch for a handler (onClick() { panel.toggle() }) when you don't want to thread a boolean. toggle(): void

entries.title: State.apply
entries.text: Fires when the bundle turns on — after the overrides compose onto the stack, so reads in the handler already see the state's values. Use for a side effect that must ride with the state (focus a revealed field), not to mutate what the state already declares. onApply()

entries.title: State.remove
entries.text: Fires when the bundle turns off, the partner of onApply — after the base values have restored. For tearing down whatever onApply set up. onRemove()

entries.title: Node
entries.text: The plain object-graph atom — a non-visual node you subclass, with class X extends Node [ … ], for logic that paints nothing: the rules for a kind of record, a service, shared state with rules to keep, machinery several views drive. It lives in the tree as a named member, shares the reactive core and the classroot/app reach, and fires init — but it paints nothing. Data itself is not wrapped in one: records live in a Dataset that views bind to, and when those records have logic of their own, the dataset is a class that extends Dataset — the special case of a class with no view that holds data. class Die extends Node [ sides: number = 6, last: number = 0, rolls: number = 0, roll() { last = 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() sides); rolls = rolls + 1 }, reset() { last = 0; rolls = 0 } ] A view then holds one as a named member (die: Die [ ]) and reads/drives it reactively. A Node may also stand on a record with a datapath of its own: its :path reads and :field = v writes resolve against that record, so a class owns the rules for a kind of data with no view involved. A class with no extends is a view, so a class of this kind always says extends Node.

entries.title: Node.trackChanges
entries.text: The values this node reports changes to: trackChanges = [ "loaded", "kind" ]. Each name must be one of the node's own reactive values — an attribute it declares, a fact it carries (scrollY, loaded, hovered), or an attribute bound to data. The checker refuses a stranger in a written list, and the runtime refuses one in a computed list when the node arms. To hear a record's field, declare an attribute over the path (kind: string = { :kind }) and name that — there is one door. Nothing else is tracked, so a node that names nothing costs nothing. array

entries.title: Node.datapath
entries.text: The data cursor: the place in a dataset this node and its descendants read and write relative to. Written as a :path (extending the inherited cursor), a { } expression yielding a place (datapath = { app.d.value.tasks[app.pick] }), or null. The nearest ancestor-or-self cursor wins, so a Node class with its own datapath stands on that record, and views inside it read the same one. A :path ending in [] replicates — and only a view replicates; on any other node that form is a compile error naming the single-record spelling. datapath

entries.title: Node.$data
entries.text: Reads the datum at a path relative to the nearest cursor — this node's own, or the nearest ancestor's — the compiled form every :path lowers to, callable by hand. $data("") is the whole record at the cursor, which is what a replicated row calls to hand its own record to a method. Reach for the :path spelling in ordinary code; reach for this when the path is computed, or when you need the record itself rather than a field of it. item() -> object { return this.datapath != null ? this.$data("") : this } $data(path: string | readonly unknown[]): unknown

entries.title: Node.$cell
entries.text: The compiled form of a write to a record field: a handler's :done = v lowers to this.$cell(["done"]).value = v, and :n += 1 reads and writes through the same place. The write lands through the dataset's set, relative to the nearest cursor, exactly where the matching read resolves. Write :field = v; this is what the compiler emits, not a call to make by hand. $cell(segs: readonly unknown[]): { value: unknown }

entries.title: Node.init
entries.text: Fires once when the node has finished constructing and its subtree exists — the place for setup that needs the built tree. Every node gets it, faceless subclasses included — the init walk visits non-View children too. Answered by onInit(). onInit()

entries.title: Node.change
entries.text: Fires at the close of a settle in which one or more tracked values ended different from where they started: after every constraint has re-run and every reader already holds the new value. One call per settle carries all of them, so a node whose two subjects move together acts once. Answered by onChange(e: ChangeEvent), where e.changed holds one ValueChange per value — its name, its previousValue (what it held at the previous close), and its currentValue (what the node holds now; reading the attribute directly gives the same thing). Silent at boot: first values are not changes, and setup belongs in onInit or, for the whole tree, the App's onReady. A handler's writes are the next settle, so a change may cause a change; a handler may not assign a value it was told about, and a ring of handlers ends on its own, because a value is delivered at most once per settle chain. Not to be confused with an input's edits, which is the instinct the name carries in from HTML and React: a field reports what the reader typed through onInput, and a control reports its own value through input(). This event is about a value the program holds. Use it only for a genuine state change — something happened and the program must act once: record that the terms were read when the reader reaches their end, open a pane when the data lands, start a fetch when a selection changes. It is not for following a value, which is a constraint, nor for moving one, which is a Spring, and it is not meant for use in conjunction with animation. onChange(e: ChangeEvent)

entries.title: Gauge
entries.text: A labeled horizontal value bar: an optional caption, then a rounded track filled to value. It follows the theme like every library control — the fill is the theme's accent, the track its trackFill, the caption textMuted — and takes a colour of its own through tint. It is for demos and dashboards that want a caption; for a meter with min/max, use ProgressBar. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], Gauge [ width = 260, label = "Storage", value = 72 ], Gauge [ width = 260, label = "Memory", value = 38, tint = #37E0C8 ] ]

entries.title: Gauge.label
entries.text: The caption to the left of the track. "" drops the caption column entirely and the track takes the full width. string

entries.title: Gauge.value
entries.text: How full the track reads, 0–100 always — a percentage, not your own units. This is the difference from ProgressBar, which takes min/max and lets you pass raw counts. number

entries.title: Gauge.tint
entries.text: The fill colour: the theme's accent unless you give one. Color

entries.title: Gauge.lead
entries.text: The caption column's width, derived from whether there is a label at all. Set it to align several bars whose captions differ in length. number

entries.title: Gauge.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Gauge.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Gauge.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The caption, so a screen reader names the reading as the eye does. string

entries.title: Gauge.accessibilityValue
entries.text: The reading, out of the gauge's fixed 0–100 range. number

entries.title: Gauge.accessibilityMin
entries.text: number

entries.title: Gauge.accessibilityMax
entries.text: number

entries.title: Card
entries.text: The box everything else sits on: the theme's surface fill, its corner radius, a hairline edge in its line token, and — the part that saves the wrapper view — a default layout that stacks and pads, so a Card's children are written as a plain list and arrive inset from every edge. Card [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 280, Text [ fontSize = 15, fontWeight = semibold, text = "Storage" ], Text [ width = 100%, wrap = true, text = "Cards size themselves to what they hold, padding included." ], Divider [ ], Button [ label = "Manage" ] ] Use Text, not TextLabel, as a direct child. A TextLabel positions itself vertically — that cap-centering y is the whole of what it adds — and the card's layout places the children it holds, so the two would own the same attribute. TextLabel belongs inside a control or a row that leaves y alone; a card's own lines are Text. Give it a width, not a height. A Card has no height of its own: it takes the one its content needs, padding counted in — so the box grows and shrinks with what is inside it, and nothing has to be kept in step by hand. Set height only to cap it (with clip = true if the content may exceed the cap). The inset is the card's own padding = 16, a View attribute: the card has an inside, and every child — stacked by the default layout, placing itself at x = center, or opted out with ignoreLayout — is positioned from it. The default arrangement is SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], which simply stacks inside that room, 8 apart. Replacing the layout does not replace the padding. Naming your own layout: member — a WrappingLayout, a row, a stack with different numbers — overrides the arrangement only; the card is still inset, because the inset was never the arrangement's. Write padding = 0 to take it away, or padding = 24 for more. fill, cornerRadius and stroke are ordinary defaults a use site may write over the same way.

entries.title: Card.fill
entries.text: The theme's surface — the token that means "the plane content sits on", one step off the window's own background in every preset, light and dark. Write over it for a card that should sink into the page rather than rise off it (fill = { provided("theme").background }), and pair that with a kept stroke so the shape still reads. Fill

entries.title: Card.cornerRadius
entries.text: The theme's controlCornerRadius, so a card's corners match the buttons and fields inside it — 7 in the house look, 4 in Redmond and MountainView. Set a number to break with the preset; the box still clips nothing unless you also say clip = true. Radius

entries.title: Card.stroke
entries.text: A one-pixel edge in the theme's line. stroke = null removes it — the right move for a card that already stands off the page by fill alone, or one nested inside another. Per-side works here as anywhere: stroke = [ null, null, stroke(1, #DBE1E9), null ] turns a card into a row with a rule under it. Stroke

entries.title: Card.padding
entries.text: Inset

entries.title: Divider
entries.text: A single line in the theme's line token, sized to the room it is given: drop one into a stack and it spans the content, drop one into a row with axis = y and it stands on end. It is a painted view, not a border — which is what lets it be a child in a list like any other, and lets a layout space it like any other. Card [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 280, Text [ text = "General" ], Divider [ ], Text [ text = "Advanced" ] ] thickness is logical pixels, not device pixels. 1 is one of the units everything else in a program is measured in, so on a 2× display the rule is two device pixels and looks like every other 1px edge in the library — there is no hairline primitive here.

entries.title: Divider.axis
entries.text: Which way the rule runs: x (the default) is horizontal and spans the parent's width; y is vertical and spans its height. A bare literal, not a string. The span is the parent's content extent — the room inside the parent's own padding — so a divider in a padded card stops where the card's content does, rather than running out under the inset. Axis

entries.title: Divider.thickness
entries.text: The rule's weight in logical pixels. 1 is the library's hairline everywhere. number

entries.title: Divider.inset
entries.text: How far in from the leading edge the rule starts — the list-separator convention, where a row's separator begins under the text rather than under the icon beside it. The rule's far end stays put, so the inset shortens it. 0 (the default) is a full-span rule. number

entries.title: Divider.color
entries.text: The rule's colour, the theme's line by default. Set it for a rule that must read heavier or lighter than the theme's edges — a section break against a row separator. Color

entries.title: Divider.width
entries.text: Derived, not authored: the span across the rule on a horizontal divider, thickness on a vertical one. Leave it alone — writing a width here fights the span, and a shorter rule is what inset is for. Length

entries.title: Divider.height
entries.text: The mirror of width: thickness on a horizontal rule, the span on a vertical one. Also derived, and also not for setting — a divider is as long as the room it was given. Length

entries.title: Divider.span
entries.text: The length the rule runs: the parent's content extent along axis, or 0 with no parent. width and height read it; a subclass that spans something else overrides it. span()

entries.title: Control
entries.text: The interaction-state base every stateful control extends. It owns how the pointer, keyboard, and focus relate to this view — and nothing semantic: checked, value, and their kin live on the concrete control. The pointer half is the language's: hovered and pressed are View's read-only interaction intrinsics (chain-based, touch-correct, cancel-safe), and on a control they answer under its policy: false while disabled, and pressed also true for a keyboard activation's flash. Style against them directly. What Control adds: disabled — inert: not focusable, no activation, never hovered or pressed. keyboard — Space or Enter on the focused control activates it, the same press() path a pointer uses, acknowledged by flashing the pressed look. It also owns two things every labelled control shares: iconLeft / iconRight — decoration, by class name. A concrete control lays them out; Control only declares that they exist, so every control that shows one names it the same way. menu — the role of dropping a menu, not decoration. Setting menu gets the disclosure mark, the anchored open, the held-open styling, and ArrowDown-to-open together, which is the part a hand-rolled copy gets wrong one piece at a time. Extend it to make your own control a first-class one — focusable, keyboard-activated, and styled off the same state pair as everything the library ships: class Counter extends Control [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, n: number = 0, fill = { pressed ? provided("theme").controlPressed : hovered ? provided("theme").controlHovered : provided("theme").control }, press() { n = n + 1 }, t: TextLabel [ x = center, fontSize = 13, text = { "" + classroot.n } ] ] App [ Counter [ x = 20, y = 20 ] ]

entries.title: Control.disabled
entries.text: Inert: not focusable, no activation, and hovered/pressed read false, so a disabled control never lights up. Constrain it rather than assigning it (disabled = { app.muted }) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also dim themselves against provided("theme").disabledOpacity. boolean

entries.title: Control.focusVisible
entries.text: Focused and the focus arrived by keyboard — the web's :focus-visible channel. Cleared by blur and by a pointer press on this control, so a clicked control shows no keyboard edge while a tabbed one does. What a AccordionPane header's focus edge reads. boolean

entries.title: Control.iconLeft
entries.text: A decorative icon for the leading slot, named by class (iconLeft = "TrashIcon"), not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored and data-bound are the same mechanism (iconLeft = { "" + :icon } in a replicated toolbar). Control only declares the attribute; the concrete control lays it out. A computed name needs use [ Name ] to survive the build, since no static reference reaches it. The name is read once, when the control is built: a name read from data gives each row its own icon, but changing the name later does not swap the icon (see IconHost). Any icon class may be named, your own included — a library icon set another way is a subclass: class BackChevron extends ChevronIcon [ dir = "left" ], then iconLeft = "BackChevron". string

entries.title: Control.iconRight
entries.text: The trailing icon slot, same vocabulary as iconLeft. Setting it wins over the chevron a menu would imply — see rightIcon. string

entries.title: Control.menu
entries.text: The menu this control drops — an instance, not a name (menu = { app.optionsMenu }). Setting it is a role, not decoration: the disclosure mark, the anchored open below the control, the held-open fill, and ArrowDown-to-open all follow together. Declare one menu and point many controls at it rather than one per opener; the menu reads opener to vary its items. View?

entries.title: Control.menuOpen
entries.text: True while menu is showing and this control is what opened it. Derived, never written — a flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu closes some other way (Escape, a pick, a press on the backdrop) and strands the control in its held-open look forever. boolean

entries.title: Control.rightIcon
entries.text: What actually renders on the right: iconRight when set, else the disclosure chevron implied by menu, else nothing. One place decides, so every menu-dropping control wears the same mark. string

entries.title: Control.flash
entries.text: The keyboard-activation pulse — the control's own state, which pressed reads as a press, so Space/Enter shows the same look a pointer press does and styling reads only hovered and pressed. boolean

entries.title: Control.flashMs
entries.text: How long flashPress() holds the pressed look. number

entries.title: Control.focusable
entries.text: A control takes focus unless it is disabled — one rule, so a disabled control drops out of the Tab order without saying so twice. boolean

entries.title: Control.accessibilityRole
entries.text: button: a control is something a person presses, and a screen reader says so with no word from the program. A control that is something else — a checkbox, a slider, a tab — names its own role. none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Control.accessibilityExpanded
entries.text: Whether the control's menu is open — follows menuOpen, so a screen reader hears a menu button as collapsed or expanded. Unset (null) on a control with no menu. boolean

entries.title: Control.openMenu
entries.text: Opens menu anchored to this control, unless there is none or the control is disabled. The seam a concrete control calls from its own press(). openMenu()

entries.title: Control.press
entries.text: The activation seam — override this, not the handlers. Pointer and keyboard both land here — a click through onClick, Space and Enter through the keyboard — so one override serves all three. The base opens menu when there is one. A value control delivers through input from here and never writes its own value directly , which is what lets a constrained control avoid fighting its constraint. On a control with a menu, an override calls super.press(): the base is what opens it from the keyboard. press()

entries.title: Control.focusShape
entries.text: The focus silhouette the ring hugs, { x, y, w, h, rad } in this control's own coordinates. null (the default) rings the whole bounds at its cornerRadius. Override to ring the part that means something — a Radio rings its dot, a Slider its thumb. focusShape()

entries.title: Control.flashPress
entries.text: Flashes the pressed look to acknowledge keyboard activation — the platform convention for buttons and menu items. Value controls whose state change is itself the feedback (Checkbox, Switch, Radio) deliberately do not call it. flashPress()

entries.title: Control.focus
entries.text: Captures the keyboard modality into focusVisible. An override calls super.onFocus(), or the focus channel goes dark. (focused itself is every view's fact, kept by the focus service.) onFocus()

entries.title: Control.blur
entries.text: Clears focusVisible. An override calls super.onBlur(), or focusVisible outlives the focus. onBlur()

entries.title: Control.pointerDown
entries.text: Claims focus, clears the :focus-visible channel, and opens menu if there is one — menus open on press, not release, as the platform does. An override calls super.onPointerDown() , or clicking the control strands the keyboard elsewhere. onPointerDown()

entries.title: Control.keyDown
entries.text: Space and Enter run press(); ArrowDown opens menu. On a slider, the arrow keys run accessibilityIncrement() and accessibilityDecrement() — the methods a screen reader's adjust gesture calls, which the slider role requires a control to have — so the keyboard and assistive technology move the value by one path; on a spinButton, Up and Down do the same. Ignores auto-repeat for activation, not for the arrows. An override handles its own keys and passes the rest on with super.onKeyDown(e), or the control loses Space, Enter and its arrows. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: Control.click
entries.text: A click runs press() unless the control is disabled — so a control that overrides press() is activated by pointer and keyboard alike without writing a handler. Override onClick only when a click means something other than activation; Button does, making it the use site's action. onClick()

entries.title: Checkbox
entries.text: A boolean control. Its value is the checked attribute; input owns the value's destination — by default the destination is the checkbox itself, so it works standalone with zero wiring: mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ] … visible = { mute.checked } Hand the value to its real owner by overriding input and constraining down: Checkbox [ label = "Mute", checked = { app.muted }, input(v: boolean) { app.muted = v } ] press() never writes checked directly — it only delivers — so a constrained checkbox never fights its constraint. row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ], Text [ text = { mute.checked ? "muted" : "audible" } ] ]

entries.title: Checkbox.baseline
entries.text: The baseline a row aligns this control by — the label's. Under align = baseline the checkbox's caption sits on the same line as its neighbours; the box rides with it. number

entries.title: Checkbox.checked
entries.text: Whether the box is ticked. Standalone it owns this and you read it back by name; constrained (checked = { app.muted }) it needs an input override to go with it — a constraint with no input leaves the checkbox's own edit assigning to a constrained attribute, which is refused at runtime. boolean

entries.title: Checkbox.label
entries.text: The text beside the box. "" renders the box alone — the form for a checkbox inside a table cell, where the column heading is the label. string

entries.title: Checkbox.size
entries.text: The box's edge length. Defaults to the theme's figure, so a toolbar checkbox can shrink to match its neighbours without a subclass. number

entries.title: Checkbox.height
entries.text: 24, the row a checkbox and its label sit in — and 44 on a touch-first device, a finger's target, the box unchanged. Length

entries.title: Checkbox.fieldValue
entries.text: Follows checked: what required and validate judge (see ValueControl). any

entries.title: Checkbox.accessibilityRole

entries.title: Checkbox.accessibilityChecked
entries.text: Follows checked; the visible label is the name. boolean

entries.title: Checkbox.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The caption of a Field around it, unless the use site names the checkbox; with neither, its label is its name. A checkbox with no label — a task's in a list — is named at its use site: accessibilityLabel = :title. string

entries.title: Checkbox.width
entries.text: Content-sized: the box, then a gap and the label when there is one. A label-less checkbox is exactly its box, so a bare mark in a table cell reserves no phantom room. Length

entries.title: Checkbox.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control — every part alike, never a recolour — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none: the one place the number lives. number

entries.title: Checkbox.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the box alone, not the box-plus-label — the Radio rule, so a long label does not drag a wide ring across the row. focusShape()

entries.title: Checkbox.input
entries.text: Where the value goes. The default writes checked; override it and the checkbox becomes a delivery channel for state you own (input(v: boolean) { app.muted = v }). This is the one member to override when the value lives elsewhere. input(v)

entries.title: Checkbox.press
entries.text: Toggles by delivering the flipped value through input — never by writing checked, which is what keeps a constrained checkbox from fighting its constraint. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Button
entries.text: A labeled action control. The action is its onClick — write it at the use site exactly as on any View; Button adds the interaction states, the themed look, and keyboard activation (Space/Enter drives the same onClick). primary = true fills with the accent; the default is the quiet control look. Button [ label = "Save", primary = true ] Button [ label = "Add", iconLeft = "PlusIcon" ] Button [ label = "Options", menu = { app.optionsMenu } ] // chevron implied Button [ iconLeft = "CloseIcon" ] // icon only Three slots in a row — iconLeft, the label, iconRight — laid out by SimpleLayout and sized from contentWidth, so an absent label or icon costs nothing and needs no special case: an invisible child is skipped and its space reclaimed. A menu supplies the right icon on its own (control.declare). The fill walks the four-rung ladder — control at rest, controlHovered, controlPressed, and controlSelected while its menu is open — so hovering a button never looks like pressing it.

entries.title: Button.baseline
entries.text: The baseline a row aligns this control by — its label's, in the control's own coordinates. A SimpleLayout or WrappingLayout with align = baseline sits the button's text on the same line as a neighbouring Text or Markdown; without this declaration the layout would refuse the button by name (a baseline is claimed, never guessed from a box). Declared here so every button carries it; an icon-only button still answers its (invisible) label's line. row: View [ layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 10, align = baseline ], Text [ fontSize = 18, text = "Ready?" ], Button [ label = "Save", primary = true ] // its label sits on the text's line ] number

entries.title: Button.label
entries.text: The button's text. "" (the default) leaves it iconless-and-wordless, which is only useful with an icon — a button with neither has nothing to press. string

entries.title: Button.primary
entries.text: Marks this as the affirmative action: it fills with the accent — accentHovered and accentPressed as the pointer hovers and presses — and takes provided("theme").accentTextColor for its ink. One per group of choices — a dialog's Save, not its Cancel. Purely a style decision; it changes nothing about behaviour. Button [ label = "Cancel" ], Button [ label = "Save", primary = true ] boolean

entries.title: Button.gap
entries.text: Space between the icon and the label, when both are present. number

entries.title: Button.padH
entries.text: Horizontal padding inside the button, each side. The button sizes to its content plus twice this, so widening it is how you make a short label less cramped. Button [ label = "OK", padH = 28 ] // a short word, given room Button [ label = "Add", iconLeft = "PlusIcon", gap = 12 ] number

entries.title: Button.inkColor
entries.text: The one ink decision, so a button's icon and its label always agree: the accent text colour when primary, the ordinary text colour otherwise. textColor follows it. Override this rather than textColor alone, or the icon and the words drift apart. class DangerButton extends Button [ inkColor = { primary ? white : crimson } ] Color

entries.title: Button.primaryFill
entries.text: The primary look's ground for the current state: the theme's accent, its hovered or pressed shade, and pressed while its menu is open. fill picks it when primary. Color

entries.title: Button.plainFill
entries.text: The plain look's ground for the current state: the theme's control colour and its hovered and pressed shades. fill picks it when not primary. Color

entries.title: Button.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Button.height
entries.text: The theme decides, when it has an opinion: provided("theme").buttonHeight sets it (a platform theme's native control height); a theme that leaves it unset gets 40. On a touch-first device it is at least 44, a finger's target. A height at the use site overrides both. Length

entries.title: Button.cornerRadius
entries.text: A theme that rounds buttons by a fixed radius sets provided("theme").buttonCornerRadius; it is capped at half the height, so a short button goes fully pill without a squared corner. Otherwise the shared controlCornerRadius every control uses. Radius

entries.title: Button.width
entries.text: Content-sized: the run — icon, label, icon — plus padH each side. Give it a width and the run centres inside it, so a dialog's equal-width row keeps every label centred. Length

entries.title: Button.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control, icon and label alike, rather than recolouring it — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none. number

entries.title: Button.fill
entries.text: The state ladder, one rung per interaction fact, first match wins: an open menu holds the selected tint, so the button stays lit while its menu is up; pressed beats hovered; at rest, the quiet control. A primary button climbs the same ladder in the accent: held — pressed, or its menu open — is accentPressed, hovered is accentHovered, at rest accent. Every rung is a theme token, so a theme restyles every button's states at once; a platform whose controls do not answer a passing pointer states its hover tones equal to its rest tones (Cupertino does). Fill

entries.title: Button.stroke
entries.text: A hairline only where the theme wants one: themes that border their secondary buttons set provided("theme").buttonStrokeColor; flat themes leave it null and get no stroke. A primary button is never bordered — the accent fill is its edge. Stroke

entries.title: Button.press
entries.text: The activation path, called by a click and by Space/Enter. It flashes the press tint, opens an attached menu if there is one, then calls onClick. Override onClick for ordinary use; override this only to change what activation means. An override calls super.press(): it is what runs onClick from Space and Enter. press()

entries.title: Button.click
entries.text: Your handler. Fires after the press is delivered, so the affordance has already run — put the work here, not in press(). onClick()

entries.title: TextLabel
entries.text: A Text that centers its ink in its parent's height — the vertical placement a label wants, as opposed to a paragraph. Use it for the text inside a control or any centered caption; use plain Text for flowing copy. Why it exists. y = center on a plain Text centers the geometric box (the ordinary meaning, matching every other view). But a label sitting in a box wants its letterforms optically centered, not the font's box with its asymmetric ascent/descent leading — otherwise the text reads a hair low. TextLabel supplies a y that centers the cap band (cap-top to baseline), the optical centre for a label: y = { parent.height / 2 - this.baseline + this.capHeight / 2 } That expression cap-centres the label: the ink sits centred by its cap band rather than by its box, which is what reads as centred for a label. It is written out here, once, instead of at every use site. It is a plain constraint over the Text's own live metric facts (baseline, capHeight, measured from the effective font), so it re-centers when the font, the size, or the parent's height changes. Override y on an instance to opt out. The centre is the cap band because that is what the platform control themes (Cupertino, Mountain View, Redmond) are matched against.

entries.title: TextLabel.y
entries.text: Centres the ink on the parent's height by its cap band — baseline and cap height — rather than by the line box, which is what a label beside a control wants and a paragraph does not. Length

entries.title: Switch
entries.text: A boolean control with a sliding thumb — same value contract as Checkbox (checked, input owns the destination), different body language: the thumb springs between its two rest points, so toggling moves rather than jumps.

entries.title: Switch.checked
entries.text: Whether the switch is on. Constrain it (checked = { app.muted }) and override input to own the destination, or leave it and read it back — a Switch works standalone with no wiring. boolean

entries.title: Switch.dragging
entries.text: True from pointer-down until the release. boolean

entries.title: Switch.dragged
entries.text: True once the pointer has moved the thumb during a press: the thumb follows the pointer, and the release settles on the side the thumb is nearer. A drag past the slop raises no click, so it never also toggles. boolean

entries.title: Switch.accessibilityRole

entries.title: Switch.accessibilityChecked
entries.text: Follows checked. A switch shows no label of its own, so its use site names it with accessibilityLabel — unnamed, the compiler warns. boolean

entries.title: Switch.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The caption of a Field around it, unless the use site names the switch: its name to a screen reader. string

entries.title: Switch.width
entries.text: A theme with a native switch size says so (provided("theme").switchWidth); otherwise 44, the common pill. Length

entries.title: Switch.height
entries.text: A theme with a native switch size says so (provided("theme").switchHeight); otherwise 24. Length

entries.title: Switch.cornerRadius
entries.text: Always a pill — half the height, whatever the height is. Radius

entries.title: Switch.fieldValue
entries.text: Follows checked: what required and validate judge (see ValueControl). any

entries.title: Switch.claim
entries.text: x: a finger drags the thumb sideways, while a vertical drag that starts on the switch still scrolls the page. both | x | y

entries.title: Switch.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control — every part alike, never a recolour — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none: the one place the number lives. number

entries.title: Switch.fill
entries.text: The track's ladder for a toggle: checked takes the accent; unchecked shows the selected tint while hovered or pressed and the quiet control tint at rest — so the track answers the pointer before the value flips. Fill

entries.title: Switch.stroke
entries.text: A hairline in the accent when checked, in the theme's line colour otherwise, so the track keeps an edge on light and dark surfaces alike. Stroke

entries.title: Switch.input
entries.text: Where the value goes. The default writes checked; override it and the switch becomes a delivery mechanism for state you own. press() never writes checked directly, so a constrained switch never fights its constraint. input(v)

entries.title: Switch.press
entries.text: Toggles, by delivering the flipped value through input. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Switch.pointerDown
entries.text: Latches the drag, and keeps Control's focus rule. An override calls super.onPointerDown(e). onPointerDown(e)

entries.title: Switch.pointerMove
entries.text: Marks the press a drag once the pointer has moved. An override calls super.onPointerMove(). onPointerMove()

entries.title: Switch.pointerUp
entries.text: Ends a drag on the nearer side, delivering through input when that changes the value. An override calls super.onPointerUp(): it is what ends the drag. onPointerUp()

entries.title: Slider
entries.text: A bounded number by drag. Same value contract as every control — value is the attribute, input owns the destination (default: itself) — and the delivery is continuous during a drag. Pressing the track jumps to that position (local coordinates); the drag then follows the pointer by root-space delta (app.pointerX), so it survives the pointer leaving the control. Arrow keys nudge by step. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ], vol: Slider [ value = 40 ], Text [ text = { volume ${Math.round(vol.value)} } ] ]

entries.title: Slider.value
entries.text: Where the handle sits, in your own units. Standalone the slider owns it; constrained (value = { app.volume }) it needs an input override with it, or the drag's own delivery is refused against the constraint. number

entries.title: Slider.min
entries.text: The value at the left end. number

entries.title: Slider.max
entries.text: The value at the right end. number

entries.title: Slider.step
entries.text: The quantum every delivered value snaps to, and the distance one arrow key moves. step = 0.01 for a fine continuous control; it is never zero — the quantizer divides by it. number

entries.title: Slider.frac
entries.text: The handle's position as 0…1, derived from the value and the range. What the track, fill, and thumb all position from; read it to hang your own decoration off the handle. number

entries.title: Slider.dragging
entries.text: True from pointer-down until the captured release. The pressed intrinsic deliberately will not do here — it is hit-chain-based, so it goes false the moment the pointer leaves the thumb, while a drag must survive exactly that. boolean

entries.title: Slider.accessibilityRole

entries.title: Slider.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The caption of a Field around it, unless the use site names the slider: its name to a screen reader. string

entries.title: Slider.accessibilityValue
entries.text: Follows value, in the slider's own units. number

entries.title: Slider.accessibilityMin
entries.text: Follows min. number

entries.title: Slider.accessibilityMax
entries.text: Follows max. number

entries.title: Slider.accessibilityStep
entries.text: Follows step — what one increment moves. A slider shows no name, so its use site sets accessibilityLabel. number

entries.title: Slider.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Slider.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Slider.fieldValue
entries.text: Follows value: what required and validate judge (see ValueControl). any

entries.title: Slider.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control — every part alike, never a recolour — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none: the one place the number lives. number

entries.title: Slider.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the circular grabber — the part the arrow keys move — rather than the whole track. focusShape()

entries.title: Slider.input
entries.text: Where the value goes, and it fires continuously through a drag, not once at release: the owner decides what to do with the stream, and the data layer owns any coalescing. Override it to redirect the value (input(v: number) { app.volume = v }); the default writes value. input(v)

entries.title: Slider.quant
entries.text: Snaps a raw value to step and clamps it into min…max. Every delivery routes through it, so an override changes what the slider can produce — logarithmic scales, detents, a magnetic centre. quant(v)

entries.title: Slider.accessibilityIncrement
entries.text: One step up, through quant and input like any other change — what the Right and Up arrows run (Control's keys), and what a screen reader's increment calls. accessibilityIncrement()

entries.title: Slider.accessibilityDecrement
entries.text: One step down — what Left and Down run. accessibilityDecrement()

entries.title: Slider.barStyle
entries.text: True when the theme asks for the Material-3 rendition: a vertical bar handle with the track shortened either side of it rather than drawn through. One theme token (provided("theme").sliderHandleStyle) selects a rendition — data, not a fork. barStyle()

entries.title: Slider.dotStyle
entries.text: True for the Fluent rendition: a round grabber with an accent dot inside that grows under hover and press. The other value of the same token. dotStyle()

entries.title: Slider.pointerDown
entries.text: Jumps the value to the pressed position, claims focus, and latches the drag. An override calls super.onPointerDown(e). onPointerDown(e)

entries.title: Slider.pointerUp
entries.text: Ends the drag. An override calls super.onPointerUp(): it is what ends the drag. onPointerUp()

entries.title: Slider.pointerMove
entries.text: Tracks the drag by root-space pointer delta, so the handle keeps up with a pointer that has left the control. An override calls super.onPointerMove(). onPointerMove()

entries.title: Slider.keyDown
entries.text: Home and End go to min and max; Page Up and Page Down move a tenth of the range, never less than a step. The arrows step, as Control gives every slider. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: RadioGroup
entries.text: One-of-N. Radios are written as the group's direct children — the group's layout arranges them, and each radio reaches its group as parent. A radio replicated from data (Radio [ datapath = :plans[], choice = { :id }, label = { :name } ]) is one too: each copy is a direct child of the group. RadioGroup [ value = "m", input(v: string) { app.size = v }, Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ], Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ], ] size: RadioGroup [ x = 20, y = 20, value = "m", Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ], Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ] ]

entries.title: RadioGroup.value
entries.text: The group's value — the chosen choice, and the only value in the pair. A Radio has none of its own; it derives on from this. Standalone the group owns it; constrained, override input beside it as with any control. string

entries.title: RadioGroup.accessibilityRole

entries.title: RadioGroup.fieldValue
entries.text: Follows value, the chosen choice: what required and validate judge (see ValueControl). any

entries.title: RadioGroup.focusable
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: RadioGroup.focusScope
entries.text: stop: the group is one Tab stop — Tab lands on the checked radio and the next Tab leaves; the arrows move to the next radio and check it, as every platform's radio group does. none | stop | capture | region | modal

entries.title: RadioGroup.focusField
entries.text: focusField()

entries.title: RadioGroup.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes. The default writes value; override it to own the destination (input(v: string) { app.size = v }) and the radios keep working untouched, because they deliver rather than store. input(v)

entries.title: RadioGroup.pick
entries.text: Selects a choice by name — the seam a Radio calls on its group. Call it to move the selection from code without bypassing input. pick(v)

entries.title: RadioGroup.focusEntry
entries.text: The radio Tab lands on: the checked one, else the first that is enabled. focusEntry()

entries.title: RadioGroup.radios
entries.text: The group's radios, for the Tab entry. A handler-only walk. radios()

entries.title: Radio
entries.text: One choice in a RadioGroup: a direct child of the group, naming itself with choice. A radio stores nothing — it derives on from the group's value and delivers its choice to the group when pressed, so turning one on can never leave another stale. App [ width = 300, height = 120, fill = white, textColor = black, size: string = "m", RadioGroup [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.size }, input(v: string) { app.size = v }, Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ] ], Text [ x = 160, y = 20, text = { "size: " + app.size } ] ]

entries.title: Radio.baseline
entries.text: The baseline a row aligns this radio by — its caption's, so a row of mixed controls and text under align = baseline reads as one line. number

entries.title: Radio.choice
entries.text: This radio's identity within its group, compared against the group's value by string. Required and unique per group — two radios sharing a choice light together. string

entries.title: Radio.label
entries.text: The text beside the dot. "" renders the dot alone. string

entries.title: Radio.on
entries.text: Whether this radio is the group's current choice. Derived from the group, never stored — which is why turning one on cannot leave another stale. boolean

entries.title: Radio.height
entries.text: Tall enough for the dot and a 2px margin either side: the theme's radioSize (18 by default) plus 4 — and on a touch-first device at least 44, a finger's target, the dot unchanged. Length

entries.title: Radio.accessibilityChecked
entries.text: Follows on: whether this choice is the group's value. boolean

entries.title: Radio.width
entries.text: Content-sized: the dot, then a gap and the label when there is one. A label-less radio is exactly its dot. Length

entries.title: Radio.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole choice, dot and label alike — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none. number

entries.title: Radio.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the round dot rather than the dot-plus-label row. focusShape()

entries.title: Radio.press
entries.text: Delivers this radio's choice to the group. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Radio.blur
entries.text: Judges the group when the focus leaves a radio, as a field is judged on leaving. An override calls super.onBlur(). onBlur()

entries.title: Radio.keyDown
entries.text: The arrows move to the next or previous radio in the group (the stop's) and check the one they land on; Space and Enter press, as on any control. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: Field
entries.text: A labeled form row: the label, then whatever control the use site nests, and under the control what is wrong with it — its error, once it has been judged: Field [ label = "Name", TextInput [ width = 220, height = 30, required = "Enter your name." ] ] The label sits in a column beside the control (labelWidth is the shared-column knob), or above it with stacked = true. The control reports itself to the field it is in, so the field shows its message without being told which control it holds; a control of your own that extends ValueControl does the same. form: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ], Field [ label = "Name", TextInput [ width = 200, height = 28 ] ], Field [ label = "Notify", Switch [ ] ] ]

entries.title: Field.baseline
entries.text: The baseline a row aligns this field by — its caption's. Two fields side by side under align = baseline keep their captions on one line whatever their controls' heights. number

entries.title: Field.label
entries.text: The caption in the left column. It is a Text, not a control's own label — a Field labels whatever you nest, so the nested control's own label should usually be empty or you will render the words twice. string

entries.title: Field.labelWidth
entries.text: The label column's width, and the knob that aligns a form. Every row in a form sets the same plain number — one value, repeated or read from a shared attribute (labelWidth = { app.formLabels }). It is deliberately not measured from the widest label: aggregating over sibling rows is exactly what the constraint system refuses, so the shared column is a value you state rather than one the form discovers. number

entries.title: Field.stacked
entries.text: The label above the control rather than in a column beside it — the usual arrangement of a form read top to bottom, and of one on a phone. boolean

entries.title: Field.fieldLabel
entries.text: The caption, provided to what the field holds: a TextInput, Switch, Checkbox, Slider or Combobox inside takes it as its name to a screen reader unless it has its own (accessibilityLabel). A control of your own reads it the same way — accessibilityLabel = { provided("fieldLabel", "") }. string

entries.title: Field.control
entries.text: The control the field holds, as it reported itself: a TextInput or ValueControl inside. Null for anything else. any

entries.title: Field.message
entries.text: What the field shows under its control: the control's error, empty when it says nothing. string

entries.title: ProgressBar
entries.text: Display-only bounded number — the read-only sibling of Slider (same value/ min/max vocabulary, no interaction, no input). Restyle by theme; set width at the use site (220 by default).

entries.title: ProgressBar.value
entries.text: Where the bar sits, in the units you choose. Clamped into min…max for display, so a value outside the range renders full or empty rather than overflowing. number

entries.title: ProgressBar.min
entries.text: The value that reads as empty. Defaults to 0. number

entries.title: ProgressBar.max
entries.text: The value that reads as full. Defaults to 100 — set it to your own total and pass raw counts as value rather than converting to a percentage yourself. number

entries.title: ProgressBar.indeterminate
entries.text: Something is under way and how far along it is unknown — a request in flight, a search running. The bar then sweeps a short segment across the track instead of filling to value, and reports no value to assistive technology. Under the person's reduced-motion setting the segment holds still, as a faint full bar. Set it from the state that is under way: indeterminate = { app.saving.loading }. boolean

entries.title: ProgressBar.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: ProgressBar.height
