entries.title: FocusRing
entries.text: The travelling focus indicator: a shape-hugging rounded outline that flies to the focused control and reshapes to its own silhouette on arrival. The ring springs position, size and cornerRadius together, which is why a Radio's row ring, a pill Switch's ring and a text field's ring each differ — the targets do. The model: The fact — the ring listens to Focus (a Focus [ onFocusChange(v: View) { … } ] member) and tracks the target's root-space geometry on every change, pointer or keyboard. A pointer focus parks the ring there silently (snap, no show) — so the next Tab's flight departs from the control the user just clicked, never from a stale perch. Roles, theme-elected — provided("theme").focusRingStyle: "both" (or true, the default) · "travel" (flight, then an idle fade) · "rest" (no flight — the ring appears in place and stays) · false (no ring; the theme's classes carry the at-rest indication — the invariant lives with the theme-and-classes pair). While keyboard modality holds and the role includes rest, the ring rests — no idle fade; a pointer press clears modality and the ring hides (web :focus-visible semantics). The flight is the flourish — provided("theme").focusAnimate = false snaps every move; the underdamped travel is default-on. It arrives automatically with any Control-descended class; declare your own FocusRing [ ] (or subclass) to replace it. Pure chrome: never focusable, never a pointer target. The silhouette is the target's focusShape() when it declares one, else its bounds at its cornerRadius. You do not instantiate this, and you do not position it. Tab between the controls below and watch it fly; the members exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition, and for the theme tokens that elect its behaviour. row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 12 ], Button [ label = "One" ], Button [ label = "Two" ], Checkbox [ label = "Three" ] ]

entries.title: FocusRing.overlayUp
entries.text: True while an overlay owns the keyboard (an open Menu). The ring stands down — the menu's own rover is the focus story, and a page ring poking around a panel reads as chrome fighting chrome. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.shown
entries.text: Whether the ring is visible. A pointer focus parks it silently — geometry current, ring hidden — so the next Tab departs from the control the user just clicked rather than from a stale perch. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.placed
entries.text: Whether the ring has ever had a target to park on. The first appearance never flies, because a flight from nowhere is a streak across the app. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.idle
entries.text: True once a travel-role ring has sat still long enough to fade out. A resting ring never sets it. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.opacity
entries.text: number

entries.title: FocusRing.ignoreLayout
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.visible
entries.text: Visible while its faded opacity still shows anything, and never while an overlay is up — a ring behind a dialog would point at something you cannot reach. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.pointerEvents
entries.text: string

entries.title: FocusRing.ringTheme
entries.text: The theme the ring draws with: the ringed control's, so a ring on a dark panel takes the panel's colours, else the App's. ringTheme()

entries.title: FocusRing.ringRole
entries.text: The theme's election, from provided("theme").focusRingStyle: "both" (the default), "travel" (flight, then fading once it settles), "rest" (appears in place and stays, no flight), or "off". "off" is legitimate only when the theme's own controls carry an at-rest focus indication — the invariant belongs to the theme-and-classes pair, not to the ring alone. ringRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.restRole
entries.text: Whether the elected role includes resting — a resting ring does not idle-fade. restRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.travelRole
entries.text: Whether the elected role includes the flight. travelRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.snapTo
entries.text: Lands the ring on its target immediately, skipping the flight. What a pointer focus, a first appearance, and provided("theme").focusAnimate = false all use — and what a target moving under a resting ring uses , so a dragged slider thumb carries the ring rigidly instead of springing after it. snapTo()

entries.title: FocusRing.draw
entries.text: Renders the outline: four corner arcs with arms whose length is a pure function of distance from the target, so the physics does the choreography. Override to replace the rendition entirely. provided("theme").focusSights = true restores the open-bracket "target sights" reading; provided("theme").focusRingInnerWidth adds the Fluent two-tone band. draw(d)

entries.title: Accordion
entries.text: Stacked pane headers with one pane open at a time, each pane sliding open and closed on a spring over its height. The load-bearing mechanic: a pane's content is present through the whole open and close , revealed and concealed by the pane's own clip as its height animates. That is what makes the motion read as a pane opening rather than as content appearing — never an instant pop, never a blank gap. The open pane is one attribute on the group — value, the open pane's name — which is exactly RadioGroup's shape. Panes are the group's direct children; each names itself (name, defaulting to its label) and derives open from the group. Content is authored as the AccordionPane's ordinary children — the AccordionPane stacks its header then the content, and clips. The pane stacks them flush, header against content, because the header is edge-to-edge and an inset that reached it would break that. So the breathing room around a pane's content is the content's own padding: Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, AccordionPane [ label = "Account", initiallyOpen = true, View [ width = 100%, padding = 12, Text [ width = 100%, wrap = true, text = "Panes slide on a spring; the content rides the whole way." ] ] ], AccordionPane [ label = "Privacy", View [ width = 100%, padding = 12, Text [ width = 100%, text = "One pane open at a time." ] ] ] ]

entries.title: Accordion.value
entries.text: The open pane's name — the group's whole value, exactly RadioGroup's shape. Assign it to open a pane from code; "" closes all of them. A AccordionPane never stores whether it is open, it derives it from here, which is why the one-open-at-a-time invariant cannot break. string

entries.title: AccordionPane
entries.text: One pane of an Accordion: a header you press and the content you write as its ordinary children. A pane derives open from the group's value — it never stores it — and slides open and closed on a spring over its height, its content present the whole way and revealed by the pane's own clip. App [ width = 300, height = 180, fill = white, textColor = black, Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, AccordionPane [ label = "Details", initiallyOpen = true, Text [ width = 100%, padding = 12, text = { "open: " + parent.open } ] ], AccordionPane [ label = "More", Text [ padding = 12, text = "Press a header." ] ] ] ]

entries.title: AccordionPane.label
entries.text: The pane header's text, and — unless you set name — its identity in the group. string

entries.title: AccordionPane.name
entries.text: This pane's identity, defaulting to its label. Set it when two panes share a label, or when the label is user-facing copy you expect to change , so the group's value does not move under you when the wording does. string

entries.title: AccordionPane.initiallyOpen
entries.text: Seeds the group: the first pane declaring initiallyOpen = true opens if nothing else has claimed value yet. A one-shot at init, not a constraint — to drive which pane is open from state, constrain the group's value instead . boolean

entries.title: AccordionPane.open
entries.text: Whether this pane is the group's current one. Derived; read it to style your content. boolean

entries.title: AccordionPane.twist
entries.text: The header chevron's angle, in radians, sprung between 0 and −π/2. It turns in step with the height animation rather than snapping , which is the whole reason it is a number and not a swap between two marks — a number can be sprung. number

entries.title: AccordionPane.width
entries.text: A pane is as wide as its accordion; only its height is its own. Length

entries.title: AccordionPane.clip
entries.text: ClipPath

entries.title: AccordionPane.defaultPlacement
entries.text: slot

entries.title: AccordionPane.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The header's text, naming the pane; the header itself is the button a screen reader presses to open it. string

entries.title: AccordionPane.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole pane, header and content alike, rather than recolouring it — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none. A disabled pane neither opens nor closes; whatever it shows stays as it is. number

entries.title: AccordionPane.tabOrder
entries.text: Contributes the pane's contents to keyboard traversal only while it is open. A closed pane is clip-occluded rather than hidden — its content must stay visible for the slide to carry it — so this is what stops Tab from descending into a pane the user cannot see . The header itself remains a stop either way. An override keeps that: a closed pane contributes nothing. tabOrder()

entries.title: AccordionPane.press
entries.text: Opens this pane by writing its name to the group. Called by a click and by Space/Enter on the header. press()

entries.title: AccordionPane.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the header — the part Space and Enter press — rather than the whole pane with its open content. The ring is the pane's only focus indicator. focusShape()

entries.title: AccordionPane.init
entries.text: Applies initiallyOpen. Fires once per pane. An override calls super.onInit(), or initiallyOpen does nothing. onInit()

entries.title: Carousel
entries.text: Pages side by side, one in view at a time. A finger drags the row of pages and it follows 1:1; on release it settles on a page on a spring — the next one when the drag went past a third of the width or was a quick flick, otherwise back where it started. Assigning page from anywhere springs the row there the same way. A carousel's children are its pages: each is laid out as wide and as tall as the carousel's content box, in order. A drag that goes up or down rather than sideways is left to the page around it (claim = x), and a press that never travels still reaches the page's own controls. Carousel [ width = 100%, height = 160, View [ fill = #F6D7C3, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "One" ] ], View [ fill = #CFE5D2, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "Two" ] ], View [ fill = #CFDCF2, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "Three" ] ] ]

entries.title: Carousel.page
entries.text: The page in view, from 0. Constrain it (page = { app.slide }) and override input to own the destination, or leave it and read it back. number

entries.title: Carousel.offset
entries.text: The row's sideways displacement in pixels: -page × width at rest, the finger's position during a drag, and the spring's in between. Every page's x derives from it. number

entries.title: Carousel.dragging
entries.text: True from pointer-down until the release. boolean

entries.title: Carousel.clip
entries.text: On: the pages beside the current one are out of view until a drag brings them in. ClipPath

entries.title: Carousel.claim
entries.text: x: a sideways drag is the carousel's, a vertical one stays the page's. both | x | y

entries.title: Carousel.input
entries.text: Where a settled swipe sends the new page. The default writes page. input(p)

entries.title: Carousel.pageCount
entries.text: How many pages there are: the carousel's laid-out children, counted when a drag needs it. pageCount()

entries.title: Carousel.pointerDown
entries.text: Latches the drag from wherever the row is, even mid-glide. An override calls super.onPointerDown(e). onPointerDown(e)

entries.title: Carousel.pointerMove
entries.text: Moves the row with the pointer, and keeps the speed. An override calls super.onPointerMove(). onPointerMove()

entries.title: Carousel.pointerUp
entries.text: Chooses the page — one step for a drag past a third of the width or a flick faster than 0.4 px/ms, otherwise none — and lets the spring carry the row there. A canceled release (the browser reclaimed the gesture) settles back on the current page. An override calls super.onPointerUp(e): it is what ends the drag. CarouselLayout Internal. The carousel's arrangement: each child a content box wide and tall, the next one a width further on, all shifted by the carousel's offset. onPointerUp(e)

entries.title: CarouselLayout
entries.text: Pages side by side, one in view at a time. A finger drags the row of pages and it follows 1:1; on release it settles on a page on a spring — the next one when the drag went past a third of the width or was a quick flick, otherwise back where it started. Assigning page from anywhere springs the row there the same way. A carousel's children are its pages: each is laid out as wide and as tall as the carousel's content box, in order. A drag that goes up or down rather than sideways is left to the page around it (claim = x), and a press that never travels still reaches the page's own controls. Carousel [ width = 100%, height = 160, View [ fill = #F6D7C3, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "One" ] ], View [ fill = #CFE5D2, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "Two" ] ], View [ fill = #CFDCF2, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "Three" ] ] ]

entries.title: CarouselLayout.place
entries.text: One box per page, from the carousel's content extent and offset. place()

entries.title: CarouselLayout.laidCount
entries.text: How many children it lays out: the carousel's pageCount(). laidCount()

entries.title: Tooltip
entries.text: The layer system's floor: any view sets tooltipLabel = "…" and this singleton renders it — hover delay, placement, flip, and theming are nobody's problem at the use site. It arrives automatically when any view in the program carries a tip, as FocusRing does; declare your own Tooltip [ ] (or subclass) to replace the rendition. It listens to the Tooltips service (a Tooltips [ onTooltip(e: TooltipEvent) { … } ] member), which owns the platform conventions (the show delay — tooltipDelay, ~1s in the Cupertino and Redmond conventions, ~500ms MountainView — instant retarget while showing, hide on press). Placement is theme data too (tooltipPlacement): "below" (the default — under the target, centered, flipping above at the edge), "above" (flipping below), or "pointer" (the Cupertino help tag — offset below-right of where the cursor rests). Always clamped inside the app. Pure chrome — never focusable, never a pointer target, always above content (the auto-splice puts it last in the App, and source order stacks). Theming (the four cities carry the tokens): tooltipFill / tooltipTextColor / tooltipStrokeColor (null = no border) / tooltipFontSize (11 in Cupertino, 12 elsewhere). Cupertino and Redmond wear bordered surface chips; San Francisco and Mountain View the inverse chip. You do not instantiate this. Set tooltipLabel on any view and the singleton appears; the members below exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition. View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 130, height = 38, cornerRadius = 8, fill = steelblue, tooltipLabel = "Saves your changes", Text [ x = center, y = center, textColor = white, text = "Save" ] ]

entries.title: Tooltip.label
entries.text: The text currently displayed, pushed in by the Tooltips service from the hovered view's tooltipLabel. A subclass reads this; nothing writes it from app code. string

entries.title: Tooltip.placement
entries.text: Where the chip sits, elected by provided("theme").tooltipPlacement: "below" (the default, centred under the target, flipping above at the edge), "above" (the Fluent default, flipping below), or "pointer" (the Cupertino help tag, offset below-right of the resting cursor). Always clamped inside the app. string

entries.title: Tooltip.pointerY
entries.text: Where the chip sits for "pointer" placement: below the resting pointer, or above it when there is no room below. number

entries.title: Tooltip.aboveY
entries.text: Where the chip sits for "above" placement: over the target, or under it when there is no room above. number

entries.title: Tooltip.belowY
entries.text: Where the chip sits for "below" placement: under the target, or over it when there is no room below. number

entries.title: Tooltip.kind
entries.text: string

entries.title: Tooltip.pressPolicy
entries.text: "dismiss" | "dismissAndDeliver" | "block" | "ignore"

entries.title: Tooltip.scrollPolicy
entries.text: "block" | "allow" | "dismiss"

entries.title: Tooltip.visible
entries.text: Shown only when asked and there is text to show — an empty tip never paints a bare box. boolean

entries.title: Tooltip.width
entries.text: Sized to its text plus padding, so the box fits the words and never the other way round. Length

entries.title: Tooltip.height
entries.text: Sized to its text plus padding, one line or several. Length

entries.title: Tooltip.x
entries.text: Beside the pointer, or centred under the element, then clamped inside the app with a 4px margin — a tip near an edge slides in rather than clipping. Length

entries.title: Tooltip.y
entries.text: Below the pointer, or below or above the element as placement says, flipping to the other side when the preferred one would leave the app. Length

entries.title: Tooltip.cornerRadius
entries.text: From the theme's tooltipCornerRadius (4 by default). Radius

entries.title: Tooltip.fill
entries.text: The theme's tooltip ground when it names one, else a dark slate — a tip is the one surface that stays dark on a light theme. Fill

entries.title: Tooltip.stroke
entries.text: A hairline only when the theme names a tooltip line; flat themes get none. Stroke

entries.title: Tooltip.pointerEvents
entries.text: string

entries.title: Menu
entries.text: The record-driven menu: items are data — the class arranges; the author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS menus: { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? } key renders right-aligned — display only; the menu registers no shortcut. icon: "ClassName" names an icon class for the leading column, and the label shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary Segmented's choices use. One field covers every mark, including the ones no font gives you; a computed name needs its class kept with use [ Name ], since no static reference reaches it. enabled: false dims the row (provided("theme").disabledOpacity) and refuses pick. { divider: true } is a separator line. submenu: [ …records… ] marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow). kind: "ClassName" renders the row's content with a named author class (app.createView — keep data-only classes with use [ Name ]), passed props as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight, pick, keyboard are the menu's, always. minWidth is the room a row needs when it has no label to measure — a kind: row's own content. The panel is at least this wide; a longer label elsewhere still wins. Only a custom row needs it. Declared once, opened by many: rows carry onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }; the menu's items constraint derives from opener — per-row variation with zero per-row instances, live while open. openAt point-positions (the context-menu rule); openFor drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both place it in the overlay layer of its context — above everything opened before it — and clamp it inside the app. A menu is a Floating (floating.declare). Dismissal: a press outside closes the whole chain and is swallowed, the Mac rule (a submenu lets a press on its parent menu through); Escape closes the chain; pick closes after delivery. App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "", edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }), ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: Menu.asList
entries.text: A list of choices rather than commands: each row is an option, not a menuItem, selected when its record says selected: true. A Combobox makes its list this way, with the listbox role given at creation (createView("Menu", { accessibilityRole: "listbox", asList: true })). boolean

entries.title: Menu.widestLabel
entries.text: The widest row label, measured — the content the panel's width is built from. number

entries.title: Menu.widestKey
entries.text: The widest key equivalent, measured; zero when no row carries one, which is what decides whether the key column exists. number

entries.title: Menu.hasSubs
entries.text: Whether any row opens a submenu — a cascade arrow needs its own trailing room. boolean

entries.title: Menu.widestCustom
entries.text: The widest minWidth any row asks for. A kind: row renders its own content and has no label to measure, so it states the room it needs in its record and the panel is at least that wide; a longer label elsewhere still wins. number

entries.title: Menu.minWidth
entries.text: The narrowest a menu gets, whatever its rows measure — a two-item menu of short words still reads as a menu. number

entries.title: Menu.items
entries.text: The rows, as records — never children. A menu arranges its own rows, so handing it views is not merely discouraged, there is nowhere to put them. The record is { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, selected?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? } (selected is read only in a list of choices: see asList); a plain array is fine (no Dataset required). Because it is an ordinary attribute it can be a constraint — derive it from opener and one menu serves every row of a table , live while it is open. MenuItemRecord[]?

entries.title: Menu.hasIcons
entries.text: Whether any row carries an icon — which is what decides the icon gutter exists at all. A menu with no icons has no gutter, and the text edge moves accordingly. boolean

entries.title: Menu.hasChecks
entries.text: Whether any row can be checked — a record carrying checked, true or false — which is what decides the check column exists, exactly as AppKit reserves its state column for any item with a state image to draw. A menu of plain commands leads its text 17 in; one with a checkable row, 24. boolean

entries.title: Menu.checkW
entries.text: What the check column adds to the leading air when it exists (7 — the Mac's 25.5 vs 17.5, measured), else 0: the amount every column to its right shifts by. number

entries.title: Menu.textEdge
entries.text: The x every row's label starts at — one line for the whole menu, icons or not, and what a kind row must align its own content to. number

entries.title: Menu.isRoot
entries.text: False on a cascade child. The root owns the backdrop, the deferred delivery, and the Escape-closes-everything behaviour; a submenu delegates all three upward. boolean

entries.title: Menu.rootMenu
entries.text: The root of this menu's cascade chain — null on the root itself. Menu?

entries.title: Menu.child
entries.text: The one lazily-created submenu instance, reused across every row that cascades. A Menu cannot declare a Menu child (it would recurse), so the cascade is built by name at first use. Menu?

entries.title: Menu.activeRow
entries.text: The row the keyboard rover currently highlights, or null when the pointer is driving. Read-only in practice. View?

entries.title: Menu.typeahead
entries.text: Whether typing a letter moves the keyboard highlight to a row — true by default, as in every desktop menu: type "ex" to land on Export. The highlight only moves; Return picks. A Combobox turns it off on its list, whose letters belong to its text field. boolean

entries.title: Menu.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Menu.takesFocus
entries.text: True: an open menu holds the focus, so a screen reader follows it, and hands it back to what had it when the menu closes. A Combobox turns it off for its list, whose field keeps the focus. boolean

entries.title: Menu.accessibilityActiveItem
entries.text: The highlighted row's item: a screen reader hears each row as the arrows reach it. View

entries.title: Menu.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The opener's name, so a menu opened from "Styling" is the "Styling" menu. string

entries.title: Menu.kind
entries.text: string

entries.title: Menu.pressPolicy
entries.text: dismiss for the root — an outside press closes the chain and goes no further; dismissAndDeliver for a submenu, so a press on its parent menu goes on to it. "dismiss" | "dismissAndDeliver" | "block" | "ignore"

entries.title: Menu.scrollPolicy
entries.text: "block" | "allow" | "dismiss"

entries.title: Menu.visible
entries.text: Derived from shown, the menu's own open fact. Visibility is never set from outside — openAt and openFor set the fact, and dismissal clears it. boolean

entries.title: Menu.height
entries.text: As tall as its panel, which is as tall as its rows — capped just inside the app's height, past which the panel scrolls its rows and the rover keeps the landing row in view. Length

entries.title: Menu.width
entries.text: Follows the rows: the text edge, the widest label, then the key column or the trailing air — the metrics of a real macOS menu, measured (the longest label trails the edge by 18; a key column sits 26 clear of the longest label and ends 16 from the edge; menu bar menus and popups measure the same). A use site's own width overrides; minWidth floors it. Length

entries.title: Menu.focusFirst
entries.text: Holds the focus on the menu itself, never on a view inside it: the menu names the row the keys are on. focusFirst()

entries.title: Menu.picked
entries.text: The delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked row's id, and the id is the whole message. Called after the menu has left the screen, so a slow action can never freeze an open menu. picked(id)

entries.title: Menu.expectedHeight
entries.text: The panel's height before it has been laid out, measured when it exists and estimated from the record count when it does not. The flip-above decision cannot wait for a settle, which is why this exists. expectedHeight()

entries.title: Menu.openAt
entries.text: Opens the menu at the pointer, given the serving view and the pointer event — the context-menu rule. Clamped inside the app like any placement. ContextMenu wraps this as open. openAt(v, e)

entries.title: Menu.openFor
entries.text: Opens the menu anchored below a control, flipping above it when there is not room below and more room above — the native select discipline. The attached-menu rule; what Control.menu uses. openFor(v)

entries.title: Menu.place
entries.text: Positions the panel at a point in the frame of the layer it paints in, moved as little as it must be to stay on the App — a menu opened in a window may hang past the window's edge, not off the App. The place is taken at open: menu chrome does not move while a menu is up. place(x, y)

entries.title: Menu.close
entries.text: Takes the menu down, closes any cascade under it, and releases the keyboard claim. An override calls super.close(). close()

entries.title: Menu.escape
entries.text: Esc closes the whole chain. escape()

entries.title: Menu.pick
entries.text: Delivers a row: dismisses first, then delivers, one painted frame later — the native menu contract, and the reason a long-running action cannot leave a menu stranded on screen. A submenu routes to the root so the whole chain closes as one. pick(id)

entries.title: Menu.openSub
entries.text: Opens a row's submenu, creating the shared child menu on first use and placing it alongside the row. openSub(row, subItems)

entries.title: Menu.closeSub
entries.text: Closes the cascade under this menu, if any. closeSub()

entries.title: Menu.rootClose
entries.text: Closes the entire chain from wherever it is called — what Escape and an outside press both do. rootClose()

entries.title: Menu.step
entries.text: Moves the keyboard rover by ±1 over the pickable rows, skipping dividers, disabled rows and custom-content rows, and scrolls the landing row into view. step(d)

entries.title: Menu.typeTo
entries.text: Moves the highlight to the first enabled row whose label starts with what has been typed: the prefix grows while typing continues and starts over after a pause, and the same letter again goes on to the next row that starts with it. typeTo(ch)

entries.title: Menu.pickActive
entries.text: Picks the roved row — Enter's action. On a row with a submenu it enters the cascade instead. pickActive()

entries.title: Menu.enterSub
entries.text: Enters the roved row's submenu and puts the rover on its first row — ArrowRight's action. enterSub()

entries.title: Menu.sideways
entries.text: Where Right and Left go past the menu's own levels: Right on a row with no submenu, Left in the top menu. Nothing by default; a MenuBar answers it by opening the menu beside this one, as every desktop menu bar does. sideways(d)

entries.title: Menu.keyDown
entries.text: Takes nothing itself: a menu's keys are its rover's, which hears them however the focus lies. Declared so that a menu holding the focus inside a group (a menu bar's) is not walked by the group's arrows. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: Menu.outsidePress
entries.text: A press outside closed it: the root closes the whole chain; a submenu closes itself and lets the press go on to its parent menu. onOutsidePress()

entries.title: MenuBar
entries.text: The record-driven menu bar: whole menus are data — menus = { [ ({ id, label, bold?, items: [ …menu records… ] }), … ] } — and the class arranges. One internal Menu serves every title; its items constraint derives from the open title's record, so item state (enabled, checked, labels) stays live while the menu is up. An item's key: is a keyboard shortcut for the whole program (Shortcuts): the menu bar is the program's shortcut table, and nothing is declared twice. Tracking is the classic desktop behavior: titles do not highlight on mere hover; a click opens (and highlights) a title; while any menu is open, moving across another title switches to it; clicking the open title closes. Delivery is the one seam: picked(id) — override at the use site. A dropped menu paints over the bar's later siblings: the bar raises itself when a menu opens (stacking is source order, and raise() is the runtime verb for it). A bar nested inside a container that sits under other content wants that container declared last, or a menu hosted at the app layer as Combobox does. App [ width = 380, height = 190, chose: string = "", bar: MenuBar [ x = 12, y = 8, menus = { [ ({ id: "file", label: "File", items: [ ({ id: "new", label: "New", key: "⌘N" }), ({ id: "open", label: "Open…" }) ] }), ({ id: "edit", label: "Edit", items: [ ({ id: "undo", label: "Undo" }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut" }) ] }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: MenuBar.menus
entries.text: The whole bar as data: [ { id, label, bold?, kind?, items: [ …menu records… ] } ], where items is exactly Menu's record shape. One internal Menu serves every title , deriving its rows from the open one — so item state stays live while a menu is up, and there is nothing to keep in step. An item's key: ("⌘S") is its keyboard shortcut, live for the whole program while the bar shows it, and arrives at picked() like a click. MenuBarMenuRecord[]?

entries.title: MenuBar.ink
entries.text: Overrides the titles' colour, for a bar drawn straight over a wallpaper where the platform text turns light. null uses the theme's text colour. The dropdown menus stay themed either way — this is the bar's own ink, not the menu's. Color

entries.title: MenuBar.openId
entries.text: Which title's menu is open, by id — "" when none is. string

entries.title: MenuBar.shown
entries.text: Whether any menu in the bar is currently open. boolean

entries.title: MenuBar.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: MenuBar.height
entries.text: From the theme's menuBarHeight (25 by default); the titles' size is menuBarFontSize (14) and their highlight's corners menuBarTitleCornerRadius (6). Length

entries.title: MenuBar.width
entries.text: Content-sized to its row of titles, so it sits in a chrome bar without a stated width. Length

entries.title: MenuBar.focusScope
entries.text: stop: the bar is one Tab stop. Tab lands on the title last used (the first, at first); Left and Right move among the titles; Enter, Space or Down opens the focused title's menu. none | stop | capture | region | modal

entries.title: MenuBar.picked
entries.text: The delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked item's id from any menu in the bar; the id is the whole message. picked(id)

entries.title: MenuBar.openMenu
entries.text: Opens a title's menu and keeps the bar itself above the menu's backdrop, which is what lets tracking continue while a menu is up. openMenu(t)

entries.title: MenuBar.trackMenu
entries.text: Switches to another title while a menu is already open — bar tracking: titles do not highlight on mere hover, but once a menu is open, crossing another title opens that one. trackMenu(t)

entries.title: MenuBar.stepMenu
entries.text: Moves to the adjacent title's menu — Left/Right while a menu is open, yielding to the open menu when a submenu is up or the rover sits on one. stepMenu(d)

entries.title: Dialog
entries.text: A modal over its context: everything behind it is held back — presses aimed past it go nowhere and do not close it — and Tab stays inside it. It closes by its buttons, or Esc. Its content is yours (its children), and an alert is the most common use, so it carries the alert verbs too: a title, a message, and buttons as records (the records door): { id, label, default?, cancel? }, rendered as themed library Buttons in the platform arrangement. Open it with a verb — show() for a dialog of your own content, ask, notice, error or open for an alert. Focus is saved on open and restored on close, one turn late, deliberately: an immediate restore would hand the in-flight keystroke back to the opener. It fades in and out. Keyboard: Return picks the default button — unless the focused view takes Return itself: a focused button or control presses itself (Return on Cancel is Cancel), and a multi-line field types a line break. Escape picks the cancel record when one exists, else just closes. Every control inside keeps its own keys (Space, the arrows). The idioms — one verb each, an optional callback receiving the picked id (the picked(id) override remains the declarative seam): dlg.notice("Saved", "Your changes were saved.") dlg.ask("Save changes?", "Unsaved changes will be lost.", (id) => …) dlg.error("Could not connect", "The server refused the connection.") ask is Cancel / No / Yes-default; error renders the title in the theme's error. Platform structure is data: dialogWidth, dialogButtonLayout = "end" (a right-aligned row — San Francisco, Material) "stack" (the stacked alert — full-width buttons stacked, default on top) "fill" (WinUI ContentDialog — equal-width buttons filling the row), dialogTextAlign = "left" "center" (the Cupertino centered title), dialogTitleFontSize / dialogBodyFontSize. Plus scrimFill + scrimOpacity (Cupertino barely dims — alerts separate by shadow; Material's scrim is 32%; Fluent's smoke 30%), the menuShadow family, error. Declare one and call it. A Dialog is not a view you show and hide around your content — it is a standing member you open with a verb, so the same instance serves every prompt in the program. App [ width = 520, height = 260, said: string = "", dlg: Dialog [ ], Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Delete…", onClick() { app.dlg.ask("Delete this file?", "This cannot be undone.", (id) => { app.said = id }) } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.said == "" ? "—" : "you chose: " + app.said } ] ] A dialog of your own: App [ width = 520, height = 300, rename: Dialog [ title = "Rename", buttons = { [ { id: "cancel", label: "Cancel", cancel: true }, { id: "ok", label: "Rename", default: true } ] }, TextInput [ width = 100%, accessibilityLabel = "New name" ] ], Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Rename…", onClick() { app.rename.show() } ] ]

entries.title: Dialog.presentation
entries.text: "center" (the default): a panel centered over its context. "full": the whole context, for a viewer or a lightbox — your content edge to edge, no title or buttons unless you set them. "center" | "full"

entries.title: Dialog.title
entries.text: The heading. Set by the verbs; read it if you are restyling. string

entries.title: Dialog.message
entries.text: The body text under the title. "" hides the line entirely rather than leaving a gap. string

entries.title: Dialog.tone
entries.text: "error" tints the title with the theme's error colour; "" is the ordinary tone. string

entries.title: Dialog.buttons
entries.text: The button records currently rendered, in authored order. The "stack" arrangement reorders them for display — default on top, cancel at the bottom — without touching this. DialogButtonRecord[]?

entries.title: Dialog.hostW
entries.text: The width of the layer it paints in: its window's, or the browser window's — not the App's, which on a page that scrolls is as tall as the page. number

entries.title: Dialog.hostH
entries.text: The height of the layer it paints in: its window's, or the browser window's. number

entries.title: Dialog.arrangement
entries.text: How the buttons lay out, elected by provided("theme").dialogButtonLayout: "end" (a right-aligned row), "stack" (full-width buttons stacked, Cupertino-style, default on top), or "fill" (equal-width buttons filling the row). Platform structure is data, not a fork. string

entries.title: Dialog.centered
entries.text: Whether the title and message are centre-aligned, elected by provided("theme").dialogTextAlign. boolean

entries.title: Dialog.kind
entries.text: string

entries.title: Dialog.pressPolicy
entries.text: "dismiss" | "dismissAndDeliver" | "block" | "ignore"

entries.title: Dialog.scrollPolicy
entries.text: "block" | "allow" | "dismiss"

entries.title: Dialog.takesFocus
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: Dialog.focusScope
entries.text: none | stop | capture | region | modal

entries.title: Dialog.defaultPlacement
entries.text: slot

entries.title: Dialog.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Dialog.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The title, so a screen reader names the dialog as it opens. string

entries.title: Dialog.accessibilityHint
entries.text: The message: a screen reader reads it after the title as the dialog opens, so "Delete this file?" is followed by "This cannot be undone." string

entries.title: Dialog.width
entries.text: The theme's dialogWidth (420), inside its context; the whole width full-screen. Length

entries.title: Dialog.height
entries.text: Its column's height; the whole height full-screen. Length

entries.title: Dialog.x
entries.text: Centered in its context. Length

entries.title: Dialog.y
entries.text: A third of the way down its context; the top, full-screen. Length

entries.title: Dialog.opacity
entries.text: Its open blend — it fades in and out. number

entries.title: Dialog.scale
entries.text: It settles from slightly small as it opens — at its program's scale where it opens in a host's layer. number

entries.title: Dialog.rotation
entries.text: Its program's turn where it opens in a host's layer; none in the full-screen presentation. number

entries.title: Dialog.pivotX
entries.text: It settles about its middle. number

entries.title: Dialog.pivotY
entries.text: It settles about its middle. number

entries.title: Dialog.picked
entries.text: The declarative delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked button's id. Fires after the dialog has left the screen, and in addition to any callback passed to the verb, so you may use either or both. picked(id)

entries.title: Dialog.open
entries.text: The general form the three idioms are built on: title, message, your own button records, a tone ("error" or ""), and an optional callback. Reach for it when the three idioms do not spell your choices — button records are { id, label, default?, cancel? } , and the two flags are what Return and Escape key off. open(t, m, btns, tone_, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.notice
entries.text: A single-OK acknowledgement. Delivers "ok". notice(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.error
entries.text: A single-OK acknowledgement with the title in the theme's error colour. Delivers "ok". error(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.ask
entries.text: The three-way prompt: Cancel / No / Yes, with Yes as the default. Delivers "cancel", "no" or "yes". ask(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.pick
entries.text: Delivers a button by id: dismisses first, then delivers, one painted frame later — the same contract as Menu.pick, so a slow action cannot freeze the dialog on screen. Guarded against double activation, so a focused default button answering Space and Return is harmless. pick(id)

entries.title: Dialog.focusFirst
entries.text: On opening, focus goes to your content's first control when it has one, else to the default button. focusFirst()

entries.title: Dialog.focusDefault
entries.text: Puts keyboard focus on the default button when the dialog opens — or the last button when no record is marked default. focusDefault()

entries.title: Dialog.pickDefault
entries.text: Picks whichever button record carries default: true — Return's action, the Cupertino rule. pickDefault()

entries.title: Dialog.pickCancel
entries.text: Picks the cancel: true record when there is one, else just closes — Escape's action. A dialog with no cancel record still dismisses on Escape, it simply delivers nothing. pickCancel()

entries.title: Dialog.escape
entries.text: Esc picks the cancel button (pickCancel). escape()

entries.title: Dialog.returnTaken
entries.text: Whether the focused view takes Return itself — a control inside the dialog (it presses itself) or a multi-line field (a line break) — so Return does not also pick the default. returnTaken()

entries.title: AppIsland
entries.text: AppIsland embeds a live Declare application: give it a program and it mounts that program as its own child app — its own reactive graph, input router, and stage — sized to this view's box. There is no coordinate sync: the tenant fills the box, so your width/height constraints size it like any view. It composes DOMIsland (the sanctioned foreign-content leaf) and builds the host's mount key from structured inputs, so callers never hand-splice the run:… wire. The page host (browser/host-client.js) sees the key on the box, resolves the program on its boot ladder — prewarm → cache → in-browser compile, identical on the dev server and a static host — and renders the child. childName (inherited from DOMIsland) is the reverse channel: the running child's appName reflected back up, so a host can title itself by what it shows. The boundary What crosses an island says its direction (the guide's Embedding chapter). DOWN: list names in provides = ["dark", "base"], and the tenant reads each with hostProvided("dark", false) — a value resolves at the island as provided() does, the island's own attribute first, then its ancestors' provisions. UP: the tenant lists names in its App's exposes = ["docH"], and the host reads them with island.exposed("docH", 0). Both are reactive, per settle, with no handshake to write. post(topic, payload) / onPost(m: IslandMessage) carry the verbs. For a host that runs a program the person browses — a documentation reader in a window — two more cross on their own, with nothing named on either side. Where it is : location is the tenant's location, both ways — set it to start the program at a place or send it to one, and read it to follow where the program has gone; departedPlace and place carry where the person had scrolled, for back and forward. Where it wants to go: the program's navigate(to) and openWindow(to) come to the island as onNavigate(n: IslandNavigation) when the island declares it, so the host decides what a link leading out of it means — a desktop opens a window. Without it, the page navigates. A host that only shows a program uses none of this. Its overlays. The program's menus, popovers and dialogs open in the nearest overlay layer up the chain — the Window the island sits in, or any view above it that provides overlays, in this program or a host further up — so they hang past the island's edge and turn and scale with the program as it is shown. With no such layer above, they stay inside the box. containOverlays = true keeps them inside the box always. The window frame, activation, and titling belong to the caller — a desktop window adds an onPointerDown that raises itself and reads childName for its title; the homepage and the viewer just size the box. This primitive is only the embedding. The keyboard goes where focus is. The program inside hears keys while focus is on the island or on one of its own views, and the host hears none then. Make the island focusable and focus it on a press (onPointerDown() { Focus.focus(this) }) to hand the program the keyboard; focusing an island whose program already holds focus leaves that focus where it is.

entries.title: AppIsland.program
entries.text: What to run: the program's path without its .declare, relative to the program that names it like any address in a program ("player" is player.declare beside it, and "../calendar/calendar" reaches the real app — no copy of the source, ever), or the reserved "raw" live-edit channel, where the running program is the host app's liveSource and recompiles as it changes. "" detaches the island and nothing mounts, which is how a closed panel stops paying for its tenant — and what bounds the recursion when a program embeds a view of itself. string

entries.title: AppIsland.containOverlays
entries.text: Keeps the program's overlays — its menus, popovers, dialogs — inside the island's box, where they would otherwise open in the nearest overlay layer above it (its window's) and hang past the box. For a host that shows programs as self-contained tiles. false by default. The tenant runs in the host page's runtime, as its own app. Where its compiled program comes from is the host's arrangement: on the distro, a prewarmed artifact or a compile; in a production build, an artifact declarec made ahead of time — for every island whose program is a literal, and for every name the program declares in its ship [ islands = [ "name", … ] ] when the value is computed. A build carries no compiler unless the program declares ship [ compiler = true ], so an island naming a program the build did not produce reports that, with the fix, rather than mounting nothing. boolean

entries.title: AppIsland.location
entries.text: Where the program is: its own location, carried both ways. Set it before the program mounts and the program starts there, as a page starts at its URL's fragment; set it later and the program follows it (its onFollowLink applies). The program's own navigation is reflected back here, so a host can show where it is, keep it, or walk it back — Back and Forward across an island are the host's to give. Assign it from a handler or onInit: a constraint here would own a value the program also writes. string

entries.title: AppIsland.place
entries.text: Set it, together with location, to return the program to a place it left: once the move has settled and the content can hold it, each pane and the island's box scroll back to where departedPlace said they were. The user's first scroll cancels a landing still in progress. Read back, it is "" again once taken. string

entries.title: AppIsland.departedPlace
entries.text: Where in the program the person was when it last left a location — how far its scrolling panes, and the island's own box, were scrolled — as an opaque value. A host that keeps a history of where the program has been (back and forward on a window) stores it with the location being left, and hands it back as place. Written by the platform; nothing to set. string

entries.title: AppIsland.slot
entries.text: The host's slot marker, derived from program — run:<program> — which is what the island host wires. Nothing to set by hand. string

entries.title: SimpleLayout
entries.text: The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along axis, in child order, spacing apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row with the ordinary y = center. Invisible children are skipped and their space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the place it would occupy, so re-showing it needs no special case. A child with flexes = true takes an equal share of the run's slack along the axis: a list that fills the room between a header and a footer, or an empty Spacer (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on each side centers the run). Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index. Padding is the view's (View.padding), and this stack obeys it without knowing it exists: it arranges inside the room the view gives it, so a run placed at 0 starts at the content origin, the cross-axis band align works in is the room between the insets, and a view that sizes itself from the stack grows by both. The inset reaches every child, on both axes, align = none included — a child placing its own x = 0 sits on the content edge, not the view's, because the content box is the parent's and not this arrangement's. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ], View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ], View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ] ]

entries.title: SimpleLayout.axis
entries.text: Which way children stack: y (the default) or x. A bare literal, not a string — axis = x, and note that x here is the axis token, not the position attribute. Axis

entries.title: SimpleLayout.spacing
entries.text: The gap between adjacent children. Negative overlaps them, which is how a stack of cards or avatars is built. number

entries.title: SimpleLayout.align
entries.text: The cross axis — y on a row, x on a stack. none (the default) leaves it to the children, who place themselves with the ordinary y = center. start center end aligns every child within the band: the view's own cross content extent — so a column width = 260 centres a width = { parent.width - 32 } child at 16, with the slack split evenly — falling back to the line, the tallest (widest) laid child's extent, on a view that derives its own cross size from these very children (reading an extent this arrangement feeds would be a cycle, and on such a view the line is that extent). A child wider than the band keeps the line, so it never hangs out both sides. baseline — a row only — sits every child on one baseline: a Text reports its own, and a composite declares which part carries it (baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }); a laid child that declares none is refused by name, at the child, and the checker says so before anything runs. A flexing child is aligned like any other (a Spacer declares a baseline of 0, so a baseline row takes it as it is). A row of figures and words that must wrap when the view is narrow — "4 sessions · 3h 40m" on a phone — is a WrappingLayout [ align = baseline ], which keeps each line on its own baseline. A bare literal. CrossAlign

entries.title: SimpleLayout.place
entries.text: The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order. Every size stays the children's own, and so does the cross axis unless align says otherwise — then the boxes carry that attribute too, and own it. Override it in a subclass for custom geometry; a Layout's place() may aggregate over children, which is the one place that is allowed. place()

entries.title: WrappingLayout
entries.text: A horizontal flow that wraps: children run left to right spacing apart, and when the next one would overflow the view's width it drops to a new row, rowSpacing down. With room for one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it stacks — cards that reflow on a phone with no media query. It owns both axes of each child (a flow is 2-D); sizes stay the children's own. justify sets each finished row along the flow — start, center, end, or fill, which spreads a row's slack into its gaps the way justified text does; indent and hangingIndent inset the first row and every row after it, the two shapes a paragraph takes. A child with flexes = true takes the rest of the row it lands on: it wraps by its content width, then grows into what the row has left, or gives up what the row is short — a strip of filters that fills the room its row's other children leave, and scrolls when that is too little. Division of labor: this is the tool for uniform, replicated collections that reflow by fitting. Managing named regions per width tier is ResponsiveLayout's. Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place(). Padding is the view's (View.padding), and a flow answers to it on both axes: rows wrap at the content width — the room between the left and right insets, never the view's own width — and a view that sizes itself from the flow grows by the vertical pair, so no row runs under the inset. box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, rowSpacing = 8 ], View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ], View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ], View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ], View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ] ]

entries.title: WrappingLayout.spacing
entries.text: The horizontal gap between children in a row. number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.rowSpacing
entries.text: The vertical gap between rows. The two gaps are independent: a uniform grid writes the same number for both, and a negative rowSpacing pulls rows into each other, which is what a large display face wants when it wraps — the row height a big face reports is looser than the line wants to sit. number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.justify
entries.text: How a finished row sits along the flow: start (the default, left), center, end (right), or fill — the row's slack is spread evenly into the gaps between its children, so every full row ends flush at the right edge, as justified text does. As in text, the last row is left at start under fill (a ragged last line), and a row of one child has no gap to widen and stays put. A bare literal. Justify

entries.title: WrappingLayout.align
entries.text: Where each child sits within its row: start (the default — the row's top), center, end, or baseline, which sits every child in the row on one baseline — a Text reports its own, a composite declares which part carries it (baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }), and a child that declares none is refused by name and placed at the row's top. A row's height grows to hold the baseline-shifted children. When the flow never wrapped — one row, which is the whole content — center and end align it in the view's own height instead, so a single row in a height = 90 bar really sits in the middle of it; a view that derives its height from this flow keeps the row as the band. A bare literal. CrossAlign

entries.title: WrappingLayout.indent
entries.text: The first row's inset from the left, in pixels — a paragraph's first-line indent. The first row's usable width shrinks by it; later rows are unaffected (see hangingIndent). number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.hangingIndent
entries.text: The inset of every row after the first — a hanging indent, the shape of a bibliography entry or a wrapped signature whose continuation lines step in under the name. The two compose: indent sets where the first row starts, hangingIndent where the rest do. number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.columns
entries.text: A grid of equal cells (default 0, off): every row holds this many children, each in a cell of the row's room shared out — the content width less spacing between them, and the row's indent. A child with flexes = true takes its cell's width; any other keeps its own and sits at its cell's left. With columns = { narrow ? 5 : 10 }, ten options are one row at a desk and two of five on a phone, every cell the same width. scale: View [ width = 100%, layout: WrappingLayout [ columns = { app.width < 600 ? 5 : 10 }, spacing = 6, rowSpacing = 6 ], View [ datapath = { app.levels[] }, flexes = true, height = 44, cornerRadius = 6, fill = gainsboro ] ] number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.place
entries.text: Runs the flow, wrapping when the next child would overflow the view's width. It owns both axes of each child — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than looping forever. Each finished row starts at its indent, is justified along the flow, and has its children aligned across it, in one pass over the row. place()

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout
entries.text: A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows. ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of plans — each one says "from this width up, arrange the children like this" — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes. Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate wiring. bar: View [ layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [ { from: 900, flow: "row", share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } }, { from: 600, flow: "row", share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } }, { from: 0, flow: "stack" }, ] } ], logo: Logo [ ], nav: Nav [ ], actions: Actions [ ], ] Each entry's from means use this plan when the view is at least this wide — the entry with the largest from that fits wins, wherever it sits in the list, and an entry with from: 0 is the fallback for anything narrower. flow is the arrangement: "row" places children left to right; "stack" places them top to bottom. share divides width in either flow — in a row it apportions the run; in a stack it sets how wide each band is, as a plain percentage of the view. The names are the view's own child names, checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is a loud error). logo: 15 gives logo 15% of it; a share of 0 drops that child while the plan is active — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is just a number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the view widens. gap sets the space between children (an entry may carry its own gap to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children keep their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as always. So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split 15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room; below 600, everything stacks. A plan need not name every child, and 20% means 20% of what is left. A child the plan leaves out keeps its natural width and the flow just places it — and the run a row's shares divide is what remains after the gaps and after those naturals . So a fixed-width logo beside two proportional regions composes without the author computing a percentage for the logo: layout: ResponsiveLayout [ gap = 10, plan = { [ { from: 0, flow: "row", share: { nav: 60, actions: 40 } }, ] } ], logo: View [ width = 200 ], // not named: keeps its 200 nav: Nav [ ], // 60% of what is left actions: Actions [ ], // 40% of what is left In an 880-wide bar that is 200 for the logo and 396 / 264 for the two regions — the row fills, exactly. Change the logo's width and the regions answer; they were never told about it. share: { logo: "auto" } says that out loud. The word means precisely what leaving the child out means — keep its natural size, divide the rest — so it buys no new geometry, only legibility: the plan reads as a complete statement of the row, and a name in a plan is checked against the tree, where an omission is mentioned nowhere. It is not share: 0, which is the opposite: 0 drops the child and reclaims its space, "auto" keeps the child at the size it chose for itself. In a stack "auto" is accepted and changes nothing — the flow axis there is height, which a share never touches. Two shares are refused, where the plan is read — both of them mistakes with no arrangement they could mean. A row's shares divide one run, so a row whose shares add to more than 100 is an error naming the plan and the total, rather than a row that runs its children off the end. And a share that is neither a number from 0 to 100 nor the word "auto" is an error naming the child, rather than a NaN width on it and a NaN position on its neighbours. The two things authors miss. share is not row-only: a "stack" entry may carry shares too, and they set each band's width — the narrow plan above could say { from: 0, flow: "stack", share: { logo: 100, nav: 100 } } to make both bands full-bleed. (A stack's shares are independent percentages of the view, not slices of one run, which is why two hundreds are fine there and a row's total is held to 100.) And share: 0 is the whole of "hide it when it's tight": a child dropped this way leaves the flow entirely and its space is reclaimed, so there is no reason to branch a tree on a width (narrow ? … : …) — appearing and disappearing is one number in one plan, and the plan is the only place the breakpoint is written down. Slack and alignment. When a row's children keep natural widths, the run may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a knob: a Spacer [ ] child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it. Shares are cut from what the naturals leave, so shares adding to 100 leave no slack at all and a Spacer beside them collapses — shares fill; naturals align. Across the flow, the layout places every child — y in a row, x in a stack, in every plan. Where each one sits there is the layout's align: start unless it says otherwise, and a plan entry may say otherwise for its own tier. A plan entry's offset shifts one named child from where align put it — a nudge that belongs to that arrangement, so it goes away with the tier, which is exactly when it stops meaning anything: actions: View [ width = 100%, layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [ { from: 420, flow: "row", gap: 18, align: "center", offset: { source: 1 } }, { from: 0, flow: "stack", gap: 14 }, ] } ], run: Button [ width = 240, height = 46 ], // the row centres the pair on it source: Text [ text = "View & edit source →" ], ] So a child under a ResponsiveLayout declares neither x nor y — the checker says so at the line, and says which of these to use instead. A child that needs a finer arrangement of its own contents is the next case down: give it a layout of its own. Nesting — who decides what. A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically. Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.) This is the answer to most things a plan cannot say by itself, and it wants no class: an ordinary inline child carries its own layout: like any other view. A class nested this way answers to its allocation, not the window — the same child reads correctly in a sidebar, a dialog, or a full-bleed row, and picks its own flow in each. One thing to get right: the parent's plan must actually give the child a width in every tier. A tier that allocates it nothing leaves it at its content width, and a child sized by its content is measuring what it is trying to arrange — so name it in the stack tier's shares (share: { acts: 100 }) or give it width = 100%. Division of labor. ResponsiveLayout manages named regions. A collection of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool: WrappingLayout (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width constraint on the card. Padding, and what from then means. The inset is the view's (View.padding), and a plan is selected against the content width, with the shares dividing it — so a padded bar's tiers answer to the room its children actually get, and from: 600 means 600 of usable room, not 600 of outer width. When the rules aren't enough. A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap. Reach for nesting first, and most of the time last: give the part that needs its own mind a layout: of its own and let it arrange itself inside the room this plan hands it (above). A child that decides for itself is almost always the answer to "this plan cannot say what I need", and it composes — the same child then reads correctly wherever it is put. Past that: whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a State applied on a width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding place() — the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.plan
entries.text: The storyboard: a list of { from, flow, share?, gap?, align?, offset? } entries. from means "use this plan when the view is at least this wide" — the largest from that fits wins, wherever it sits in the list, and from: 0 is the fallback. flow is "row" or "stack". share divides width in either flow — not row-only: a "stack" entry may carry shares, and they set each band's width. It names the children by their own child names , checked when the layout first arranges — a name with no child is a loud error. A share of 0 drops that child while the plan is active — out of the flow, its space reclaimed — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is one number rather than a narrow ? … : … branch, and they return by themselves when the view widens. A child a plan does not name keeps its natural width, and a row's shares divide what is left after it — the gaps and the naturals both come out before the percentages are cut, so 60 means 60% of the remainder and a fixed-width logo composes beside two proportional regions with no arithmetic by hand. "auto" is the word for that said out loud (share: { logo: "auto", nav: 60, actions: 40 }): identical geometry to leaving the child out, and the opposite of 0 — 0 drops the child, "auto" keeps it at the size it chose for itself. In a stack "auto" is accepted and changes nothing, since a stack's shares are widths and its flow axis is height. align and offset are per tier. A plan entry's align — a string, "start", "center", "end" or "baseline" — overrides the layout's own for that tier, as its gap does. Its offset names children the way share does and shifts each one across the flow — down in a row, right in a stack — by a signed number of pixels from where align placed it. A name with no child, or an offset that is not a number, is an error naming it. Two values are refused where the plan is read. A row whose shares add to more than 100 is an error naming the plan and the total — a row's shares divide one run and cannot claim more of it than there is. (A stack's do not compete: each is an independent percent of the view, so { logo: 100, nav: 100 } is the full-bleed idiom, not an overflow — but a single share above 100 is refused in either flow.) And a share that is neither a number from 0 to 100 nor "auto" is an error naming the child, instead of a NaN width. array

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.gap
entries.text: The default space between children, overridable per plan entry. number

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.align
entries.text: Where children sit across the flow — y in a row, x in a stack: start (the default), center, end, or baseline. A bare literal here; a plan entry overrides it with a string (align: "center"). center and end work in the band: the view's own cross content extent, or the tallest (widest) laid child on a view that sizes itself from these very children — the same band as SimpleLayout's align. baseline sits every child of a row on one text line, each child declaring its own (a Text does; a composite says which part carries it), and is refused on a stack tier, which has no line. There is no none: this layout places the cross axis in every tier, so it always says where. CrossAlign

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.place
entries.text: Selects the active plan from the view's own width — never the window's — and arranges accordingly: both axes of every child, along the flow by the plan and across it by align and offset. That is what makes nesting work: the parent's plan decides how much room a child gets, and the child's own plan answers to the room it got, automatically. A plan can only name direct children; managing a grandchild is the child's plan's business. place()

entries.title: Spacer
entries.text: When a row (or stack) does not fill its container, the leftover space has to go somewhere. A Spacer says where, structurally: put one between two groups and they push apart ("logo left, actions right"); put one on each side of a run and it centers; put one first and the run right-aligns. Several spacers split the slack evenly. When there is no slack — a plan whose shares fill the width, an auto-sized container — a Spacer is simply zero and invisible in effect. It is nothing but an empty view that flexes: Spacer [ ] is View [ flexes = true ], named for what it is for. Any view can flex the same way (View.flexes); a Spacer is the one with nothing in it. It paints nothing and has no size of its own; it declares a baseline of 0, so a baseline row takes it like any other child. For a minimum height (a strut), use an empty view: View [ width = 0, height = 44 ].

entries.title: Spacer.baseline
entries.text: 0 — the top of an empty box. Declared so that a row aligned on its baselines takes a Spacer as it takes any child: it sits at the line and, having no height, moves nothing. number

entries.title: Spacer.flexes
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: Spacer.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Spacer.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Table
entries.text: The list collection, componentized: the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or written) collection, carrying the selection model so no app hand-rolls it again: Selection is the Table's value — selected (the primary item) and selection (all of them, presented order), holding items: the record for a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via input; identity by the usual ladder (a record's id by convention, else the object itself — the reconciler's own rule). The three facts: selection, the anchor (where ranges extend from), and the keyboard position active — moved by arrows, extended by shift, walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection). selects declares the mode: none single multi (default single). Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children reaching their table as parent, replicated over data or written by hand. The row template stays free of any selection wiring. Windowing composes: put virtualize on the row template and selection, ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — items are read from the data through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (rows are assumed uniform in height). Table [ width = 300, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value }, selects = "multi", input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel }, TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 30, t: TextLabel [ x = 8, text = :label ] ] ] App [ width = 320, height = 200, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "label": "Ada" }, { "id": 2, "label": "Grace" }, { "id": 3, "label": "Alan" } ] } }, t: Table [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 100, datapath = { d.value }, selects = "multi", TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 26, Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = :label ] ] ], Text [ x = 20, y = 140, text = { (t.selection ?? []).length + " selected" } ] ]

entries.title: Table.selected
entries.text: The primary selected item — the record most recently selected, or null. Items, not views: selection survives sorts, filters, and windowing because it was never a set of instances. object

entries.title: Table.selection
entries.text: Every selected item, in presented order — null when nothing is selected. Records for a replicated table, the row views themselves for a written one. Never assign it; deliver through input. array

entries.title: Table.active
entries.text: The item the keyboard stands on — moved by arrows, and distinct from the selection, which is what makes ⌘-walk-then-Space possible. object

entries.title: Table.selects
entries.text: The mode: "none", "single" (the default), or "multi". Multi is what enables shift-ranges, ⌘-toggles, and the ⌘-walk. string

entries.title: Table.activeIndex
entries.text: The keyboard position as a logical index. A program that moves the keyboard itself sets it together with active, the record at that position. number

entries.title: Table.activeView
entries.text: The row view at the keyboard position, reported by the row itself (in a DataGrid, the cell). Null while no row presents it. View?

entries.title: Table.focusScope
entries.text: stop: the table is one Tab stop, holding focus itself while the arrows move the active row; a row's own controls are not stops in the walk past it. Enter opens the active row (activateRequested); a program that opens a row into controls focuses the first of them, and Tab then walks that row's controls; Esc returns focus to the table. none | stop | capture | region | modal

entries.title: Table.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Table.accessibilityActiveItem
entries.text: The activeView: a screen reader hears the row the arrows land on while the table keeps the focus. View

entries.title: Table.accessibilityMultiselectable
entries.text: True when selects is "multi", so a screen reader says more than one row can be chosen. boolean

entries.title: Table.scrolls
entries.text: none | y | x | both

entries.title: Table.clip
entries.text: ClipPath

entries.title: Table.idOf
entries.text: A item's identity: its scalar id field by convention, else the object itself — the same ladder the reconciler uses, so nothing needs declaring for selection to survive a re-sort . idOf(m)

entries.title: Table.same
entries.text: Whether two items are the same one, by idOf. same(a, b)

entries.title: Table.isSelected
entries.text: Whether a item is in the selection, by identity. isSelected(m)

entries.title: Table.isActive
entries.text: Whether a item is the keyboard position, by identity. isActive(m)

entries.title: Table.selectable
entries.text: Whether an item can be selected and stood on — true for every item by default. Clicks, ranges, arrows, Home and End pass over an item it refuses, so a heading between rows is never selected. Override it to say which items are rows a person picks: selectable(m: object) -> boolean { return m.heading == null }. selectable(m)

entries.title: Table.input
entries.text: Where the selection goes. The default writes selected and selection; override it to own the value (input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel }) and every gesture — click, range, keyboard — routes through your override, because they all land here. input(sel)

entries.title: Table.clearSelection
entries.text: Delivers an empty selection through input. clearSelection()

entries.title: Table.itemAt
entries.text: The item at a logical index. itemAt(i)

entries.title: Table.itemArray
entries.text: The full item universe, read from the data through any row's cursor — never from instances. This is the windowing contract: a table over a virtualized collection can range-select rows that have never been built. itemArray()

entries.title: Table.itemCount
entries.text: How many items there are — the full logical count, not what is materialized. itemCount()

entries.title: Table.rowClick
entries.text: The click protocol: plain click selects exactly one item, ⌘/Ctrl toggles, Shift extends from the anchor. Called by a TableRow; override to change what a click means. rowClick(i, m, toggle, range)

entries.title: Table.step
entries.text: Arrow-key travel: plain moves and selects, Shift extends the range, ⌘ moves the position alone so Space can toggle it. Scrolls the destination into view. step(to, e, dir)

entries.title: Table.showRow
entries.text: Scrolls a row into view by index — using its instance when one exists, and arithmetic when it does not , so arrow travel into unmaterialized rows works and materializes on arrival. showRow(i)

entries.title: Table.deleteRequested
entries.text: Delivery seam — the app declares what deleting is. Fires on Delete or Backspace while there is a selection and the table itself holds focus, so a text field's Backspace is never mistaken for it. Does nothing by default: refusal by inertness. deleteRequested()

entries.title: Table.activateRequested
entries.text: Delivery seam — the app declares what opening is. Fires on Enter on the walked row, under the same focus condition. The list idiom's other half. activateRequested()
