entries.title: Table.keyDown
entries.text: Arrows, Home/End, Space (multi), Delete/Backspace and Enter. An override should call through or the table loses its keyboard. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: TableRow
entries.text: One row of a Table: a direct child of it, replicated over data (datapath = :rows[]) or written by hand. A row carries no selection wiring of its own — it reads whether it is selected or active from its table, and hands clicks to the table's rowClick. It is never a tab stop: the table holds focus, so the arrow keys land on the container. App [ width = 320, height = 170, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "label": "Ada" }, { "id": 2, "label": "Grace" } ] } }, t: Table [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 220, height = 60, datapath = { d.value }, TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 28, Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = { :label + (parent.selected ? " ✓" : "") } ] ] ], Text [ x = 20, y = 110, text = "Click a row: its own selected fact follows." ] ]

entries.title: TableRow.selected
entries.text: Whether this row's item is in its table's selection — derived from the table, never stored. boolean

entries.title: TableRow.active
entries.text: Whether this row is its table's keyboard position. boolean

entries.title: TableRow.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: TableRow.accessibilitySelected
entries.text: Follows selected. boolean

entries.title: TableRow.focusable
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: TableRow.width
entries.text: As wide as its table; a row never sizes itself. Length

entries.title: TableRow.fill
entries.text: Selected takes the selected tint, hovered the hover tint, otherwise none — a row is transparent so the table's own ground shows through. Fill

entries.title: TableRow.stroke
entries.text: The active row shows an accent ring only while the table's focus is visible (keyboard, not pointer) — the rule every control's focus ring follows. Stroke

entries.title: TableRow.item
entries.text: The item this row presents: its record when replicated, the row view itself when written by hand. item()

entries.title: TableRow.tableIndex
entries.text: This row's logical index in data order — its rowIndex when replicated, so it is true under windowing; -1 for a row windowing has parked, which presents no record. A method rather than an attribute because its consumers are gestures, and the written-row fallback walks children, which no constraint may do. tableIndex()

entries.title: TableRow.pointerDown
entries.text: Focuses the table, not the row — rows are never tab stops, so the arrow keys must land on the container. An override calls super.onPointerDown(), or the arrow keys have nowhere to land. onPointerDown()

entries.title: TableRow.click
entries.text: Delivers the click to the table's rowClick with the modifier state. Override rowClick on the table rather than this, unless a particular row needs to opt out. onClick()

entries.title: Combobox
entries.text: Filter-as-you-type over a collection: a text field owning a query plus a dismissable option list owning a choice — a derived selection over data. Composition, not invention: TextInput for the entry, the Menu machinery for the list (overlay, raise, light-dismiss, Escape closes — the whole dismissal discipline rides along), and the matches are a derived collection — a constraint over the items array, so the live match count is free and no rendered row is ever scanned. Combobox [ width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee", items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.assignee = v } ] Items are members (the selection model's currency): records — shown by their label (or id) — or plain strings. value holds the chosen member; input(v) is the delivery seam: the default writes value, a use-site override redirects and the attribute stays untouched. Typing filters live (case-insensitive substring); opening without typing shows the full list (the disclosure-button path). Picking echoes the label into the field and closes; editing again re-filters from the new text. Keyboard: arrows rove the list (the Menu rover), Enter picks the roved row — or, when none is roved, the first match of what was typed (the type-then-Enter path); over the whole list it keeps the choice already made; Escape closes the list (then a second Escape leaves the control — the focus-scope ascent). The list is never a tab stop of its own. The list is a collection like any other — bind 100k options and virtualize applies to it the same way (via the Menu it composes). App [ width = 320, height = 160, picked: string = "", people: array = { ["Ada Lovelace", "Grace Hopper", "Alan Turing", "Barbara Liskov"] }, Combobox [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee", items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.picked = "" + v } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.picked == "" ? "—" : app.picked } ] ]

entries.title: Combobox.items
entries.text: The options, as members: records — shown by their label, else id — or plain strings. The currency of the selection model, so whatever you put in is what comes back out of input. array

entries.title: Combobox.value
entries.text: The chosen member, not the typed text — the whole record when you supplied records. null until something is picked. Standalone the combobox owns it; constrained, override input beside it. object

entries.title: Combobox.placeholder
entries.text: The entry's placeholder text while empty. string

entries.title: Combobox.purpose
entries.text: What the choice is — country, region, name — given to the entry, so autofill and a password manager recognise the field, and a phone brings up the keyboard that suits it. Text that arrives whole and names exactly one item, as autofill's does, picks that item. InputPurpose

entries.title: Combobox.query
entries.text: What the user has typed since the last pick. Not the value — the draft that filters the list. string

entries.title: Combobox.filtering
entries.text: Whether the user has typed since the last pick. False means a bare disclosure, which shows the whole list rather than filtering against a stale query — the difference between clicking the chevron and typing. boolean

entries.title: Combobox.matches
entries.text: The filtered options, as a derived collection: a constraint over items, so the live match count is free and no rendered row is ever scanned. Case-insensitive substring against each member's label. array

entries.title: Combobox.matchCount
entries.text: How many options currently match — read it straight, rather than counting list rows, which is both wrong under virtualization and refused by the compiler. number

entries.title: Combobox.list
entries.text: The option list — a Menu created at the app layer on first open, not a child of the combobox, so it paints over everything rather than only over later siblings. All the overlay behaviour arrives with it: light dismiss, Escape, the arrow rover, the viewport flip, the long-list scroll. View?

entries.title: Combobox.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Combobox.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The caption of a Field around it, else the placeholder, unless the use site names the combobox — its name to a screen reader, carried by the field inside, which is what holds the focus. string

entries.title: Combobox.accessibilityExpanded
entries.text: Whether the list is open — what a screen reader hears as the combobox expanded or collapsed. boolean

entries.title: Combobox.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Combobox.focusable
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: Combobox.height
entries.text: From the theme's comboboxHeight (30 by default), and at least 44 on a touch-first device, a finger's target. Length

entries.title: Combobox.fieldValue
entries.text: Follows value, the chosen member: what required and validate judge (see ValueControl). any

entries.title: Combobox.labelOf
entries.text: How a member is displayed: a record's label, else its id, else the value itself. Override to display members your own way. labelOf(m)

entries.title: Combobox.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes. Receives the chosen member. The default writes value; an override redirects it and leaves the attribute untouched. input(v)

entries.title: Combobox.focusField
entries.text: focusField()

entries.title: Combobox.pickIndex
entries.text: Picks the nth current match: echoes its label into the entry, closes the list, and delivers the member through input. The index is into matches, never into items. pickIndex(i)

entries.title: Combobox.ensureList
entries.text: Creates the shared list on first use and wires its delivery back to pickIndex. ensureList()

entries.title: Combobox.syncList
entries.text: Pushes the current matches into the list — called on every keystroke. syncList()

entries.title: Combobox.closeList
entries.text: Closes the list without picking. closeList()

entries.title: Combobox.listShown
entries.text: Whether the list is currently up. listShown()

entries.title: Combobox.listRoved
entries.text: Whether the keyboard rover is sitting on a row. This is what makes Enter mean two things : pick the roved row when there is one, else take the first match of what was typed — the type-then-Enter path. With nothing typed, Enter keeps the choice already made. listRoved()

entries.title: Combobox.open
entries.text: Opens the full list unfiltered — the disclosure-button path. open()

entries.title: Combobox.toggle
entries.text: Opens the list, or closes it if it is already open. toggle()

entries.title: ContextMenu
entries.text: The right-click / long-press menu: Menu's machinery whole — overlay, raise, pointer-anchored placement with viewport clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule (an outside press closes and is swallowed), Escape closes the chain — with a gesture-opened entry. It has no overlay machinery of its own; whatever it does, Menu does. Declared once, opened by many. The serving view declares the gesture — that declaration is what routes it (the claim model: contextMenu engages the right-click/two-finger path, hold is the touch long-press gate, and each engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on the view the menu serves: rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ], … Row [ …, onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ] open(v, e) anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener (items = { … opener … } for per-row menus with zero per-row instances); picking delivers through picked(id) and closes. Everything else — items, opener, picked, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is Menu's, documented there. App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "", rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { [ ({ id: "open", label: "Open" }), ({ id: "rename", label: "Rename" }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "delete", label: "Delete" }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8, fill = darkslategray, onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, Text [ x = 12, y = center, text = "Right-click or hold me" ] ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.chose == "" ? "—" : app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: ContextMenu.open
entries.text: Opens the menu anchored at the pointer, given the serving view and the pointer event — Menu.openAt under the name the two-line wiring reads best with. The serving view declares the gesture, and that declaration is what routes it : onContextMenu engages the right-click and two-finger path, onHold the touch long-press. Neither engages anywhere a handler is not declared, so a context menu costs nothing on views that do not offer one. open(v, e)

entries.title: DataGrid
entries.text: Records as rows, one column per field you choose: headers that sort, reorder and resize by drag (touch-correct), selection and keyboard travel from Table, and a windowed collection, so ten thousand rows cost a screenful of views. A DataGrid has no children. What it shows comes from two attributes: items, the records, one row each; and columns, plain records, one column each. App [ width = 440, height = 220, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail", "state": "open" }, { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" }, { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid", "state": "open" } ] } }, DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, selects = "multi", items = { app.d.value.rows }, columns = { [ { id: "id", title: "ID", width: 50 }, { id: "title", title: "Title", width: 220 }, { id: "state", title: "State", width: 110 } ] } ] ] Drag a header sideways to reorder; drag the divider between two headers to resize; click a header to sort. Items are records, kept matched to their rows by each record's id. Taken from a Dataset, they are the dataset's own records: an edit made in a cell writes the record, and everything that reads it follows. Columns are records with an id (the field the column shows, and its name), a title, a width, and optionally a cell or edit. Being data, they can be built, stored, or chosen by the person, like any records. A cell shows its field as text, unless its column names a class: cell: "DoneCell" draws that class in every row of the column, each copy bound to its own row's record (so :done is that row's done). Cells in one column can differ by row: the class decides how to look for its record, with a State or a classFor inside it. edit: true makes a column's cells text fields that write the record as you type, with a spreadsheet's keys: Enter, F2 or a typed character starts the edit, Up and Down move it a row, Esc puts the text back. A heading row is a record with a heading field — { id: "g1", heading: "Overdue" } — drawn across the full width, with no cells, passed over by selection and the arrow keys. headingClass names a class of your own to draw it. Sorting names a derivation. A header click sets sortOn and sortDir; your app derives the sorted items from them, and the grid shows the order it is given. Order and widths are the grid's state, order and widths, delivered through arrangeInput and resizeInput, so an app can persist a person's layout.

entries.title: DataGrid.headerH
entries.text: The header row's height. number

entries.title: DataGrid.items
entries.text: The records, one row each, in the order shown. Usually a dataset's list — items = { app.tasks.value.rows } — or one derived from it (sorted, filtered, grouped). A record whose heading field is set is a heading row. array

entries.title: DataGrid.columns
entries.text: The columns, as records, in their first order: id (the field shown, and the column's name), title (the header; the id when absent), width (in pixels; 120 when absent), and optionally cell (the name of a class drawn in each of the column's cells) or edit (true for text fields). The column model follows this list: add, remove or change a record and the grid follows. array

entries.title: DataGrid.headingClass
entries.text: The name of the class that draws a heading row — "" for the grid's own, the record's heading text in the theme's muted ink. The class is placed across the row, with the heading record as its data. string

entries.title: DataGrid.order
entries.text: The presented column order, as column ids — null means the order of columns. Part of the grid's value-pattern state: delivered through arrangeInput, so an app that overrides that owns the order and can persist it. array

entries.title: DataGrid.widths
entries.text: Per-column width overrides, { id: width } — null means the widths in columns. A width of 0 drops the column entirely , which is the deliberate narrow-screen degrade: priority, not squish. widths = { app.narrow ? { notes: 0 } : null } is a responsive layout. object

entries.title: DataGrid.sortOn
entries.text: The column id the sort names — "" when unsorted. Sorting names a derivation; it does not reorder anything. The truth stays in the data: your app derives the sorted items from this, and the grid displays the order it is given. string

entries.title: DataGrid.sortDir
entries.text: "asc" or "desc", alongside sortOn. string

entries.title: DataGrid.activeCol
entries.text: The active cell's column — with Table's active row, the grid's keyboard position. Left and Right move it. number

entries.title: DataGrid.inHeader
entries.text: Whether the keyboard position is in the header row: Up from the first row goes there, Left and Right move along the headers, Enter or Space sorts by the column, Down comes back. boolean

entries.title: DataGrid.datapath
entries.text: The grid's own rows: its items, wrapped so each record becomes a row. Set by the grid; not yours to point elsewhere. datapath

entries.title: DataGrid.sortInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for sorting. The default writes sortOn/sortDir; override it to own the sort — which is what you do when the sort belongs to a server query. sortInput(on, dir)

entries.title: DataGrid.arrangeInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for reordering, receiving the new column-id order. Override it to persist a user's column layout. arrangeInput(ord)

entries.title: DataGrid.resizeInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for resizing, receiving a column id and its new width. Widths are plain values — nothing measures cells — so an override is free to clamp, snap, or store them. resizeInput(id, w)

entries.title: DataGrid.headerClick
entries.text: Toggles the sort on a column: same column flips direction, a new column starts ascending. Routes through sortInput. headerClick(id)

entries.title: DataGrid.selectable
entries.text: Table's, answered here: a heading record is not selectable, every other record is. An override narrows it with super.selectable(m), so headings stay out. selectable(m)

entries.title: DataGrid.columnRecords
entries.text: The derived column model — the columns records, ordered and widthed by state, with running x offsets. The one truth every header cell and grid cell positions from. columnRecords(cols, ord, w)

entries.title: DataGrid.currentOrder
entries.text: The column ids in their present order. currentOrder()

entries.title: DataGrid.activeCell
entries.text: The active cell, when its row is built. activeCell()

entries.title: DataGrid.enterCell
entries.text: Enters a cell: an edit cell's field takes the focus (starting with a typed character, when one is given); in any other cell, its first control does, or — for Space — is pressed. enterCell(cell, typed)

entries.title: DataGrid.editStep
entries.text: Moves an edit to the same column one row up or down — the spreadsheet expectation — passing over headings. Scrolls the destination into existence first, so it works over a windowed collection. editStep(row, col, d)

entries.title: DataGrid.colWidthOf
entries.text: The present width of a column by id. colWidthOf(id)

entries.title: DataGrid.keyDown
entries.text: Left and Right move the active cell; Enter, F2 or a typed character edits a text column; Enter or F2 moves into a cell's control, and Space presses it; the rest is Table's. An override passes the keys it does not take to super.onKeyDown(e). onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: DataGridRow
entries.text: A row of a DataGrid, one per item: the grid makes it, never the program. It holds one DataGridCell per column, placed from the column model. Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are TableRow's and Table's.

entries.title: DataGridRow.rec
entries.text: The row's record, as a derived attribute, so its cells follow the record's changes. object

entries.title: DataGridRow.accessibilityRole

entries.title: DataGridRow._reportsActive
entries.text: Internal. Off: in a grid the keyboard is on a cell, and the cell reports itself, not the row. boolean

entries.title: DataGridRow.height
entries.text: From the theme's gridRowHeight (28 by default); the header row is gridHeaderHeight (30). Length

entries.title: DataGridRow.cellAt
entries.text: The cell in a column, by its place in the column model. cellAt(col)

entries.title: DataGridHeadingRow
entries.text: A heading between a DataGrid's rows — the row the grid makes for a record with a heading field. It spans the grid, has no cells, and is passed over by selection and the arrow keys. It draws the grid's headingClass, or its own: the heading text, muted.

entries.title: DataGridHeadingRow.rec
entries.text: The heading record. object

entries.title: DataGridHeadingRow.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.text: boolean

entries.title: DataGridHeadingRow.focusable
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: DataGridHeadingRow.height
entries.text: The theme's gridRowHeight, the same as an ordinary row. Length

entries.title: DataGridHeading
entries.text: The grid's own heading: the record's heading text, semibold, in the theme's muted ink. A headingClass of your own replaces it; its data is the heading record.

entries.title: DataGridHeading.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: DataGridHeading.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: DataGridCell
entries.text: One cell of a DataGrid row: placed and sized from its column, with the row's record as the data of what it draws — the column's cell class, an edit field for an edit column, or the field as text. The grid makes it; a program writes the class it draws.

entries.title: DataGridCell.row
entries.text: The DataGridRow this cell is drawn in, or null outside one. DataGridRow?

entries.title: DataGridCell.dataGrid
entries.text: The DataGrid its row belongs to. DataGrid?

entries.title: DataGridCell.gridFocused
entries.text: Whether the grid holds keyboard focus in its body (not its header), so a cell can show where the keyboard is. boolean

entries.title: DataGridCell.activeHere
entries.text: Whether it is the grid's active cell while the grid has focus. boolean

entries.title: DataGridCell.x
entries.text: Its column's offset in the row. Length

entries.title: DataGridCell.width
entries.text: Its column's width. Length

entries.title: DataGridCell.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: DataGridCell.clip
entries.text: ClipPath

entries.text: The outline that marks the active cell. Stroke

entries.title: DataGridCell.cornerRadius
entries.text: From the theme's gridCellCornerRadius (3 by default): the active cell's outline. Radius

entries.title: DataGridCell.kind
entries.text: What the cell holds: "own" (the column's class), "edit" (a text field) or "text". kind()

entries.title: DataGridCell.drawn
entries.text: drawn()

entries.title: DataGridCell.editor
entries.text: The text field of an edit cell, or null. editor()

entries.title: DataGridCell.firstControl
entries.text: The first focusable view inside the cell's own class, or null — what Enter moves into and Space presses. firstControl()

entries.title: DataGridCell.writeText
entries.text: Writes a text value into the cell's field in its row's record. writeText(v)

entries.title: DataGridCell.takeActive
entries.text: Makes this the grid's active cell — what a control inside it does when it takes the focus. takeActive()

entries.title: DataGridText
entries.text: What a DataGrid column with no cell draws: its field, as text.

entries.title: DataGridText.field
entries.text: The field shown — its column's id. string

entries.title: DataGridText.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: DataGridText.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: DataGridEdit
entries.text: What an edit: true column of a DataGrid draws: a text field writing its field into the row's record as you type. Up and Down (or Return) move the edit to the same column in the row above or below; Esc puts back the text the edit began with.

entries.title: DataGridEdit.field
entries.text: The field edited — its column's id. string

entries.title: DataGridEdit.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: DataGridEdit.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: DataGridEdit.write
entries.text: Writes a text value into the field. write(v)

entries.title: SearchField
entries.text: A text field for searching, that a screen reader announces as a search field, with "Search" as its placeholder until you give it your own. Its look is the theme's: a stadium — round at both ends, searchFieldCornerRadius = "round" — unless the theme gives that token a radius (a square-cornered house style gives it its fieldCornerRadius), with searchFieldHeight, searchFieldPadding, and searchFieldFill and searchFieldStroke (the theme's surface and line when unset). Everything else is TextInput's: text, onInput, onEnter, the value pattern. App [ width = 400, height = 100, q: string = "", find: SearchField [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, placeholder = "Search messages", onInput(t: string) { app.q = "" + t } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 64, text = { app.q == "" ? "type to search" : "searching for " + app.q } ] ]

entries.title: SearchField.height
entries.text: The theme's searchFieldHeight. Length

entries.title: SearchField.cornerRadius
entries.text: The theme's searchFieldCornerRadius: "round" (the default) for round ends at any height, or a radius, capped at half the height. Radius

entries.title: SearchField.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: SearchField.placeholder
entries.text: "Search" unless you name what is searched ("Search messages") — it is also the field's name to a screen reader when no accessibilityLabel is set. string

entries.title: SearchField.padding
entries.text: The theme's searchFieldPadding at each end, so the text sits clear of round ends. Inset

entries.title: SearchField.fill
entries.text: The theme's searchFieldFill, else its surface. Fill

entries.title: SearchField.stroke
entries.text: The theme's searchFieldStroke, else its line, turning to its accent while the field has the focus. Stroke

entries.title: Segmented
entries.text: A row of mutually exclusive choices — the control you reach for when the options are few, named, and worth showing all at once. Its choices are data, like Menu's items and DataGrid's columns: Segmented [ width = 300, value = { app.page }, choices = { [ ({ id: "controls", label: "Controls" }), ({ id: "table", label: "Table" }), ({ id: "grid", label: "DataGrid" }) ] }, input(v: string) { app.page = v } ] Tabs A segmented control that switches what is shown below it — pages, panes — is a row of tabs: use a TabBar, which is a Segmented in every other way and is heard as tabs. Why data, and not Segment children Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask the view tree that: childViews carries set membership only, so .length is live while anything reaching into the collection is refused — aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]. The compiler names the answer. Equal widths Segments divide the control's width evenly — a segmented control divides evenly, where a row of buttons sizes to its content. Equal width keeps the convention that segment labels are short and similar in length, and it lets the pill travel at constant width between segments. So a Segmented does not size itself to its labels : set width, or accept segMin × choices.length. The pill The highlight springs a normalized lane — a float index — not pixels. x is then lane × segW, so a resize recomputes segW and the pill snaps to the right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. The chosen segment wears a raised surface pill with a hairline. App [ width = 340, height = 130, page: string = "one", Segmented [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, value = { app.page }, choices = { [ ({ id: "one", label: "One" }), ({ id: "two", label: "Two" }), ({ id: "three", label: "Three" }) ] }, input(v: string) { app.page = v } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { "showing: " + app.page } ] ]

entries.title: Segmented.choices
entries.text: The segments, as records: { id, label } or { id, icon } — the same vocabulary Menu's items use. A choice shows a label or an icon, never both. A choice may also carry a location, which makes that segment a real link (see SegmentedItem.location). array

entries.title: Segmented.value
entries.text: The active choice. Constrain it to your own state and override input to own the destination, or leave it alone and read value back — a Segmented works standalone. Compared against each choice's id by identity, so any value type works. object

entries.title: Segmented.disabled
entries.text: Disables the whole control. A segment is not separately disable-able — a disabled group leaves the tab order entirely rather than offering unreachable stops. boolean

entries.title: Segmented.rad
entries.text: The control's corner radius, from the theme's segmentedCornerRadius (8 by default); the pill and each segment's hover sit 2 inside it. number

entries.title: Segmented.segMin
entries.text: The per-segment width used when you set no width on the control. Because a Segmented does not self-size to its labels, this is what decides the default width: segMin × choices.length. number

entries.title: Segmented.count
entries.text: How many choices there are, floored at 1 so the width arithmetic never divides by zero. number

entries.title: Segmented.segW
entries.text: One segment's width — the control's width divided by the count. What the pill and every segment position from. number

entries.title: Segmented.idx
entries.text: Which choice is live, as an index into choices, from the data — the only place the question can be asked. −1 (nothing selected) parks the pill at 0 and hides it rather than springing to a phantom slot. number

entries.title: Segmented.lane
entries.text: The pill's position as a float index, sprung toward idx. The whole reason the pill is correct at any size: x is lane × segW, so a resize recomputes the width and the pill snaps to the right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. number

entries.title: Segmented.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Segmented.focusScope
entries.text: stop: the control is one Tab stop — Tab lands on the selected segment and the next Tab leaves; the arrows move among the segments, wrapping, as in any stop. Space or Enter picks where they land, so an inactive choice is reachable and selectable entirely from the keyboard , and nothing changes until it is asked to — a choice that is a place is followed on Enter, as a link is, not on the arrow. none | stop | capture | region | modal

entries.title: Segmented.height
entries.text: From the theme's segmentedHeight (30 by default); the labels' size is segmentedFontSize (13). Length

entries.title: Segmented.cornerRadius
entries.text: The control's rad. Radius

entries.title: Segmented.fill
entries.text: The track: the theme's trackFill, else control. The pill is segmentedSelectedFill, else surface. Where the theme gives segmentDividerColor (none by default), a divider stands between segments; one beside the pill fades as the pill reaches it, so they part around the selection as it slides. Fill

entries.title: Segmented.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control — track, pill and every segment alike, never a recolour — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none. number

entries.title: Segmented.width
entries.text: Content-sized: every segment at least segMin wide, so short labels never squeeze. Length

entries.title: Segmented.datapath
entries.text: Roots the control on its own items data, so the segments replicate from choices without the author writing a datapath. datapath

entries.title: Segmented.focusEntry
entries.text: The segment Tab lands on: the selected one, else the first. focusEntry()

entries.title: Segmented.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes, receiving the picked id. The default writes value; override it to own the destination. input(v)

entries.title: Segmented.pick
entries.text: Selects a choice by id, routing through input. The seam a segment calls. pick(v)

entries.title: Segmented.segs
entries.text: The segment views, for the Tab entry. A handler-only walk — a constraint may not aggregate the view tree. segs()

entries.title: TextSizeSwitch
entries.text: The reading-size control: three sizes — smaller, the default, larger — each shown as the letter A at that size, with the size in use marked. It is a Segmented, so it holds its value the way every segmented control does, Tab reaches it as one stop, and the arrows move between the sizes. The value is a scale, one of sizes. An app keeps the scale it reads its text at and binds the switch to it: App [ fontScale: number = 1, TextSizeSwitch [ value = { app.fontScale }, input(v: object) { app.fontScale = v as number } ], Text [ fontSize = { 15 app.fontScale }, text = "Read me" ] ]

entries.title: TextSizeSwitch.sizes
entries.text: The three scales, smallest first, the default in the middle: [0.9, 1, 1.2] unless the app reads at another default. number[]

entries.title: TextSizeSwitch.choices
entries.text: One segment per size, each showing its A and named for a screen reader by what it does. array

entries.title: TextSizeSwitch.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: "Text size": the group's name. string

entries.title: TextSizeSwitch.width
entries.text: Three segments of 34 each, so the letters keep their room whatever the theme's segment minimum. Length

entries.title: ChevronIcon
entries.text: The disclosure mark: a menu drops, a pane opens, a select expands. Every disclosure in the chrome is this one class turned by its dir, which is what makes them agree. For a direction that is itself the state — a sort order, a trend — reach for ArrowIcon instead; the two must not look alike.

entries.title: ChevronIcon.dir
entries.text: The resting orientation: "down" (the default), "up", "left" or "right". Sugar over angle. string

entries.title: ChevronIcon.angle
entries.text: The rotation in radians, and the primitive, so it can be sprung — an Accordion twisty turns in step with its pane sliding open rather than snapping between two states. The turn lives in the recording deliberately: the mark rotates inside its 16-box while the box stays put. (The View-level rotation attribute turns the whole box — the wrong tool for a glyph whose frame should not move.) number

entries.title: ChevronIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the chevron. Override to replace the mark while keeping the class's role. draw(d)

entries.title: CheckIcon
entries.text: The tick — a checked menu row, a Checkbox's mark, a confirmation. Ink stays local : a menu row inverts its check on the highlighted row while a checkbox always uses the accent text color, so the host sets ink rather than the icon assuming it.

entries.title: CheckIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the tick. One shape, one stroke, one join — so a checkbox's mark and a menu row's check cannot drift apart. draw(d)

entries.title: CloseIcon
entries.text: The dismiss mark: a window close box, a chip's remove affordance, a dialog's corner.

entries.title: CloseIcon.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: "Close": a control that shows only this mark is the Close button to a screen reader. A control with words of its own is named by them. string

entries.title: CloseIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the cross. draw(d)

entries.title: PlusIcon
entries.text: Add. Pairs with MinusIcon at the same stroke and cap, so a stepper's two ends match.

entries.title: PlusIcon.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: "Add": a control that shows only this mark is named Add. A control with words of its own is named by them. string

entries.title: PlusIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the plus. draw(d)

entries.title: MinusIcon
entries.text: Remove, and the partially-checked state of a tri-state box. Pairs with PlusIcon.

entries.title: MinusIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the bar. draw(d)

entries.title: LightbulbIcon
entries.text: The help affordance — the one FILLED mark in a stroked set: a continuous teardrop of glass over a three-bar tapering base.

entries.title: LightbulbIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the bulb. This one mark is filled, and does not answer to weight — the contour carries its weight in the outline itself, so there is no stroke to widen. The bulb keeps its own visual weight at every rung. draw(d)

entries.title: SunIcon
entries.text: "Light" in the appearance triad — a disc with rays, sharing its radius and stroke with MoonIcon and AutoIcon so the three read as one family at 14px.

entries.title: SunIcon.rays
entries.text: How many rays surround the disc. Eight by default; lowering it reads lighter at small sizes. number

entries.title: SunIcon.solid
entries.text: false (the default) draws the ring; true fills the disc. The ring is drawn a touch smaller than the filled disc on purpose — a stroke straddles its path, so an outline at the filled radius reads as the larger mark. boolean

entries.title: SunIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the disc and its rays. draw(d)

entries.title: MoonIcon
entries.text: "Dark" in the appearance triad. The crescent is the region between two equal circles , the second offset by (3, −3) — so both arcs meet exactly at the circles' intersection points and the horns close to a point instead of leaving the ragged tail an arc pair leaves.

entries.title: MoonIcon.solid
entries.text: false (the default) strokes the closed path — the tapered-horn rendition; true fills it for a solid crescent. One path, two renditions — nothing about the geometry changes, only what is done with it. boolean

entries.title: MoonIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the crescent. draw(d)

entries.title: AutoIcon
entries.text: "System" in the appearance triad — the same disc, half of it taken away. The ring stays around the empty half so it reads as part of one object rather than as a gap. The one mark of the three whose meaning is its fill, which is why a mixed outline-and-filled language is right for the triad.

entries.title: AutoIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the half-filled disc. draw(d)

entries.title: TextSizeIcon
entries.text: The letter A, drawn: two legs and a crossbar, standing on the box's baseline. Its three named sizes are TextSmallIcon, TextMediumIcon and TextLargeIcon; a control names them in data.

entries.title: TextSizeIcon.glyph
entries.text: The letter's height in the 16-unit box. The three named sizes set it; the letter keeps its proportions and its baseline at every height. number

entries.title: TextSizeIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the letter. draw(d)

entries.title: TextSmallIcon
entries.text: The small A of a text-size control.

entries.title: TextSmallIcon.glyph
entries.text: Seven and a half units: the smallest of the three. number

entries.title: TextSmallIcon.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: "Smaller text", for a control that shows only this mark. string

entries.title: TextMediumIcon
entries.text: The default A of a text-size control.

entries.title: TextMediumIcon.glyph
entries.text: Ten and a half units: between the other two. number

entries.title: TextMediumIcon.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: "Default text size", for a control that shows only this mark. string

entries.title: TextLargeIcon
entries.text: The large A of a text-size control.

entries.title: TextLargeIcon.glyph
entries.text: Thirteen and a half units: the largest of the three, nearly the whole box. number

entries.title: TextLargeIcon.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: "Larger text", for a control that shows only this mark. string

entries.title: Icon
entries.text: A small monochrome mark, drawn rather than typed. A font's glyphs are not marks: they are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a ✓ sits on the text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The library's own marks — Checkbox.mark, Menu.check, the Combobox disclosure — are all Icons. An icon is placed like any view. In a row, the row's align = center centers it with the text beside it; placed by hand, it takes y = center as any view does. Writing one Subclass and override draw. Author the shape in a 16×16 box — unit converts it to whatever size the host asked for: class SparkIcon extends Icon [ draw(d: DrawContext) { d.scale(unit, unit) d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke() } ] Overriding a method is how a subclass refines an icon — a subclass cannot re-declare a child it inherits (the compiler refuses it) — so the shape lives in draw and everything adjustable is an attribute. Size changes the drawing, not the shape Every icon is one path. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing redrawn at a breakpoint: unit scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for, so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly. The stroke is the deliberate exception. d.lineWidth = weight / unit sits inside d.scale(unit, unit), so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant weight in device pixels at every size. An icon's line therefore matches the 1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows. The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5% at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px — chrome sizes — that is invisible. Past ~32 an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a mark — so this set is built for chrome sizes , and a large display icon (an empty-state mark, an about-box graphic) would want the opposite: d.lineWidth = weight outside the scale, so the line grows with the drawing. What is not an Icon Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification swell, they are polychrome (gradient(hue1, hue2) behind a hue-parameterised drawing), and their width animates every frame. Each of those alone rules them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and reads spindly; ink is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing this set forbids. The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is chrome vocabulary versus identity. A mark that says close, expand, checked, this is the dark theme belongs here, at a size the host states. A mark that says this is Calendar does not, and belongs to the app that owns the identity. Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows take WindowIcon and CodeIcon from this set, while its dock keeps DockIcon. Two rules Scale inside the body, never with the View's scale. A recording rasterizes into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution, while scale is a transform applied after — so scale = { width / 16 } would rasterize 16 pixels and stretch them. Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is most of them. Scaling inside the recording allocates the raster at true size instead. Never animate an icon's width. Reading size inside draw makes the recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records and reallocates the backing canvas every frame, which drops a magnifying dock of icons from 60 to ~25fps. A static size re-records once and costs nothing after: 120 icons re-recording their content every frame run frame-bound at 16.6ms. Colour is not a rule — ink follows the provided text colour, so an icon beside a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

entries.title: Icon.iconSize
entries.text: The mark's size, in px — a provided value (a host states it once, every icon beneath answers): defaults to the nearest provided iconSize, overridable at the use site. number

entries.title: Icon.textColor
entries.text: The effective text colour the mark's ink follows — a provided value, so an icon beside a muted label goes muted on its own; set ink to override. Color

entries.title: Icon.ink
entries.text: The mark's colour. Follows the provided textColor, so an icon beside a muted label goes muted on its own. The trap: that attribute falls back to black platform-wide, so an icon in a context that never states a text colour renders black and vanishes on a dark surface. State ink unless you know the context sets one — IconHost does it for every icon built by name. Color

entries.title: Icon.weight
entries.text: Stroke width in final device pixels, not authored ones. Divide by unit inside draw (d.lineWidth = weight / unit) and the scale cancels, so the line lands at a constant weight at every size and matches the 1px rules and text it sits among. number

entries.title: Icon.unit
entries.text: The 16-box-to-host-size scale factor. Multiply the path by it; divide the stroke by it. Every icon is one path at one size, scaled — there are no per-size variants. number

entries.title: Icon.width
entries.text: Sized by the provided iconSize, so a menu states 16 once and every icon in it answers; a use site may set its own. Length

entries.title: Icon.height
entries.text: Square, always — the height follows the width. Length

entries.title: IconHost
entries.text: Turns an icon's class name into a live view. A control names its icon (iconLeft = "TrashIcon") rather than nesting one: a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form that is the same whether it is written or read from data. IconHost builds the named icon with createView, as a menu record's icon field does. It reserves no space when empty, so a control's contentWidth measures only the slots that are filled and an icon-less button needs no special case. The name is read once, when the host is built. A name read from data gives each row of a toolbar its own icon, but changing the name later does not swap the icon. An icon that must change at runtime — a play/pause toggle — is two icons, each with visible constrained.

entries.title: IconHost.kind
entries.text: The icon class name to build ("TrashIcon"). "" builds nothing and the host collapses to zero width, so an icon-less control needs no special case. Consumed once, at construction — assigning a new name later does not re-materialize the icon. A name that is only ever computed needs use [ Name ] to survive the build. string

entries.title: IconHost.iconSize
entries.text: The size the built icon takes — a provided value (a menu row 16, a button 18); defaults to the nearest provided iconSize. number

entries.title: IconHost.ink
entries.text: The colour handed to the icon this host builds. A value passed to createView is set once, and the ink must follow the control's state, so it travels as a provided value: this provides textColor, which the icon's drawing reads. Defaults to provided("theme").text rather than the platform's inherited black, which is what stops a host-built icon from rendering invisibly on a dark surface. Color

entries.title: IconHost.width
entries.text: Zero when there is no icon to host, so an empty slot reserves nothing and an icon-less button needs no special case; else the provided iconSize. Length

entries.title: IconHost.height
entries.text: The icon's size whether or not one is hosted, so a row's height does not jump when an icon appears. Length

entries.title: IconHost.visible
entries.text: Present only when a kind is named. boolean

entries.title: IconHost.init
entries.text: Builds the named icon. Fires once. An override calls super.onInit(), or nothing is built. onInit()

entries.title: SegmentedItem
entries.text: One choice of a Segmented, materialized from that control's choices data — never authored directly , which is why it carries almost nothing of its own. It is a full Control: its own tab stop, activated by Space or Enter, so a user can tab to an inactive choice and select it. It renders rest, hover and press only. The chosen state is the sliding pill behind these, not a fill of its own — which is exactly what lets the pill travel between segments instead of popping.

entries.title: SegmentedItem.on
entries.text: Whether this segment is the group's current choice, derived from the parent by identity. boolean

entries.title: SegmentedItem.ink
entries.text: This segment's text and icon colour, brightening when it is on or hovered. One attribute, so a label and an icon can never disagree. Color

entries.title: SegmentedItem.location
entries.text: Makes this segment a real link: give a choice a location and the segment declares link = "#…" to it, so it renders as a real anchor the crawler follows, ⌘-click opens, and a click or Enter navigates. A view-switching control is often the only edge into half of an app, so the switch has to say where it goes. Empty for an ordinary segmented control, and an empty location is no link at all. string

entries.title: SegmentedItem.height
entries.text: As tall as the control. Length

entries.title: SegmentedItem.width
entries.text: Every segment the same width — the control's segW, its width divided by its count. Length

entries.title: SegmentedItem.x
entries.text: Placed by index: the control's inset plus i segment widths. Length

entries.title: SegmentedItem.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: SegmentedItem.accessibilityChecked
entries.text: Follows on: a segment is one radio of its group. boolean

entries.title: SegmentedItem.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: Empty for a segment that shows text (the text names it); a segment showing an icon is named by its record's label. string

entries.title: SegmentedItem.disabled
entries.text: Disabled with the control; an item never disables alone. boolean

entries.title: SegmentedItem.link
entries.text: "#" + this segment's location, or empty — the segment is a link exactly when its choice names a place, and never while the group is disabled. string

entries.title: SegmentedItem.replace
entries.text: The group's own replace: whether following this segment's link overwrites the history entry instead of pushing one. boolean

entries.title: SegmentedItem.press
entries.text: Delivers this segment's id to the group. press()

entries.title: SegmentedItem.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the segment's pill inset, not its whole box. focusShape()

entries.title: SegmentedItem.click
entries.text: Presses. A segment whose choice carries a location also follows its link. onClick()

entries.title: SegmentedItem.keyDown
entries.text: Space and Enter pick; the arrows move among the segments (the stop's). onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: ArrowIcon
entries.text: An arrow, not a chevron — the two mean different things and must not look alike. A chevron discloses; an arrow points at a direction that is itself the state: sort ascending, a trend, a transfer. The shaft is what a chevron lacks. The two often sit adjacent — a sort-direction control beside a sort-menu popper — and one shape for both reads as a mistake.

entries.title: ArrowIcon.dir
entries.text: Which way it points: "up" (the default), "down", "left" or "right". string

entries.title: ArrowIcon.angle
entries.text: The rotation in radians, sprungable like ChevronIcon's. number

entries.title: ArrowIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the arrow. draw(d)

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch
entries.text: The light/dark control: one icon that shows the appearance you are in — a sun in light, a moon in dark — and a press flips to the other. Two states, not three. The third state other switches carry, "follow the system", is not a choice here but the default: an app derives its appearance from its environment (the OS, or the host it is embedded in) until the reader presses the switch, and from then on keeps what the reader chose. That is the rule the platform's own apps follow, and it is why the control needs no Auto button: nobody has to choose to follow the system, because until they choose anything else, they already are. App [ themeMode: string = "auto", // "auto" until the reader chooses isDark: boolean = { app.themeMode == "auto" ? app.systemDark : app.themeMode == "dark" }, theme = { app.isDark ? SanFranciscoDark : SanFrancisco }, AppearanceSwitch [ dark = { app.isDark }, input(v: boolean) { app.themeMode = v ? "dark" : "light" } ] ]

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.dark
entries.text: The appearance the switch shows: true shows the moon, false the sun. Bind it to the app's effective appearance (dark = { app.isDark }) — the value the page is actually wearing, whether that came from the environment or from the reader. boolean

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.width
entries.text: A square: the theme's appearanceSwitchSize (32 unless a theme says otherwise). Length

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.height
entries.text: The same as the width. Length

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.cornerRadius
entries.text: The theme's control radius, capped at half the height. Radius

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.accessibilityRole
entries.text: none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: string

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.accessibilityChecked
entries.text: Follows dark: to a screen reader the sun and the moon are one switch, "Dark appearance". boolean

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.tooltipLabel
entries.text: Says what a press will do — "Switch to dark" or "Switch to light" — rather than naming the current state, which the icon already shows. string

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.fill
entries.text: Nothing at rest — the icon stands on the surface beneath it — the control's hover tint under the pointer, and its pressed tint while held. Fill

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.input
entries.text: Where a press delivers the new appearance — the flipped value of dark. The default writes dark; override it to record the reader's choice in the app (input(v: boolean) { app.themeMode = v ? "dark" : "light" }), after which the environment stops deciding. press() never writes dark directly, so a constrained switch never fights its constraint. input(v)

entries.title: AppearanceSwitch.press
entries.text: Flips the appearance, by delivering !dark through input. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Floating
entries.text: The base of every overlay in the library — Popover, Sheet, Dialog, Toast, and the menus — and of a program's own (class Viewer extends Dialog [ … ]). It is declared where it belongs, in its owner, and paints above everything in its context: in the overlay layer the nearest Window provides, else in the App's own layers — overlays in the order they open, toasts above them. It carries, once, what every overlay needs: Opening and closing — show() and close(); shown says whether it is open now. A closed overlay builds no view of its own until it is first shown. Motion — it animates in and out on openT (0 closed, 1 open), and stays built until its closing motion lands: closing stops it taking input at once. Input — pressPolicy and scrollPolicy say what a press and a scroll aimed past it do (outsidePress, scrollBelow), while it is open. An outside press that dismisses closes it. Keys and focus — while open it holds the keyboard (a key it uses does not also reach the program's Keys members); Esc closes the topmost open overlay; one that takes focus focuses its first stop on opening and gives focus back on closing. Anchoring — anchorBox(v) is a view's box in the overlay's frame, for an overlay that opens next to something; toLayer(v, x, y) maps a point the same way, through a window turned or scaled; keepOnApp(x, y, w, h) moves a box back onto the App. Its colours are theme tokens — the panel of a Dialog, Sheet or Popover paints the theme's surface (a Menu's, menuFill else surface; a Toast's, tooltipFill), and the backdrop scrimFill at scrimOpacity. One overlay of its own colour is given a theme with the token changed: theme = { ({ ...provided("theme"), surface: #111111 }) }. Forms — it is a boundary: a field inside belongs to a Form inside it, not to one around the place it is declared. App [ width = 420, height = 220, Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Show", onClick() { app.note.show() } ], note: Popover [ anchorTo = { app.children[0] as View }, Text [ text = "A popover is a Floating." ] ] ]

entries.title: Floating.kind
entries.text: What kind of overlay it is: "floating" (menus, popovers), "modal" (dialogs, sheets) or "notice" (toasts). Floating and modal overlays share a layer and stack in the order they open — a menu opened from a dialog paints above it; notices paint above them all. A class-level fact. string

entries.title: Floating.shown
entries.text: Whether it is open now. Open it with show() and close it with close() — or make it state: shown = { app.editing } with input(open: boolean) { app.editing = open }, and it opens and closes as the state does (SwiftUI's isPresented). boolean

entries.title: Floating.present
entries.text: Whether it is built and drawn: open, or closing until its motion lands. Content built fresh for each opening reads it, so it stays through the closing motion instead of emptying the panel as it goes: entry: Form [ exists = { app.formSheet.present } ]. boolean

entries.title: Floating.openT
entries.text: The open blend, 0 closed and 1 open, sprung — what a subclass draws its motion from. number

entries.title: Floating.host
entries.text: The view it paints in, chosen when it opens. View?

entries.title: Floating.opener
entries.text: The view it was opened for, when it was opened for one. View?

entries.title: Floating.pressPolicy
entries.text: What a press outside it does while it is open — outsidePress's value then. "dismiss" | "dismissAndDeliver" | "block" | "ignore"

entries.title: Floating.scrollPolicy
entries.text: What a scroll outside it does while it is open — scrollBelow's value then. "block" | "allow" | "dismiss"

entries.title: Floating.takesFocus
entries.text: Whether opening moves focus into it (its first stop) and closing gives it back — to the view that had it, or, when that view is gone or hidden by then, to the next Tab stop after its place. boolean

entries.title: Floating.sharesProgram
entries.text: Whether, open in a host's layer (a program running in a window, say), it is shown at its program's scale and turn there — as a menu or a popover is. false for what attaches to the window itself, edge to edge (a Sheet). true by default. boolean

entries.title: Floating.ignoreLayout
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: Floating.visible
entries.text: Follows present: it is drawn while open, and while its closing motion runs. boolean

entries.title: Floating.paintsIn
entries.text: Follows host: it paints in the layer it opened into. View

entries.title: Floating.scale
entries.text: Its program's scale where it opens in a host's layer (_baseScale) — a subclass multiplies its own motion into it. number

entries.title: Floating.rotation
entries.text: Its program's turn where it opens in a host's layer (_baseRotation), in degrees. number

entries.title: Floating.outsidePress
entries.text: pressPolicy while it is open, none once it closes — a closing overlay takes no presses. none | dismiss | dismissAndDeliver | block | ignore

entries.title: Floating.scrollBelow
entries.text: scrollPolicy while it is open, none once it closes. none | block | allow | dismiss

entries.title: Floating.input
entries.text: Where opening and closing go — the value pattern, as a control's value goes through its input. The default writes shown. To make whether it is open your own state, constrain shown and override this to write that state, so its own closings (Esc, a press past it) reach it: shown = { app.editing }, input(open: boolean) { app.editing = open }. Constraining shown without it is a compile error. An override must deliver: write the state shown follows, or — with shown not constrained — call super.input(open); otherwise show(), close(), Esc and a press past it do nothing. To act on closing, override closed() instead. input(open)

entries.title: Floating.show
entries.text: Opens it, through input(true): picks its layer, builds it, holds the keyboard, and takes focus if it takes focus. show()

entries.title: Floating.showFor
entries.text: Opens it for v — opener becomes v. showFor(v)

entries.title: Floating.focusFirst
entries.text: Where the focus goes when an overlay that takesFocus opens: the first view inside that takes focus, else the overlay holds the focus itself, so Tab has nowhere to go behind it and Esc still closes it. An override that may find nothing to focus calls super.focusFirst() for that case. focusFirst()

entries.title: Floating.close
entries.text: Closes it at once, through input(false) (it stops taking input); it is torn down when its closing motion lands. An override calls super.close(). Work for every closing belongs in closed(): the state shown follows can close it without coming through here. close()

entries.title: Floating.closed
entries.text: Called once it is closed — override to act on closing. It runs before focus is given back, so focus moved here (to what the closing created) stays where it was put. closed()

entries.title: Floating.isTop
entries.text: Whether it is the topmost open overlay — the one Esc closes. isTop()

entries.title: Floating.anchorBox
entries.text: A view's box in this overlay's frame: { x, y, w, h }. anchorBox(v)

entries.title: Floating.toLayer
entries.text: A point in v's own frame, in the frame of the layer this paints in: { x, y }. Exact through a turned or scaled window, and from a program hosted in a window into its host's. toLayer(v, px, py)

entries.title: Floating.screen
entries.text: The App the layer belongs to — the host's, for a program whose overlays open in its host's window. An overlay may leave its window, never the screen. screen()

entries.title: Floating.toScreen
entries.text: A point in v's own frame, in the screen's frame. toScreen(v, px, py)

entries.title: Floating.keepOnApp
entries.text: Where a box at (x, y), w by h, in the layer's frame, must be to stay on the screen with 4 to spare: { x, y }, moved as little as it can be. An overlay inside a window may hang past the window's edge, but not off the screen. keepOnApp(x, y, w, h)

entries.title: Floating.escape
entries.text: What Esc does when this is the topmost open overlay — closes it; a dialog picks its cancel button instead. escape()

entries.title: Floating.outsidePress
entries.text: An outside press (or, with scrollPolicy = "dismiss", an outside scroll) asked it to close. onOutsidePress()

entries.title: OverlayStrata
entries.text: Internal. The App's overlay layers — overlays, then notice — made by the first Floating that opens and kept above everything else the App holds. Menus, popovers, dialogs and sheets share the first, in the order they open (a menu opened from a dialog paints above the dialog); toasts paint in the second, above them all. It keeps the open overlays in the order they opened, so Esc knows which is on top. Not written in a program.

entries.title: OverlayStrata.stack
entries.text: The open overlays, oldest first. array

entries.title: OverlayStrata.handled
entries.text: The last key event an overlay acted on — so one Esc closes one overlay, however many hear it. object

entries.title: OverlayStrata.ignoreLayout
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: OverlayStrata.ignoreScroll
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: OverlayStrata.width
entries.text: The window's width when the layers are the App's (or the App's, where it is narrower); a window's own, inside one. Length

entries.title: OverlayStrata.height
entries.text: The window's height when the layers are the App's (or the App's, where it is shorter), so an App that is a whole scrolling page still opens its sheets and dialogs on screen; a window's own, inside one; the App's, where there is no window (headless). Length

entries.title: OverlayStrata.pointerEvents
entries.text: string

entries.title: OverlayStrata.opened
entries.text: Puts an overlay on top of the stack. opened(v)

entries.title: OverlayStrata.closedIt
entries.text: Takes an overlay off the stack. closedIt(v)

entries.title: OverlayStrata.top
entries.text: The open overlay the keyboard goes to — the one Esc closes — or null: the latest that took the keys and still holds them (Keys.claimant()). A toast, which takes nothing, is never it; nor is a dialog open in one window while focus is in another. top()

entries.title: Popover
entries.text: A bubble anchored to a view, holding your own content — a picker, a few settings, an info card. It opens next to its anchor (below, else above where there is no room), follows it as it moves, and closes when you press anywhere outside it, the press going on to what you pressed. On a phone-width screen it presents as a sheet rising from the bottom instead. App [ width = 420, height = 240, b: Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Font…", onClick() { app.pick.showFor(this) } ], pick: Popover [ Text [ text = "Size" ], Slider [ width = 180 ] ] ] It is a Floating: it takes focus on opening (its first control) and gives it back on closing; Tab stays inside it; Esc closes it.

entries.title: Popover.anchorTo
entries.text: What it opens next to when shown without one — showFor(v) names it per opening instead. View?

entries.title: Popover.placement
entries.text: Which side it prefers: "below" (the default) or "above"; it takes the other side when the preferred one has no room. string

entries.title: Popover.gap
entries.text: The space between the anchor and the bubble. number

entries.title: Popover.asSheet
entries.text: Whether it presents as a bottom sheet — by default when the screen is narrower than 560. As a sheet, a press outside it closes it and goes no further. boolean

entries.title: Popover.anchorView
entries.text: The view it is anchored to now: the opener, else anchorTo. View?

entries.title: Popover.ab
entries.text: The anchor's box in the popover's frame. object

entries.title: Popover.hostW
entries.text: The width of the layer it paints in: its window's, or the browser window's — not the App's, which on a page that scrolls is as tall as the page. number

entries.title: Popover.hostH
entries.text: The height of the layer it paints in: its window's, or the browser window's. number

entries.title: Popover.roomBelow
entries.text: Whether it fits below its anchor. boolean

entries.title: Popover.roomAbove
entries.text: Whether it fits above its anchor. boolean

entries.title: Popover.below
entries.text: Whether it sits below its anchor now. boolean

entries.title: Popover.accessibilityRole
entries.text: A dialog: it takes the focus and holds it while it is open, as a dialog does. none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.title: Popover.accessibilityLabel
entries.text: The name of what opened it, so a popover opened from "Text size" is the "Text size" dialog. string

entries.title: Popover.kind
entries.text: string

entries.title: Popover.pressPolicy
entries.text: dismissAndDeliver — a press outside closes it and goes on; dismiss as a sheet. "dismiss" | "dismissAndDeliver" | "block" | "ignore"

entries.title: Popover.scrollPolicy

entries.title: Sheet
entries.text: A modal panel attached to an edge of its context — a form, a detail, a set of choices. On a phone-width screen it rises from the bottom, and a downward swipe on its handle puts it away; on a wide screen it slides in from the end edge (edge = "end") or, for a sheet whose edge is the bottom, floats as a card in the middle. A sheet at the start edge (edge = "start") is a navigation drawer: it slides in from the start edge at every width, and a swipe back toward that edge on its trailing edge puts it away. Behind it the context dims; a press there closes the sheet, and nothing behind it scrolls while it is open. Tab stays inside it; Esc closes it; focus goes to its first control when it opens and back when it closes. App [ width = 640, height = 420, Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "New entry…", onClick() { app.entry.show() } ], entry: Sheet [ edge = "end", Text [ fontWeight = bold, text = "New entry" ], TextInput [ width = 100%, accessibilityLabel = "Title" ], Button [ label = "Save", primary = true, onClick() { app.entry.close() } ] ] ]

entries.title: Sheet.edge
entries.text: Which edge it belongs to: "bottom" (the default — on a wide screen it floats as a centered card), "end" (on a wide screen it slides in at the end edge, full height), or "start" (it slides in at the start edge, full height, at every width — a drawer). On a phone-width screen a bottom or end sheet rises from the bottom. "bottom" | "end" | "start"

entries.title: Sheet.widePresentation

entries.title: Shortcuts
entries.text: Keyboard shortcuts, declared as data: records with the key that triggers each, the label a person reads, and the id the action receives. A set covers the view it is declared on and everything inside it. A key press is looked up from the focused view outward: the nearest set that declares that key takes it, and the press goes no further. The walk goes on past the program — a program running in a desktop window reaches the desktop's shortcuts — so a host offers its keys to whatever runs inside it without passing anything down. App [ width = 520, height = 240, saved: number = 0, keys: Shortcuts [ title = "Notes", items = { [ ({ id: "save", key: "⌘S", label: "Save" }), ({ id: "clear", key: "⇧⌘K", label: "Clear" }) ] }, picked(id: string) { if (id == "save") app.saved = app.saved + 1 } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 20, text = { "Saved " + app.saved + " times — press ⌘S" } ] ] A key with a command modifier (⌘, ⌃, ⌥) or a function key works anywhere; a plain key ("?") does not fire while a text field has focus — typing is the field's. While an open menu, dialog or sheet holds the keyboard its keys are its own: a set declared inside it is in force — a form in a sheet keeps its own keys — and every set outside it stands down. A shortcut's chord is not also the browser's (⌘S does not save the page) — except those the browser keeps for itself, such as ⌘W and ⌘N in Safari, which a label may still show. A MenuBar declares the keys of its items for its whole program: the menu bar is the program's shortcut table, and nothing is declared twice. Keys.shortcutsInForce() lists what is in force where focus is — a panel of the available shortcuts reads it.

entries.title: Shortcuts.items
entries.text: The shortcut records: { id, key, label }, and enabled: false for one that shows but does not fire. key is spelled with the modifier glyphs in any order — "⌘S", "⇧⌘Z", "⌥⌘←", "F5" — or in words, "Cmd+Shift+Z". ⌘ is the command key: ⌘ on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere. ShortcutRecord[]

entries.title: Shortcuts.on
entries.text: The view whose subtree the set covers, when that is not the view it is declared on. A MenuBar sets its own to the App. View?

entries.title: Shortcuts.title

entries.title: Shortcuts.picked
entries.text: Receives the id of the shortcut pressed. Override it at the use site. picked(id)

entries.title: Shortcuts.init
entries.text: Registers the set with the keyboard service. An override calls super.onInit(), or no shortcut in the set fires. onInit()

entries.title: Toast
entries.text: A short message that appears at the bottom of its context and goes away by itself — "Saved", "Copied", "Message deleted · Undo". It takes no focus and blocks nothing: presses beside it go where they were aimed, and it stays above an open dialog, still clickable. An optional action record ({ id, label }) adds one button; its id arrives at picked. App [ width = 520, height = 260, toast: Toast [ ], Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Save", onClick() { app.toast.say("Saved", null) } ] ]

entries.title: Toast.message
entries.text: The text it shows. string

entries.title: Toast.action

entries.title: Toast.duration

entries.title: Toast.hostW

entries.title: Toast.held
entries.text: Whether the toast is held open: the pointer is over it, or its action has the focus. A toast whose time runs out while held stays, and goes a moment after it is let go, so a person reaching for "Undo" is never cut off. boolean

entries.title: Toast.kind

entries.title: Toast.stroke

entries.title: Toast.picked

entries.title: Window
entries.text: A window inside a program: a raised surface with a title bar you drag it by and a button at its end that closes it — and, when resizable, edges that resize it. It is the theme's surface, hairline, rounding and shadow, as a dialog or a popover is, with the title bar the same surface and a hairline under it. It is also a world of its own. A menu, popover, dialog or sheet declared inside it opens over it: above its content and past its edges, turning and scaling with it. A toast belongs to the whole program and shows at the bottom of the App. Tab stays among the window's controls; F6 moves to the next window, Shift-F6 back; a press inside it gives it the keyboard, back on the control that last had focus there, and brings it to the front. A dialog or sheet open in it holds back presses aimed at this window only — another window, or what lies behind, still takes them. Esc closes it when focus is inside it and nothing open inside it takes Esc first. Its children go into its body, the pane below the title bar, and place themselves there as in any view — give one a layout or a padding of its own. Whether it is open is state, by the value pattern: open on its own, or open = { … } with input writing where your state lives. Its x, y, width and height are its own to move and resize, so set them as literals. App [ width = 640, height = 360, fill = { provided("theme").background }, notesOpen: boolean = true, Button [ x = 20, y = 316, label = "Show notes", disabled = { app.notesOpen }, onClick() { app.notesOpen = true } ], Window [ x = 30, y = 30, width = 280, height = 190, title = "Settings", more: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "reset", label: "Reset" }), ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy settings" }) ] } ], View [ width = 100%, padding = 16, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 12 ], Checkbox [ label = "Show line numbers" ], Checkbox [ label = "Wrap long lines" ], Button [ label = "More", menu = { parent.parent.more } ] ] ], Window [ x = 330, y = 60, width = 280, height = 220, title = "Notes", resizable = true, open = { app.notesOpen }, input(v: boolean) { app.notesOpen = v }, View [ width = 100%, padding = 16, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ], TextInput [ width = 100%, placeholder = "Title" ] ] ] ] Without a frame frame = false keeps the world and drops the frame: no surface, title bar, close button or resize edges, and no bringing itself forward or closing on Esc — its fill, stroke, shadow and rounding are yours, and so are moving, sizing and stacking it (raise() brings it to the front). What a program with windows of its own design builds on — the Desktop app's are these. App [ width = 560, height = 260, fill = #E6E9EE, Window [ x = 40, y = 40, width = 240, height = 160, rotation = -4, frame = false, title = "Tilted", cornerRadius = 10, fill = white, shadow = { shadow(0, 6, 20, 0x00000033) }, Text [ x = 16, y = 16, text = "A window of its own design" ], TextInput [ x = 16, y = 52, width = 200, accessibilityLabel = "Note" ] ] ]

entries.title: Window.close

entries.title: Window.show
entries.text: Opens it, through input(true), and brings it to the front. show()

entries.title: Window.holdsFocus

entries.text: Gives the window the keyboard: focus goes back to the control that last had it inside the window, else to the first. What a press inside the window does; a program's own way of bringing a window to the front calls it too. enter()

entries.title: Window.bringForward
entries.text: Brings it in front of the windows beside it — its siblings that are windows — and keeps it beneath whatever its parent holds above them. A press in a framed window, focus arriving in it and show() all call it. bringForward()

entries.text: A press inside the window, on nothing that takes it, gives the window the keyboard — and a framed one comes to the front. An override calls super.onPointerDown(). onPointerDown()

Built by a TabBar from its choices — never authored directly: App [ width = 300, height = 80, view: string = "day", TabBar [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, value = { app.view }, choices = { [ ({ id: "day", label: "Day" }), ({ id: "week", label: "Week" }) ] }, input(v: string) { app.view = v } ] ]
