entries.title: TabBar
entries.text: A Segmented that is a row of tabs, switching what is shown below it — see Segmented § Tabs. It looks and moves like a Segmented and takes the same choices, value and input; to a screen reader it is a tab list, each segment a tab. The keys are a Segmented's: the arrows move among the tabs and Space or Enter picks one, so a pane changes only when asked. App [ width = 360, height = 150, page: string = "general", TabBar [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, value = { app.page }, choices = { [ ({ id: "general", label: "General" }), ({ id: "privacy", label: "Privacy" }) ] }, input(v: string) { app.page = v } ], View [ x = 20, y = 70, visible = { app.page == "general" }, accessibilityRole = tabPanel, accessibilityLabel = "General", Checkbox [ label = "Open at login" ] ], View [ x = 20, y = 70, visible = { app.page == "privacy" }, accessibilityRole = tabPanel, accessibilityLabel = "Privacy", Text [ text = "Nothing is shared." ] ] ]

entries.title: Tree
entries.text: An outline whose rows open and close to show their children — a file browser, the sidebar of a mail program or a Finder window. Like Segmented's choices and Menu's items, what it shows is data: nested records, each { id, label, icon?, children? }. Tree [ width = 240, accessibilityLabel = "Files", items = { app.folders }, value = { app.picked }, input(v: string) { app.picked = v }, expanded = { app.openFolders }, expandInput(ids: array) { app.openFolders = ids } ] The Tree holds two values, and both follow the value pattern: value, the id of the selected row, and expanded, the ids of the rows that are open. Neither is written into the records — the records say what the outline holds, the two values say where the person is in it — so the same records can stand under two trees open in different places. Each value works standalone, or is owned by the program through input and expandInput. The rows on screen are the open part of the outline, flattened into a dataset and replicated as TreeRows. Every row is built, none virtualized: a tree is for tens or hundreds of rows, not hundreds of thousands. For a long flat collection use a Table. Keyboard The Tree is one Tab stop: Tab lands on the selected row (else the first) and the next Tab leaves. Focus itself moves from row to row, so a screen reader announces each: Up and Down move to the previous and next visible row; Home and End to the first and last. Right opens a closed row; on an open one it moves to its first child. Left closes an open row; on any other it moves to the row's parent. Enter and Space select the row focus is on. With the pointer, a click selects a row, a click on its chevron opens or closes it without selecting, and a second click on a row with children opens or closes it. Naming it A tree is something a person moves through, so a screen reader needs its name: set accessibilityLabel where you place it ("Files", "Mailboxes"). The rows are named by their labels. App [ width = 320, height = 300, picked: string = "notes", Tree [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 280, accessibilityLabel = "Documents", expanded = ["docs"], value = { app.picked }, input(v: string) { app.picked = v }, items = { [ ({ id: "docs", label: "Documents", children: [ ({ id: "notes", label: "Notes.txt" }), ({ id: "plans", label: "Plans", children: [ ({ id: "q3", label: "Third quarter" }), ({ id: "q4", label: "Fourth quarter" }) ] }) ] }), ({ id: "pics", label: "Pictures", children: [ ({ id: "beach", label: "Beach.jpg" }) ] }), ({ id: "todo", label: "To do" }) ] } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 260, text = { "selected: " + app.picked } ] ]

entries.title: Tree.items
entries.text: The outline, as records: { id, label, icon?, children? }, where children is an array of the same records, nested to any depth. id is a string and unique across the whole tree — selection and the open rows are held by it. icon names an icon class, as Menu's items do (icon: "CheckIcon"); a name computed at run time needs use [ Name ] to survive the build. A row with a children array is a parent even when the array is empty. array

entries.title: Tree.disabled
entries.text: Disables the whole tree: it dims, its rows take no pointer or key, and it leaves the Tab order. boolean

entries.title: Tree.indent
entries.text: How far each level sits inside its parent, 16 by default. number

entries.title: Tree.value
entries.text: The id of the selected row, "" for none. Constrain it to your own state and override input to own it, or leave it alone and read it back. Selecting a row inside a closed parent leaves the parent closed: open the ancestors through expanded to show it. string

entries.title: Tree.expanded
entries.text: The ids of the open rows. A row whose parent is closed stays hidden whatever this says, and opens again as it was when its parent does. Constrain it and override expandInput to own it, exactly as value with input. array

entries.title: Tree.hasIcons
entries.text: Whether any record, at any depth, carries an icon. Decides whether there is an icon column at all, so that every label in the tree starts on the same line whether or not its own row has an icon. boolean

entries.title: Tree.accessibilityRole
entries.text: tree. none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary

entries.text: The tree's name, "" by default: the use site names it, since only the program knows what the tree holds. string

entries.title: Tree.width
entries.text: 240 by default. The rows are as wide as the tree, so the tree does not size itself to its labels; a label too long for its row ends in an ellipsis. Length

entries.title: Tree.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole tree to the theme's disabledOpacity. number

entries.title: Tree.focusScope
entries.text: stop: the tree is one Tab stop, and focus moves among its rows with the keys above. none | stop | capture | region | modal

entries.title: Tree.datapath
entries.text: Roots the tree on its own shown data, so the rows replicate without the author writing a datapath. datapath

entries.title: Tree.input
entries.text: Where the selection goes, receiving the picked id. The default writes value; override it to own the destination. input(v)

entries.title: Tree.select
entries.text: Selects a row by id, routing through input. What a click, Enter and Space call. select(id)

entries.title: Tree.expandInput
entries.text: Where the open rows go, receiving the whole new list of ids. The default writes expanded; override it to own the destination. expandInput(ids)

entries.title: Tree.isOpen
entries.text: Whether a row is open, by id. isOpen(id)

entries.title: Tree.openRow
entries.text: Opens a row by id, routing through expandInput. Does nothing to a row already open. openRow(id)

entries.title: Tree.closeRow
entries.text: Closes a row by id, routing through expandInput. Its descendants keep their own open state for when it opens again. closeRow(id)

entries.title: Tree.toggle
entries.text: Opens a closed row, closes an open one. What a click on the chevron and a second click on a row call. toggle(id)

entries.title: Tree.flatten
entries.text: The visible rows, in order: the outline walked from the top, descending only into open rows. Each row record wraps its source record (item) and adds what the row shows from the outline — level (1 at the top), hasChildren, open, the parent row's id, and its place among its siblings, pos of size. The tree's own dataset of these rows, re-derived whenever items or expanded changes, is what the TreeRows replicate over; the rows stack flush. flatten(list, open)

entries.title: Tree.anyIcon
entries.text: Whether any record in a list, at any depth, carries an icon. anyIcon(list)

entries.title: Tree.rowAt
entries.text: The row view at a visible index, or null. A handler-only walk — a constraint may not aggregate the view tree. rowAt(i)

entries.title: Tree.rowFor
entries.text: The row view showing an id, or null when that row is not visible. A handler-only walk. rowFor(id)

entries.title: Tree.focusRow
entries.text: Moves focus to a row, and scrolls it into view when the tree scrolls. The keyboard's moves land here. focusRow(v)

entries.title: Tree.focusEntry
entries.text: The row Tab lands on: the selected one when it is visible, else the first. focusEntry()

entries.title: TreeRow
entries.text: One row of a Tree, materialized from the tree's visible rows — never authored directly . It is a Control, so focus lands on the row itself and a screen reader announces it as a tree item, with its level, whether it is open, and whether it is selected. A row is the library's row look: a rounded highlight, controlHovered under the pointer and controlSelected when selected, the label in the theme's text at the menu's size. A row with children leads with a chevron that turns on a spring as it opens and closes, the same turn as an Accordion pane's; a row without one leaves the space blank, so labels at one level line up. App [ width = 280, height = 140, Tree [ x = 20, y = 20, accessibilityLabel = "Mailboxes", expanded = ["in"], items = { [ ({ id: "in", label: "Inbox", children: [ ({ id: "work", label: "Work" }), ({ id: "home", label: "Home" }) ] }), ({ id: "sent", label: "Sent" }) ] } ] ]

entries.title: TreeRow.rowId
entries.text: This row's id, from its record. string

entries.title: TreeRow.level
entries.text: How deep the row sits, 1 at the top. number

entries.title: TreeRow.hasChildren

entries.title: TreeRow.open

entries.title: TreeRow.selected
entries.text: Whether this row is the tree's value. boolean

entries.title: TreeRow.inset
entries.text: Where the row's content begins: its level's indent, plus a small margin. number

entries.title: TreeRow.twist
entries.text: The chevron's angle, in radians, sprung between 0 (open, pointing down) and −π/2 (closed, pointing right), so it turns as the row opens rather than swapping marks. It starts where it belongs, so a row that appears does not turn into place. number

entries.title: TreeRow.ink
entries.text: The label's colour: the theme's text, which stays readable on the selected tint in every theme. Color

entries.title: TreeRow.width
entries.text: As wide as the tree. Length

entries.title: TreeRow.height

entries.title: TreeRow.disabled

entries.title: Splitter
entries.text: The divider between two panes — a mail list and the message beside it, a sidebar and the page — that a person drags to give one pane more room. It is only the divider: you arrange the panes yourself, and the pane before it reads value for its size. Drag it, or Tab to it and use the arrow keys; it keeps value inside min…max either way. App [ width = 600, height = 300, fill = { provided("theme").surface }, row: View [ width = 100%, height = 100%, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x ], side: View [ width = { app.row.split.value }, height = 100%, fill = { provided("theme").background }, Text [ x = 16, y = 16, text = "Mailboxes" ] ], split: Splitter [ value = 200, min = 120, max = 400, accessibilityLabel = "Sidebar width" ], main: View [ width = { app.row.width - app.row.side.width - app.row.split.width }, height = 100%, Text [ x = 16, y = 16, text = "Message" ] ] ] ] At rest it is a hairline in the theme's line; under the pointer, while dragged and while focused from the keyboard it becomes a 2 px line in accent. Its own footprint along the axis is the slim strip a pointer can catch (thickness), with the line centred in it. The same value pattern as every control: standalone it owns value, as above; constrained to your own state it needs input with it — Splitter [ value = { app.sideW }, input(v: number) { app.sideW = v } ].

entries.title: Splitter.value
entries.text: The size of the pane before the divider, in pixels. Standalone the splitter owns it; constrained (value = { app.sideW }) it needs an input override with it, or the drag's own delivery is refused against the constraint. number

entries.title: Splitter.min
entries.text: The smallest value a drag or a key can deliver. number

entries.title: Splitter.max
entries.text: The largest value a drag or a key can deliver. number

entries.title: Splitter.step
entries.text: How far one arrow key moves the divider, in pixels. 10 by default. number

entries.title: Splitter.axis
entries.text: Which way the divider moves: x (the default) is an upright divider between panes side by side, moved left and right; y lies across between panes one above the other, moved up and down. A bare token, as on Divider. Axis

entries.title: Splitter.thickness
entries.text: The strip along axis that catches the pointer — 8 px by default. The line drawn inside it is 1 px at rest and 2 px when active, so a wider strip makes it easier to catch without making it heavier. number

entries.title: Splitter.home
entries.text: The value the splitter had when it was built — what a double-click puts back. number

entries.title: Splitter.saved
entries.text: Where toggle() restores to: the value the pane had when it was collapsed. number

entries.title: Splitter.dragging
entries.text: True from pointer-down until the captured release. pressed will not do here: it goes false when the pointer leaves the strip, and a drag must survive exactly that. boolean

entries.title: Splitter.active
entries.text: Hovered, dragged, or focused from the keyboard — the state the accent line shows. boolean

entries.title: Splitter.accessibilityRole

entries.title: Splitter.accessibilityMax
entries.text: Follows max. number

entries.title: Splitter.height

entries.title: Splitter.cursor
entries.text: col-resize on an upright divider, row-resize on one that lies across. string

entries.title: Splitter.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the divider to the theme's disabledOpacity. number

entries.title: Splitter.input
entries.text: Where the value goes, continuously through a drag and once per key. Override it to redirect the value (input(v: number) { app.sideW = v }); the default writes value. input(v)

entries.title: Splitter.setTo
entries.text: Clamps a value into min…max, rounds it to a whole pixel, and delivers it through input when it differs from value. Every change the splitter makes routes through it. setTo(v)

entries.title: Splitter.toggle
entries.text: Collapses the pane before the divider to min, remembering where it stood; called again from there, it restores that size. What Enter runs. toggle()

entries.title: Splitter.accessibilityIncrement
entries.text: One step larger for the pane before the divider — what Right (or Down) runs, and what a screen reader's increment calls. accessibilityIncrement()

entries.title: Splitter.accessibilityDecrement
entries.text: One step smaller — what Left (or Up) runs. accessibilityDecrement()

entries.title: Splitter.span
entries.text: The length the divider runs across its axis: the parent's content height on an upright divider, its content width on one that lies across. span()

entries.title: Splitter.focusShape
entries.text: Hugs the 2 px line itself, stopping short of the ends so the ring stays inside the panes' edges: on a focused divider the ring reads as a halo around the accent line. focusShape()

entries.title: Splitter.init
entries.text: Records home. An override must call super.onInit(), or a double-click has nothing to restore. onInit()

entries.title: Splitter.pointerDown
entries.text: Claims focus, as every control does, and starts the drag. An override calls super.onPointerDown(e). onPointerDown(e)

entries.title: Splitter.pointerMove
entries.text: Moves the divider by the pointer's root-space movement since the press, so it keeps up with a pointer that has left the strip. An override calls super.onPointerMove(e). onPointerMove(e)

entries.title: Splitter.pointerUp
entries.text: Ends the drag. A drag the browser takes back (e.canceled, a touch that became a scroll) puts the value back where it started. An override calls super.onPointerUp(e): it is what ends the drag. onPointerUp(e)

entries.title: Splitter.click
entries.text: Does nothing: a press on the divider that does not move is not a command. onClick()

entries.title: Splitter.dblClick
entries.text: Restores home, the size the pane was built with. onDblClick()

entries.title: Splitter.keyDown
entries.text: The window-splitter keys: Left and Right (Up and Down on axis = y) move by step through accessibilityDecrement() and accessibilityIncrement(); Home and End go to min and max; Enter runs toggle(). onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: DatePicker
entries.text: A field that shows a date and opens a month to pick one from. Press it — or Enter, Space or Down on it — and a Popover opens below it holding a MonthCalendar, with the focus on the chosen day; picking a day sets it and closes, and the focus goes back to the field. Esc, or a press past it, closes without picking. App [ width = 340, height = 380, due: string = "", DatePicker [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.due }, input(v: string) { app.due = v } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.due == "" ? "no date" : "due " + app.due } ] ] It looks like a Combobox's field: the theme's field fill and line, its height and corners, a chevron at the end. The date shows in the program's language (app.language) at medium length, "Oct 18, 2026".

entries.title: DatePicker.value
entries.text: The chosen day, "YYYY-MM-DD", or "" for none. Constrain it to your own state and override input beside it, or leave it and read it back. string

entries.title: DatePicker.min

entries.title: DatePicker.max
entries.text: The last day that can be picked; "" for no limit. string

entries.title: DatePicker.weekStart

entries.title: DatePicker.placeholder
entries.text: What the field shows with no date, "Select a date" by default. string

entries.title: DatePicker.display
entries.text: The date as the field shows it, or "" with none. string

entries.title: DatePicker.edge
entries.text: The picker's edge colour: the theme's error while it says what is wrong, the accent while its calendar is open, else the line colour. Color

entries.title: DatePicker.keyDown

entries.title: MonthCalendar
entries.text: A month of days to pick one from: the month and year with buttons to the months either side, a row of weekday initials, and six weeks of days. Days of the months either side fill the first and last weeks, in muted ink, and pressing one picks it and shows its month. Today wears a ring; the chosen day is filled. Its value is a date as an ISO string, "YYYY-MM-DD", or "" for none — the value pattern, as every control has it: standalone it keeps its own, constrained it delivers through input. App [ width = 300, height = 340, day: string = "2026-10-18", MonthCalendar [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.day }, min = "2026-10-05", input(v: string) { app.day = v } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 310, text = { app.day } ] ] The days are one Tab stop, as a screen reader's grid: Tab lands on the chosen day, else today, else the 1st. The arrows move a day left and right and a week up and down, into the next or previous month when they cross its edge; Page Up and Page Down move a month (with Shift, a year); Home and End go to the start and end of the week; Enter or Space picks. The month buttons are Tab stops of their own, before the days. Names come from the program's language (app.language): the month, the weekday initials, and each day's full date, which is what a screen reader says on it.

entries.title: MonthCalendar.value
entries.text: The chosen day, "YYYY-MM-DD", or "" for none. Constrain it to your own state and override input beside it, or leave it and read it back. string

entries.title: MonthCalendar.min
entries.text: The first day that can be picked, "YYYY-MM-DD"; days before it are disabled. "" for no limit. string

entries.title: MonthCalendar.max
entries.text: The last day that can be picked; days after it are disabled. "" for no limit. string

entries.title: MonthCalendar.weekStart
entries.text: The day a week starts on: 0 Sunday (the default), 1 Monday, and so on. number

entries.title: MonthCalendar.daySize
entries.text: The width and height of a day, 32 by default. number

entries.title: MonthCalendar.today
entries.text: Today, "YYYY-MM-DD", from the calendar's own clock, so it turns over at midnight. string

entries.title: MonthCalendar.shownMonth
entries.text: The month on screen, "YYYY-MM": the value's month, else today's, until the month buttons, the keys or a pick move it. Set it to show another month. string

entries.title: MonthCalendar.title
entries.text: The shown month and year as the language writes them, "October 2026" — the header's text and the name of the grid. string

entries.title: MonthCalendar.gridW
entries.text: The width of seven days, which the header and the weekday row share. number

entries.title: MonthCalendar.width
entries.text: The width of seven days. Length

entries.title: MonthCalendar.input
entries.text: Where a pick goes, receiving the day. The default writes value. input(v)

entries.title: MonthCalendar.pad2
entries.text: A number as two digits. pad2(n)

entries.title: MonthCalendar.isoOfDate

entries.title: MonthCalendar.addMonths

entries.title: MonthCalendar.clamp
entries.text: A day moved inside min and max. clamp(iso)

entries.title: MonthCalendar.weeks
entries.text: The six weeks on screen, as records — each day's iso, its day of the month, whether it is inMonth, today, selected or disabled, and its full name — the data the grid replicates. weeks()

entries.title: MonthCalendar.weekdayNames
entries.text: The seven weekday initials, from weekStart. weekdayNames()

entries.title: MonthCalendar.step
entries.text: Shows the month n months on. step(n)

entries.title: MonthCalendar.pick
entries.text: Picks a day: shows its month and delivers it through input. pick(iso)

entries.title: MonthCalendar.entryDay
entries.text: The day Tab lands on in the shown month: the chosen day, else today, else the 1st — kept inside min and max. entryDay()

entries.title: MonthCalendar.cellFor

entries.title: MonthCalendar.go
entries.text: Answers a key on a day: works out the day it moves to, shows that day's month, and moves the focus to it once the month is on screen. False for a key it does not move by. go(from, e)

entries.title: MonthCalendar.moveTo
entries.text: Shows a day's month and moves the focus to the day. moveTo(iso)

entries.title: Disclosure
entries.text: A section that opens and closes under a line that names it — "Advanced options", "Show details". Press the line and the section slides open below it, its chevron turning as it goes; press again and it slides shut. Accordion is a stack of these that keeps one open; a Disclosure stands alone, and any number may be open. The content is the disclosure's ordinary children, present through the whole slide and carried by the disclosure's clip, exactly as an Accordion's AccordionPane carries its own: App [ width = 320, height = 200, Disclosure [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 280, label = "Advanced options", Checkbox [ label = "Keep a log" ], Checkbox [ label = "Check for updates" ] ] ] To a screen reader the line is a button that says whether it is expanded; Tab reaches the content only while it is open.

entries.title: Disclosure.label
entries.text: The line's text, and the section's name. string

entries.title: Disclosure.detail
entries.text: A summary of what the section holds, set at the line's right end — "3 set", "12 files" — so it reads whether the section is open or shut. Empty, the default, shows nothing. string

entries.title: Disclosure.open
entries.text: Whether the section is open. Constrain it to your own state and override input to own the destination, or leave it alone and read it back. boolean

entries.title: Disclosure.twist
entries.text: The chevron's angle, in radians, sprung between −π/2 (closed) and 0 (open), so it turns in step with the slide. number

entries.title: Disclosure.clip
entries.text: The section is carried by this clip while it slides: present the whole way, revealed and concealed by the disclosure's own height. ClipPath

entries.title: Disclosure.defaultPlacement

entries.title: Stepper
entries.text: A number you change a step at a time — a quantity, a font size, a count of copies. It shows the value between a − and a + on the same rounded track a Segmented sits on, and is one Tab stop: App [ width = 300, height = 100, copies: number = 2, Stepper [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.copies }, min = 1, max = 99, accessibilityLabel = "Copies", input(v: number) { app.copies = v } ], Text [ x = 160, y = 26, text = { app.copies + " copies" } ] ] From the keyboard, Up and Down step it, Page Up and Page Down move ten steps, and Home and End go to min and max. To a screen reader it is a spin button, named at its use site, saying its value and range; its adjust gesture steps it the same way. − and + are for the pointer, and dim at the ends of the range.

entries.title: Toolbar
entries.text: A row of commands that is one Tab stop — a text editor's Bold, Italic and Underline, a drawing app's tools. Tab lands on its first command (or the one last used), the arrows move along the row, Home and End go to its ends, and the next Tab leaves it, so a long row of commands costs one stop. It sits on the same rounded track a Segmented does, its ToolButtons quiet until hovered: use [ PlusIcon, MinusIcon ] App [ width = 360, height = 100, bold: boolean = false, italic: boolean = false, Toolbar [ x = 20, y = 20, accessibilityLabel = "Formatting", ToolButton [ label = "B", toggle = true, on = { app.bold }, input(v: boolean) { app.bold = v }, accessibilityLabel = "Bold" ], ToolButton [ label = "I", toggle = true, on = { app.italic }, input(v: boolean) { app.italic = v }, accessibilityLabel = "Italic" ], ToolbarDivider [ ], ToolButton [ icon = "PlusIcon", label = "Add" ], ToolButton [ icon = "MinusIcon", label = "Remove" ] ] ] Its children are yours: ToolButtons, a ToolbarDivider between groups, or any control — a Segmented, a Stepper — which the arrows reach like the rest. To a screen reader it is a toolbar, named at its use site.

entries.title: Breadcrumb
entries.text: The path to where you are — Home › Guide › Layout — each step a way back up. The steps are records, outermost first; the last is where you are, shown in the stronger ink and not pressable. A step with a location is a real link (⌘-click, copy link, the crawler); one without is a button that hands its id to input: App [ width = 400, height = 80, at: string = "layout", Breadcrumb [ x = 20, y = 20, items = { [ ({ id: "home", label: "Home" }), ({ id: "guide", label: "Guide" }), ({ id: "layout", label: "Layout" }) ] }, input(id: string) { app.at = id } ] ] To a screen reader it is a navigation landmark named "Breadcrumb", its steps links or buttons, the last one the current page.
