entries.title: Form
entries.text: The place a set of fields is submitted from. The controls inside it — every TextInput and ValueControl that exists and is not disabled — join it by being inside it; there is nothing to register. It holds no values: they live wherever the program keeps them (the App, a model class, a dataset). It knows what is wrong, says so on submit, sends, and carries a service's refusals back to the fields they name. App [ width = 360, height = 240, fill = white, email: string = "", signIn: Form [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 12 ], Field [ label = "Email", stacked = true, TextInput [ width = 300, name = "email", purpose = email, required = "Enter your email address.", text = { app.email }, onInput(v: string) { app.email = v }, validate(v: string) -> string { return v.includes("@") ? "" : "Enter an email address like name@example.com." } ] ], Button [ label = "Sign in", primary = true, onClick() { parent.submit() } ], send() { app.email = "" } ] ] The normal case sends to a service. Give the form its source — the DataSource that sends — and submit() judges every member, sends when nothing is wrong, keeps pending while the request is out, and reads a refusal's body back onto the members by name. A message that names no member becomes the form's error. The source's own onLoad is where a success goes on, as ever. A form with no service leaves source out and says what sending is: send() runs when submit() finds nothing wrong, and the program saves however it likes there — to a Dataset, a file, the host page (the example above). An outside check (a name already taken in local data) is said with refuse. Slow work there sets pending itself while it runs. Membership is the form's subtree, with three edges: an overlay (a Sheet, Dialog, Popover) is a boundary: a control in it belongs to a Form inside the overlay, not to one around the place it is declared. A control set apart on purpose names its form: form = { app.payment }; a control inside another control is part of it: a Combobox's entry field belongs to the combobox, which is the member; a member that is not shown (it, or a view above it, has visible = false) or is disabled does not count: it is not judged, and its problems hold nothing up.

entries.title: Form.source
entries.text: The DataSource the form sends — a write: method = "POST", its body built from the program's values. pending follows the request the form sent; when the service refuses, its errorBody goes through refusal onto the members. Leave it null to send another way (send()). DataSource?

entries.title: Form.failedMessage
entries.text: What error says when the request failed with nothing readable — no reply at all, or a reply that is not a refusal. Say it in the program's own words. string

entries.title: Form.members
entries.text: The controls in the form, counted or not. Kept by the controls themselves. any[]

entries.title: Form.problems
entries.text: Every counted member's current problem, in reading order: { name, message, control } each. It does not wait for judging, so it is the fact a summary, a banner or a count is built on. FormProblem[]

entries.title: Form.enterMoves
entries.text: Return in a single-line field takes the person to the next field — in reading order, among the fields that count — and submits from the last; an on-screen keyboard's Return key says "Next" on the way and "Go" on the last. Off (the default), Return submits from any field, as on the web. A field that declares its own onEnter decides for itself. boolean

entries.title: Form.valid
entries.text: Whether nothing is wrong: no member has a problem and validate() is satisfied. boolean

entries.title: Form.error
entries.text: The message that belongs to no field: a refusal that names none (an account locked), a name no counted member has, the form's own validate() on submit, or failedMessage when the request failed without a readable reply. Shown wherever the program places it. string

entries.title: Form.submitted
entries.text: Whether submit() has been tried since the last success. A presentation that shows nothing until a submit reads it. boolean

entries.title: Form.pending
entries.text: True while the request the form sent is out; submit() does nothing meanwhile. A form with no source sets it itself around slow work in send(), and back to false when the work is done. Keep the Submit button focusable while pending (say so in its label); submit() already ignores the press, so a form sends once with no flag of your own — a sending beside pending is a second copy of it. boolean

entries.title: Form.next
entries.text: next(from) takes the focus from a field to the next one that counts, in reading order, or submits the form when from is the last. What Return does under enterMoves; a field's own onEnter may call it. next(from)

entries.title: Form.validate
entries.text: The form's own rule, for what belongs to no one field — return "" when it is fine, or the sentence. A rule that does belong to a field goes on that field (validate there may read any other value). validate()

entries.title: Form.submit
entries.text: Judges every member now, so every problem shows at once, each under its own field — fields the person never reached and fields autofill filled without focusing included. Withdraws the last refusals. If anything is wrong, showProblems(); otherwise send(). Does nothing while pending. Return in a single-line TextInput inside the form calls it (or moves on, under enterMoves), unless the field declares an onEnter of its own. submit()

entries.title: Form.send
entries.text: What submit() does when nothing is wrong. By default it sends source (and does nothing when there is none). A form with no service overrides it to save its own way; one with a source that also wants to do something first calls super.send() after. A send of the program's own has succeeded when it refused nothing — once pending is false, if it set it — and the fields are then judged afresh, so a field emptied for the next entry says nothing. send()

entries.title: Form.showProblems
entries.text: What submit does when something is wrong. By default: when more than one field has a problem, it announces how many; it takes the focus to the first (in reading order), whose own message a screen reader then hears; a form-level error is announced. Override it to focus a summary of your own, scroll, or stay silent. showProblems()

entries.title: Form.refusedWith
entries.text: refusedWith(body) is the program's own reaction when the service refuses, given the body: undo a reservation the refusal names, empty a field the service will not take again. The order is fixed: the refusal is laid on the members first (each named field's refused, the rest in error), then refusedWith runs, then showProblems() — so what it changes is what the person is then shown. refusedWith(body)

entries.title: Form.refuse
entries.text: refuse(problems) lays problems on the form from anywhere: each { name, message } lands on the counted member of that name as its refused, and the rest become error. A refusal reaches it from source by itself; a service that answers success with errors in the body (GraphQL does) calls it from the source's onLoad. refuse(list)

entries.title: Form.refusal
entries.text: refusal(body) reads a refusal's body into problems. It understands one field ({ "field", "message" }), a list ({ "errors": [ … ] } with field, path, a JSON pointer or JSON:API's source.pointer, and message, detail or title), and a bare { "message" }, which names no field. A pointer is read as a dotted name (#/address/city is address.city) and matched exactly. Override it to map a service's own shape, its codes to the program's sentences, or another language. refusal(body)

entries.title: ValueControl
entries.text: The base of a control that holds a value a person sets — a checkbox, a switch, a choice of one, a date, a number — and so can be checked, required, refused by a service, and gathered into a Form. It is a Control (focus, keyboard, disabled) with the words a field needs, the same words a TextInput has: required, validate(v) and refused say what can be wrong; problem is what is wrong now, valid that nothing is, and error is problem once the control has been judged — left, judge()d, or submitted with its form; name is its address in its form: the key a service names it by. A concrete control says what its value is by setting fieldValue (a Checkbox's is checked, a Combobox's its value), and when that counts as empty by empty if the default does not fit. Extend it for a value control of your own: class Rating extends ValueControl [ width = 120, height = 24, stars: number = 0, fieldValue = { stars }, empty = { stars == 0 }, input(v: number) { stars = v }, press() { input(stars % 5 + 1) }, TextLabel [ text = { "★".repeat(classroot.stars) + "☆".repeat(5 - classroot.stars) } ] ] App [ Rating [ x = 20, y = 20, required = "Rate your stay." ] ] A control inside another control is part of it, not a member of a form of its own: the entry field of a Combobox belongs to the combobox, which is the member.

entries.title: ValueControl.name
entries.text: The control's address in its form — the key a service names it by when it refuses a value ({ "field": "country", "message": "…" }). A path is allowed ("address.country"). It is independent of the control's name in the view tree; leave it empty for a control no service names. string

entries.title: ValueControl.required
entries.text: true, or the message to say, when the control may not be left empty: required = "Choose the country.". Empty is what empty says. With true the message is "Required"; say a message of your own wherever a person will read it. Screen readers hear the control as required either way. boolean | string

entries.title: ValueControl.judgeOn
entries.text: When error first says what is wrong: leave (the default) once the control has been left, edit at every moment. JudgeOn

entries.title: ValueControl.judged
entries.text: Whether the control has been judged: left, judge()d, or submitted with its form. Writable: set it back to false for a fresh try (a security code emptied after a decline). boolean

entries.title: ValueControl.fieldValue
entries.text: The value the rules judge: validate(v) receives it, required asks whether it is empty, and a refusal is said of it. Each concrete control sets it from its own value. any

entries.title: ValueControl.empty
entries.text: Whether fieldValue counts as empty for required: blank(fieldValue) by default. A control whose empty is something else says so (a rating of 0). boolean

entries.title: ValueControl.refused
entries.text: An outside message about the value — usually a service's refusal, laid here by a form's refuse or the control's own refuse(message). It is the control's problem while the value is the one refused, and stops counting when the value changes. string

entries.title: ValueControl.problem
entries.text: What is wrong with the value now, whatever has been judged: the refusal, then required, then validate. Empty when nothing is. The fact any presentation can be built on; a Form lists its members' problems. string

entries.title: ValueControl.valid
entries.text: Whether problem is empty. boolean

entries.title: ValueControl.error
entries.text: problem once the control is judged, else empty — the default display rule, and what a Field shows under the control and a screen reader hears with it. Under judgeOn = edit it is problem at every moment. string

entries.title: ValueControl.form
entries.text: The form the control belongs to: the nearest Form above it, unless set — set it (form = { app.payment }) for a control that sits outside its form's views, as in a sheet of its own. any

entries.title: ValueControl.accessibilityError
entries.text: Follows error: the control is invalid to a screen reader while it says something. string

entries.title: ValueControl.accessibilityRequired
entries.text: Follows required. boolean

entries.title: ValueControl.blank
entries.text: blank(v): null, "", false or an empty list. blank(v)

entries.title: ValueControl.validate
entries.text: The control's own rule: given the value, return "" when it is fine, or the sentence that says what is wrong. It runs when required is met, and it is reactive — a rule that reads another value (app.form.country) judges again when that value changes. validate(v)

entries.title: ValueControl.refuse
entries.text: refuse(message) says an outside message about the current value (see refused); "" withdraws it. refuse(message)

entries.title: ValueControl.judge
entries.text: Judges the control now, as leaving it would. judge()

entries.title: ValueControl.focusField
entries.text: Puts the focus where a person fixes this control's value — the control itself, or its entry field when it has one. A form calls it to take the person to a problem. focusField()

entries.title: ValueControl.retire
entries.text: A control that goes leaves its form and its Field. An override calls super.onRetire(). onRetire()

entries.title: FieldLayout
entries.text: How a Field arranges what it holds: the caption in its column beside the control, or above it when the field is stacked; the control, or a row of them; and the message under the control, as wide as what it holds. A Field makes its own; nothing else needs one. App [ fill = white, Field [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Name", stacked = true, TextInput [ width = 220, required = "Enter your name." ] ] ]

entries.title: FieldLayout.place
entries.text: place()

entries.title: Cupertino
entries.text: The compact-desktop record — a preset is data riding one machinery, never a code path: Cupertino metrics — compact controls, 6px radii, the tight hairline focus halo hugging the control (gap 0), a muted disabled treatment. A Mac control does not answer a passing pointer, so the hover tones equal the rest tones (controlHovered, accentHovered); pressing darkens a control in light and lightens it in dark. The type stack (the platform UI face via -apple-system) is the consuming app's fontFamily, not a theme token.

entries.title: CupertinoDark
entries.text: The dark half of Cupertino: the same tokens, with values for a dark ground. Everything said there applies; provide this record where the app is dark, or let AppearanceSwitch choose between the two.

entries.title: ThemeDefaults
entries.text: The value every optional library token takes when the theme in force does not state it. The runtime lays any provided theme over this record, so a library class reads provided("theme").segmentedHeight and always gets a number: a theme states only what it changes, and no read site carries a fallback of its own. The required tokens — the palette (accent, surface, text, line, control and their states) and controlCornerRadius, focusRingStyle — are not here: a missing colour is an error to see, never a light default under a dark theme. A token whose natural default is another token (trackFill is control unless a theme says otherwise) has no value here; its reader says so with ??. One that no preset states is listed as null all the same, so every token a theme can carry is declared somewhere and reading one that is not is a compile error. This record is not a preset: no program names it.

entries.title: MountainView
entries.text: The Material 3 record: pill buttons (buttonCornerRadius saturates at half the height), square-ish fields, the grow-on-check switch thumb (switchThumbOffSize < the checked size), the bar-handle slider with its track gap, M3's 38% disabled opacity, and the offset focus indicator (width 3, gap 2). Hover and pressed on the accent are Material's state layers: the button's ink over its fill at 8% and 16%. Roboto is the consuming app's fontFamily.

entries.title: MountainViewDark
entries.text: The dark half of MountainView: the same tokens, with values for a dark ground. Everything said there applies; provide this record where the app is dark, or let AppearanceSwitch choose between the two.

entries.title: Redmond
entries.text: The Fluent-fidelity record (Windows 11): 4px radii on everything, the Windows accent blue (light-on-dark flips to the pale #4CC2FF with dark text on it), compact 32px buttons, the 40×20 toggle with its 12px off-thumb, the round slider grabber with the accent dot (sliderHandleStyle = "dot"), and Fluent's two-tone focus rectangle — a 2px outer stroke over a 1px inner separator (focusRingInnerWidth), black over white in light, white over black in dark. Windows focus does not fly: focusRingStyle = "rest" — the indicator appears in place and stays. An accent button's hover and pressed tones are Fluent's secondary and tertiary accent fills — the accent at 90% and 80% over the page. Segoe UI is the consuming app's fontFamily, not a theme token.

entries.title: RedmondDark
entries.text: The dark half of Redmond: the same tokens, with values for a dark ground. Everything said there applies; provide this record where the app is dark, or let AppearanceSwitch choose between the two.

entries.title: SanFrancisco
entries.text: Declare's own look — named for where Declare is made — and the theme a widget renders when nothing provides one: control.declare defaults theme to SanFrancisco (the light record), so an app that never mentions a theme is San Francisco light, always. These declarations are the preset itself, written in the language; the runtime serves them by name. A record is complete, not a delta: every token the standard library consults is stated, so a preset reads whole with nothing to chase. A control's hover and pressed step darker in light and lighter in dark. The accent steps darker in both: it is the fill behind white labels, which a lighter blue would wash out. Links are blue on the page itself, so they take their own linkColor, lighter than the accent in dark.

entries.title: SanFranciscoDark
entries.text: The dark half of SanFrancisco: the same tokens, with values for a dark ground. Everything said there applies; provide this record where the app is dark, or let AppearanceSwitch choose between the two.

entries.title: boot
entries.text: Runs a Declare program in this page: fetches or compiles it, builds the app, mounts it in options.host (or the whole page), and resolves to the page's Tenant handle on it — null if it could not come up, after showing why. import boot from "/declare/bundles/declare-boot.js".

entries.title: boot.main
entries.text: The program's .declare file, relative to the page — or its directory, for a program kept as a directory. Its own relative addresses (images, data) resolve beside it. string

entries.title: boot.host
entries.text: The element the app fills, marked data-declare-embed. The app then leaves the page's title, URL, history, scroll and keys alone. Without it the app takes the whole page (the element with id host). Several apps on one page each take their own element. HTMLElement (optional)

entries.title: boot.provides
entries.text: Values the program reads with hostProvided(name, default), there from its very first evaluation. A data-declare-provide JSON attribute on the element does the same; these win over it. Later changes go through Tenant.provide. Record<string, unknown> (optional)

entries.title: boot.onPost
entries.text: Hears the program's app.postToHost(topic, payload). Without it, such a message is dropped with a console note. (message: IslandMessage) => void (optional)

entries.title: boot.onNavigate
entries.text: Carries out every link the program follows out of itself (app.navigate) and every window it opens (app.openWindow). It runs synchronously inside the click, so it may open a window itself. Without it, the browser does: the page navigates, or a new window opens. (navigation: IslandNavigation) => void (optional)

entries.title: boot.location
entries.text: The program's starting location — what its app.location reads before anything moves it. A whole-page app takes the URL's fragment first. string (optional)

entries.title: boot.backend
entries.text: The renderer, when the page chooses: "DomBackend" or "CanvasBackend". Otherwise the address's ?render= decides, then the program's own default. "DomBackend" | "CanvasBackend" (optional)

entries.title: observe
entries.text: Watches a value out of a running program: read is called under tracking, and onChange runs with its result once per settle in which that changed. Returns the unwatch. import boot, { observe } from "/declare/bundles/declare-boot.js".

entries.title: Tenant
entries.text: The page's handle on a program it booted: what boot() resolves to, and what the host element carries as el.__declareTenant. It speaks to the program in an island's words — values down and up, and messages both ways.

entries.title: Tenant.app
entries.text: The App itself, for reading and writing its attributes from page script (tenant.app.hue = 120), and for observe. Under the GPU renderer it is a stand-in that relays reads and writes to the program's worker. any

entries.title: Tenant.post
entries.text: Sends the program a message: it arrives as onHostMessage({ topic, payload }) on its App. post(topic: string, payload?: unknown)

entries.title: Tenant.provide
entries.text: Changes a value the program reads with hostProvided(name, default); every reader re-derives. undefined withdraws it, and readers fall back to their defaults. provide(name: string, value: unknown)

entries.title: Tenant.exposed
entries.text: Reads a value the program offers up — one its App lists in exposes — or dflt when it offers no such name. Tracked, so observe(() => tenant.exposed("total", 0), cb) follows it. exposed<T>(name: string, dflt?: T)

entries.title: IslandHandle
entries.text: The handle foreign content inside a DOMIsland uses to reach the program around it — the island element's el.__declareIsland, there once the island has mounted. It reaches what a Declare tenant reaches; its verbs keep the island's own names.

entries.title: IslandHandle.provides
entries.text: The names the island offers down, from its provides list. provides()

entries.title: IslandHandle.hostProvided
entries.text: The value the island provides under name now, or undefined when it does not list the name. hostProvided(name: string)

entries.title: IslandHandle.watchProvided
entries.text: A standing watch over a provided value: callback runs now with the value, then at the close of every settle that changed it. Returns the unwatch. watchProvided(name: string, callback: (value: unknown) => void)

entries.title: IslandHandle.expose
entries.text: Offers a value up: the program reads it with the island's exposed(name, default), whose default's kind the value must match. undefined withdraws it. expose(name: string, value: unknown)

entries.title: IslandHandle.post
entries.text: Sends the program a message: it arrives as the island's onPost({ topic, payload }). post(topic: string, payload?: unknown)

entries.title: IslandHandle.onPost
entries.text: Hears the island's post(topic, payload). Returns the unsubscribe. onPost(callback: (message: IslandMessage) => void)

entries.title: App [ … ]
entries.text: App root instance the root program root one root A program is one tree, and App [ … ] is its root — one per program. With width and height unset it fills its host, which is the common case: the page, the window, the island it is mounted in. Everything else nests inside its brackets, and app (lower case) names the running instance from any depth — which makes it the place for the few values the whole app shares, such as the current selection or a mode. Any instance may declare its own members, the App included — attributes, methods, handlers, children — with no class at all; the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass. The top-level forms (class, include, use, script, style, theme, schema, ship, defaultFlags) may come before or after it, in any order. Records belong in a Dataset, and state that is a thing in its own right in a model class (a class with no extends) — the App is not meant to hold every value. App [ members ] One root, one program. A second `App [ … ]` is not a second window; it is a syntax error at the point the first program ended. A program without a root is not a program — a file of classes alone has nothing to run. `classroot` has no meaning on the App: it names the root of a *class* you define. From the App, reach values by a bare name, `this`, or `app`.

entries.title: Type [ … ]
entries.text: [ ] brackets square brackets instance instantiate component instance members Square brackets hold a node's members — attributes, declarations, methods, handlers, children — and the nesting of brackets is the tree. Naming a type with a bracketed body instantiates it: Text [ text = "OK" ] is a Text, bg: View [ … ] a View reachable as bg. Every member inside is one of the five shapes (set, declare, child, method, handler), separated by commas. An instance is a full node in its own right: it may declare new attributes and methods without a class, because the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass for it. Name a class when you instantiate it more than once or need to name its type — or when a long instance declaration makes its parent hard to read, so pulling it out (possibly into its own file) keeps the program's structure visible. Type [ members ] name: Type [ members ] A type must exist: a built-in, a library class, or a class this program declares or includes. Members are separated by commas; the compiler names the spot when one is missing. A trailing comma before `]` is legal, and the formatter removes it. Members share one namespace: a child cannot take an attribute's name, and two children cannot share one. A second child with the same name is refused, and the message says where the first is.

entries.title: class
entries.text: class declare a class define a component component definition This is the one way to define a class. Everything inside the brackets is a member: name = value sets an attribute the base already has, name: Type = value declares a new one, name: Type [ … ] is a named child, name() { … } a method, onThing() { … } a handler for an event the node fires. Instantiate the class by naming it with a [ ] body, as many times as you like; each instance may set any attribute and add members of its own. A class is not a file and not a module. It is a top-level declaration, and a program is one tree of them — include merges another file's classes into the same program, and there is nothing to export. Any instance may declare members with no class at all, because the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass. Name a class when you instantiate it more than once or need to name its type, or when pulling a long instance out keeps its parent readable. With no extends, the base is View: a class that draws. A class with no view names its base: extends Node, or extends Dataset for a document. class Name [ members ] // a view class Name extends Base [ members ] // any other base A class extends a library class or one declared in this program — declared anywhere in it, later in the file included. Omit `extends` and the base is `View`. A class may not contain itself, directly or through another class: the tree it describes would never finish. One name, one class. A second declaration of the same name is refused, and so is a class named like a built-in. `children` is a structural member of every View and cannot be a class's own member. A bare `name = value` sets an attribute the base has; an attribute the base does not have must be **declared**, with a type — `name: Type = value`. A class is instantiated where its base fits: a `layout:` member takes a Layout, a view's place a View.

entries.title: extends
entries.text: extends subclass inherit base class inheritance Single inheritance from another class — a library class or one of your own. The subclass sees every attribute, child, method, and event of the base. Re-stating an attribute with name = value overrides its default; re-stating a method replaces it; and a base's named child is reached by name, not redeclared. Omit extends altogether and the base is Node — a model class with no box. extends is not a top-level form in its own right: it is part of a class declaration. The base may be declared later in the file, or in an included one. Any concrete built-in is a base — View, Node, Layout and TweenLayout, Dataset, Spring, Keys, State and the rest — as is any class descending from one; only the abstract bases (Stream, Media) are refused. class Name extends Base [ … ] The base must be a class: a built-in or a declared one. Any built-in class is a base — View, Layout, Node, Dataset, Spring, Keys, State alike; only an abstract base (Stream, Media), which no runtime class implements, is refused. A subclass may not take a built-in's name.

entries.title: <Class/>
entries.text: inline view inline views view in text view in a sentence view in prose chip in text widget in text component in markdown inline-block tag in content Inside rich-text content, a self-closing tag whose name is a view class the program declares is one real view of that class, placed in the flowing line as an atomic box the words wrap around. There is no whitelist to extend and no attribute to set: the class existing is what makes the tag mean it, matched by the name exactly as written, in both formats (HTMLText's html and Markdown's text). A tag naming no class of yours keeps the meaning it already had — the HTML whitelist, an autolink, a literal < — and a <span class> stays a style, never a view. The tag's attributes are the class's, each converted from its string by the attribute's declared type, exactly as a source literal is: id='142' is the number in a number attribute, tint='#DDF4E4' a Color, align='center' an enum member, width='50%' a percent of the width the text flows in, a bare open is true. The tag is the use site, so an attribute takes use-site precedence over what the class body sets for that attribute — a literal or a { } constraint — and only the winner installs; an attribute the tag does not mention keeps the class's own behaviour. x/y are refused — the flow places the view, as a layout places its children — and an unknown attribute, a value that will not convert, a read-only attribute, or a percent on an attribute with no axis goes to the class's unsupported policy. The view owns its width/height while the flow owns its x/y, it never splits across a line, a taller one grows its line, a size change re-flows the text, and it reads the surrounding run's text face as provided values. Content is reactive: a tag still present keeps its view and its state, with only changed attributes rewritten (a tag that gains or loses an attribute is built again, since what it claims is settled at build), and key='…' fixes that identity when the order moves. Markup carries no expressions, so a live value is either concatenated into the content (with escapeHtml around every interpolated value) or derived inside the class from an identity the content names. HTMLText [ html = "Filed under <Chip label='docs'/> today." ] Markdown [ text = "Fixed by <Issue id='142'/>." ] <Chip key='a' label='docs'/> // key: this view's identity across a content change Placement belongs to the flow, so a tag may not set `x` or `y`. A tag names attributes the class actually has; anything else goes to `unsupported`. An inline view is self-closing: a tag with content between it and a closing tag is not one. A percent needs an axis to resolve against, so it belongs on a width or a height. A read-only attribute is computed from its declaration, so no tag may set it.

entries.title: name = value
entries.text: set an attribute assignment attribute value equals bare value Sets an attribute the class already has. The right-hand side is one of three things, and the spelling says which: a bare literal (a number, a percent, a color, a string, a keyword — set once), a { } constraint (TypeScript that stays true), or a :path read from bound data. A bare [ … ] list fills an array-typed attribute. One family of names may be set on a node that does not declare them: the built-in provided values — the text face (fontSize, fontFamily, fontWeight, textColor, letterSpacing), theme, iconSize, and the rich-text attributes. Setting one on a container provides it to every descendant that reads it (see provided). A set attribute with a { } is owned by its constraint: the runtime keeps it current, and a direct write to it is refused with a message naming the fix — derived state is never assigned; change its inputs. In a handler, name = value is the setter: the write lands when the handler returns, together with every other write it made, in one settle. name = literal name = { expression } name = :path The attribute must exist on the class — to introduce a new one, declare it with a type. A bare value must be of the attribute's kind; the message names the vocabulary it takes. A `script { }` constant is not a bare literal — reach it through braces. A list belongs to an array-typed attribute; a scalar one refuses it.

entries.title: name: Type = value
entries.text: declare an attribute new attribute reactive attribute colon type typed attribute Declares a new reactive attribute — the way state enters a program. The type is a TypeScript type, the same vocabulary a signature uses: TypeScript's built-ins (number, string, Map<string, Row>), Declare's own (Color, Length, Radius), a class, a declared schema, a literal union ("open" "closed"), an array, a tuple, or a function type. The default is a bare literal or a { } expression. A declaration's { } default is only a formula: reading it inlines the expression, and an assignment simply replaces it — the right tool for a value you may take over later, which is how TextInput.initial differs from its read-only text = { … } twin. Compare set: a set attribute is owned by its { } and refuses assignment. name: Type = value name: Type // no default: undefined until written rows: Row[] = [] panel: Menu? = null // a class — the attribute holds an instance A declaration carries a type; the colon is not optional. The type must be one the program can name; the message says where types come from. An attribute the class already has is set, not declared again. A built-in read-only intrinsic (`hovered`, `pressed`, `dark`, …) is computed for you and cannot be shadowed by a declaration.

entries.title: name: Type [ … ]
entries.text: child named child anonymous child nested view subview A child is a member that is itself an instance. Named, it is reachable from its siblings and its class as name; anonymous, it is placed and painted but never addressed. Children paint in declaration order — later siblings on top; there is no z-index — and a parent with a layout: member arranges them, while one without positions them by their own x/y. A child is also how anything that is not a view joins the tree: a Dataset, a Spring, a Keys or Focus service, a stream. A source of events is a child, so it lives and dies with the node that declares it; there is nothing to subscribe to and nothing to unregister. name: Type [ members ] Type [ members ] // anonymous A child may not take an attribute's name — members share one namespace. Two children cannot share a name. A child cannot be named after a scope noun.

entries.title: name(a: T) -> R { … }
entries.text: method function member call define a method method signature A method is a typed signature, name first, and a statement body. Every parameter carries a written type — a primitive, a class, an event payload, a function type (f: (id: string) -> void), or an array of one; a ? after the type says the value may be absent, and the body must check. Omit -> R for a method that returns nothing. A method runs when called; an attribute stays true. A computed value is therefore not a method but a declaration with a { } default. A constraint that calls a method stays live through it: every read inside the method is a wired dependency, rebased onto what you passed — which is the difference between a method and a script { } function, whose body the compiler never reads. name() { statements } name(v: number, c: Menu?) -> string { statements } Parameters are typed; a bare name has no type. An attribute's value is one expression; statements live in methods.

entries.title: onEvent(e: Payload) { … }
entries.text: handler event handler onClick on event events A handler is a method named on + an event this node fires — onClick, onPointerMove, onInit, onKeyDown — and it is a method in every respect: a subclass's onInit replaces its base's, and reaches it with super.onInit() when it wants the base's to run. The payload, when there is one, is typed by the event, and the compiler names the type when you write the wrong one. Handlers only assign attributes; every constraint that reads those attributes follows, which is the whole update model. The on prefix is a convention: a method so named that answers no event of its node is an ordinary method, and the compiler warns, naming the handler when the name is one slip from it. Nothing bubbles. A handler runs on the node that declares it, for events that node fires; a parent that wants a child's click declares the handler on the child (or the child calls up through parent or classroot). Events from outside the tree come through a member you declare — a Keys [ onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) { … } ] gives a node app-wide keyboard handling. onClick() { statements } onPointerMove(e: PointerEvent) { statements } The pointer's handlers are `onPointer…`, one for a mouse and a fingertip alike. The payload's type is the event's.

entries.title: super.name(…)
entries.text: super base method call the base override overriding a method parent class method inherited method A method a subclass declares replaces the base's method of the same name, handlers included. super.name(args) calls the one it replaced: the nearest method of that name beneath the body in the extends chain. It is an ordinary call, so the body decides where it goes — before its own work, after it, in the middle, conditionally, or not at all — and passes whatever arguments it likes. Inside the base's method, this is still the instance, so the base's own calls reach the subclass's overrides, as in any class language. A built-in's own runtime methods are replaced and reached the same way: class Fetcher extends DataSource [ fetch() { …; super.fetch() } ] wraps the DataSource's fetch rather than rewriting it, and the runtime's own calls to fetch() land on the override. A use site that overrides a class's method (Stepper [ input(v: number) { … } ]) reaches the class's with super the same way. A constraint that calls a method stays live through super too: the base body's reads are wired like the override's. name(v: T) { super.name(v) } fetch() { log = log + "fetching"; super.fetch() } `super` reaches a method up the chain: one written in this program or the library, or the built-in's own runtime method. A built-in fires its events; a handler has no base body to call. `super` is a call, not a value. A `{ }` value has no base method to reach.

-> return type method return arrow in a signature function type The return-type marker in a signature, and the arrow of a function type. quant(v: number) -> number { … } returns a number; omit it for a method that returns nothing. In a type position, (a: T) -> R is a function type — a parameter that takes a callback, or a declared attribute holding one. It is not a lambda arrow and not a binding operator: inside a { } body or a script block, => is ordinary TypeScript. The language's other arrow, <->, is the two-way binding operator on a text field's value. name(a: T) -> R { … } f: (id: string) -> void // a function type, in a parameter or a declaration Parameters in a function type are typed like a method's.

{ } braces curly braces constraint expression binding live value TypeScript in brackets Braces hold TypeScript, and as an attribute's value the expression is a constraint — re-evaluated when, and only when, something it reads changes, and kept true from then on. width = { parent.width - 40 } stays true through every resize; nothing subscribes, diffs, or re-renders. Dependencies are extracted statically by the compiler, which reads through the methods you call — a script function is the one opaque call. Inside the braces you are in plain TypeScript at full expression strength: ternaries, template literals, array chains, closures, casts. The bare-value vocabulary stops at the brace — a color is 0x4169E1, not navy; a size is computed from the parent, not written as a percent. A :path may appear inside a body, which is how anything conditional over replicated data is written. name = { expression } name: Type = { expression } No percentages in braces: read the parent and scale. No `#hex` in braces: a color in TypeScript is a number. No named colors in braces either; the message gives the number. A body is one expression; statements belong in a method. An attribute may not derive from itself — that is a cycle by construction; derive from a base. A bare name must resolve: a member up the enclosing brackets, a parameter, or one of the few globals a body may use. A constraint cannot notice a script `let` change; hold changing state in an attribute. A script call is opaque: pass values, never a node.

entries.title: :path
entries.text: :path datapath colon path data read replication [] suffix bound data :@ the record itself computed key whole record A colon-prefixed path reads from bound data, relative to the nearest enclosing datapath. datapath selects a place in a dataset; descendants read fields relative to it; and a path ending in [] replicates its node — one instance per record, reconciled by the record's id. This is what replaces items.map(…): a collection of children comes from data, never from code in the tree. Between the root and the [], a path may select in the JSONPath subset — [0], [-1], [1:4], [ ], ['quoted key']. A :path in a value is a read. In a handler or method, :field = v (and +=, ++) writes that field of the record the node is attached to, through the dataset's set — a field, a nested field or a non-negative index; a slice, wildcard or [] is refused, and so is an assignment inside a { } value. A text field's <-> is the other write, with a draft and validation. :@ is the record itself — JSONPath's current node — for a record that is a plain value (a string in a list of tags) or to hand a whole record to a method. [( expr )] is a key computed by TypeScript, anywhere in a path: :@[(field)] reads the field field names, :rows[(i)].title the title of the record i indexes, and both follow the expression as well as the data. Plain [ ] stays JSONPath; the parentheses mark the computed form, which needs braces — text = { :@[(k)] }. Both are written like any path: :@[(k)] = v, and :@ = r replaces the record. Without a schema a path is dynamic: an unresolved read yields null and the bound attribute falls back to its default; with one, every path is checked at compile time. text = :title // a read, relative to the nearest datapath View [ datapath = :rows[], … ] // [] replicates: one instance per record text = { :on ? :title : "—" } // a read inside a body input(v: boolean) { :done = v } // a write, in a handler or method Text [ datapath = :tags[], text = :@ ] // :@ — the record itself text = { "" + :@[(classroot.field)] } // [( … )] — a key computed by TypeScript A computed key is TypeScript, so its path is written in braces. `[]` replicates and may appear only at the end of a path. A dataset's literal body is strict JSON — quoted keys, no trailing commas. A dataset needs data: a literal body, or a derived `contents`. A literal is not a place: a cursor points into declared data. Declare the records in a Dataset and point at its `.value`.

entries.title: key
entries.text: key key = record identity identity reconcile reconciliation Replication reuses an instance across sorts, filters and edits when it can tell which record is which. By convention that is the record's id field, with nothing declared. When a collection's identity lives under another name, key = :field on the replicated node names it — a single :path, read per record. It is replication metadata, so it is legal only beside a many-path datapath. View [ datapath = :people[], key = :email ] Only a node that replicates can carry a `key`. A key is one `:path` to the identity field, never a literal or a many-path.

<-> two way two-way binding bidirectional double arrow live commit Two-way binding, opt-in and for leaf editors only. The left side is an editor's value; the right names a place in data — a :path, or a { } yielding a field name — resolved against the nearest enclosing datapath. Edits in the field write back through the cursor, and a change in the data shows in the field. It is the only arrow in the language that writes. Deliberately narrow: to drive an ordinary attribute from a control, use the value pattern — derive down with text = { app.note }, deliver up with input(v: string) { app.note = v } — so data flow stays traceable. One-way :path everywhere else. TextInput [ text <-> :title ] TextInput [ text <-> { fieldName } ] // a { } yielding a field name The left side is an editor's value; a Text is not an editor. There must be data to edit: a `datapath` above the editor. The right side is a place, not a value: a `:path`, or a `{ }` yielding a field name.

entries.title: gradient(…) · stroke(…) · shadow(…) · frost(…)
entries.text: gradient stroke shadow stop frost value constructor value constructors constructor call The value constructors build the composite values decoration attributes take: a gradient, a stroke, a shadow, a frosted backdrop, a gradient stop. They are the only call forms a bare value admits, and each has one shape — the message names it when the call is wrong. Inside a { } the same names are ordinary functions, with colors written as numbers. Their names are reserved: no member may be called gradient, stroke, shadow, stop, or frost. A stroke is drawn inside the box, so it never enlarges the layout; a shadow is cast outside it, escaping any clip, as a CSS box-shadow does. A stroke attribute also takes four of them — [top, right, bottom, left], clockwise from the top, null for a bare side — which is the one-or-four shape cornerRadius and padding share. All three take either form from a { } constraint as readily as from a literal, which is how a border in a theme token is written: stroke = { [ stroke(1, provided("theme").line), null, stroke(1, provided("theme").line), null ] } rules a row top and bottom. fill = gradient(#F8F8F8, #D8D8D8) // bare: colors in the bare vocabulary fill = { gradient("180deg", 0xF8F8F8, 0xD8D8D8) } stroke = stroke(1, #B0B0B0) // drawn inside the box stroke = [ stroke(1, #B0B0B0), null, stroke(1, #B0B0B0), null ] // per side, top first shadow = shadow(0, 4, 12, #00000033) // dx, dy, blur, color backdrop = frost(26, 1.5) // blur, saturate A fill takes a color, a gradient, or null; an unknown call is not a fill. Each constructor has one arity; a short call is refused with the shape.

entries.title: 12 · 50% · center · navy · #336699 · "text" · true
entries.text: literal literals bare value percent named color hex color string literal keyword literal enum token The bare-value vocabulary the compiler owns: numbers, percents, the position literals center and end, colors by name or hex, strings, booleans, null, and the enum tokens each attribute names. A bare literal is the value itself, set once. Inside { } none of this exists — there you are in TypeScript, where a color is 0x336699 and a size is arithmetic on the parent. A "…" string ends at its line; long text is a """ block. An 8-digit 0x literal is an alpha color, never a number — which is why #RRGGBBAA and 0xRRGGBBAA mean the same thing and a Length refuses it. width = 240 // a number width = 100% // a percent, of the parent x = center // a position literal, on x/y fill = navy // a named color fill = #336699 // a hex color; #RRGGBBAA carries alpha text = "one line" // a string ends at its line text = """ several lines """ // a block string axis = y // an enum token An enum attribute takes one of its tokens; the message lists them. An 8-digit 0x is an alpha color, not a number. A quoted string ends at its line.

entries.title: this · parent · classroot · app
entries.text: this parent classroot app scope noun scope nouns nouns root children reserved names A bare name resolves outward through the enclosing brackets, innermost first — the brackets are the scope exactly as they are the tree — and the compiler rewrites the read to an explicit path at compile time. Four reserved words say it explicitly: this, the node the code is written on; parent; classroot, the instance of the class being defined, from any depth inside it; and app, the running application, from anywhere. Built-ins never resolve outward: every view carries width, so a bare width is always this node's. classroot is legal only inside a class body. One structural member every View carries, children, is reserved as well. this.width // the node the code is written on parent.width // its parent classroot.label // the instance of the class being defined app.theme // the running application `classroot` names the root of a class you define; it has no meaning on the App. A scope noun cannot name a child. A scope noun cannot be declared. A bare name must resolve up the enclosing brackets.

entries.title: include
entries.text: include include another file split a program multiple files import a file Merges another file's top-level declarations — its classes, scripts, styles, themes, schemas — into this program, once, however many times it is named. It is not a module system: there are no exports, no namespacing, and no root instance comes across. Everything merges into one program, and a class in an included file may extend one declared here. The path resolves relative to the including file. The standard library needs no include — its classes are auto-included by name — but a library file may be included explicitly, as the library's own files include each other. include [ "path.declare" ] include [ "a.declare", "b.declare" ] The file must exist, relative to the including one. A path is a quoted string.

entries.title: use
entries.text: use use directive keep a component tree shaking constructed by name createView Keeps classes the production build would otherwise drop. The build tree-shakes anything no tag instantiates; a class your code constructs by name at runtime — app.createView("Badge"), an icon named by a string in a control's iconLeft — is mentioned nowhere in the tree, so it would be removed. use says it is still needed. The symptom without it is a class that works in dev, where everything is present, and is missing from the built app. A menu's kind or icon record field, an IconHost's kind, and every createView call are the places to look. use [ Name, Other ] An entry names a built-in or a declared or included class.

entries.title: ship
entries.text: ship ship block package production build self-contained islands files compiler at run time inspector in production declarec States what a self-contained package of this program must carry beyond what its source names. A production build (declarec) reads the block; the dev server and the static site, which carry every source and a compiler, read none of it. Each member is a fact about the program, never a build option: islands — the programs an AppIsland may mount when its program is computed (program = { app.current }), spelled as program spells them. Each is compiled ahead and shipped beside the app with everything it would carry alone — its data, its own islands, its own ship block — once, however many hosts name it. A literal program = "name" needs no entry. files — what the program reads that no literal names, or that lives outside its folder: a docs model two levels up, its own source for a viewer. Each is copied into the package and served from there; the program's paths are untouched. A .declare source ships with its highlighted reader form too, so a viewer in the package reads it as on the site. A literal url = "data.json" beside the program needs no entry. compiler = true — the program compiles source at run time (live editing, programs typed in). The package carries the compiler and the library's source; otherwise it carries neither, and an island naming an unbuilt program is a reported error. inspector = true — the program answers questions about itself in production: the Inspector (compiled ahead), the __declare bridge, source positions, and error prose all ship. It does not imply the compiler. The block may appear before or after the root, and an included class may carry its own — a help panel that reads the docs model says so where it lives — and the program's merged block is the union. ship [ islands = ["name", "../../other/other"] ] ship [ files = ["../../docs/model.json", "app.declare"] ] ship [ compiler = true, inspector = true ] A member is one of the four. `islands` and `files` are lists of quoted paths. An entry is a name in quotes, never bare. `compiler` and `inspector` are true or false. Each member is named once.

entries.title: defaultFlags
entries.text: defaultFlags flags default flags renderer canvas kernel crawler render The program's own defaults for the platform's flags, the same ones a request names in its URL (?render=canvas) and declarec takes (--render=canvas), with the same values. A flag the request or the command names wins; one it leaves out, the program's block decides; one neither names takes the platform's default. render — dom or canvas: the renderer a browser runs the program on. A program whose screen is all drawing, redrawn every frame — a game — can run smoother as one canvas. kernel — wasm or js: the reactive kernel a production build carries. crawler — true or false: whether a production build, or a run page on the dev server, embeds the program's crawled content for readers that don't run it. accessibility — true or false: whether the program carries its accessibility layer — what screen readers are given, the accessibility warnings, reduced motion. A game drawn every frame, with nothing a screen reader could use, sets it false and pays nothing for it. The block is read before the program runs, so it says nothing about how the program behaves, and the program runs the same whichever values a host uses. A program running as another's AppIsland takes the outer program's renderer and kernel, and the Mac host runs its own. A program has at most one block. It may sit in any of the program's files, before or after the root. defaultFlags [ render = canvas ] defaultFlags [ kernel = js, crawler = true ] A member is one of the three. A value is one of its member's words. Each member is named once. A program has one block.

entries.title: script
entries.text: script script block typescript block helper function plain typescript import A top-level block of plain TypeScript, wholly outside the reactive system: pure functions of their arguments (date arithmetic, formatting, parsing), stateful helpers, whole libraries. A program may hold any number of blocks, inline and files mixed; they share one scope in source order. A file is written module-style (export allowed); an inline block refuses export, since its top-level names are already visible to every { }. A block may import ES modules — a relative file, or an npm package by bare specifier — bundled at compile by a Node host (the dev server, declarec, verify); the in-browser compile refuses imports by name. A constraint may call into script, opaquely: it depends on the values it passes, never on what the function does inside. So pass values, not nodes, and hold state that changes in an attribute — nothing notices a script let change. This is where arithmetic, formatting, and imported JavaScript live, so the tree stays about the tree. What does not belong here is anything the program's look or model depends on. A color, a font list or a size used in more than one place is a theme token read with provided("theme"), a style, or an attribute — a script constant cannot be themed, switched for dark mode, or read by explain. A derivation over the app's data — an order's total, a running balance — is a method on the node that holds the data. The compiler reads through a method, so its dependencies are known and explain can show them; it cannot see inside a script function, and its results arrive untyped. script { … } // inline TypeScript script [ "file.ts" ] // the same, from a file `export` has no meaning in an inline block. A script `let` is not reactive state; a constraint reading it is refused. A body may not write a script variable — each body holds a copy, so the write lands nowhere. A script constant is not a bare literal; reach it through braces.

entries.title: font
entries.text: font declare a font web font font family typeface font face A typeface is an object in the tree, not a top-level declaration: a Font with FontFace children, usually on the App, or a Font [ family = "…" ] with no faces for a system font. A family attribute holds it — fontFamily = { app.brand }, or a list in a { }, { [app.brand, "sans-serif"] } — so switching fonts is an assignment. loaded and failed are the font's facts; wait and late say what loading is worth. A FontFace's weight is a keyword, a number 1–1000, or range(lo, hi) for a variable font file. See the Font and FontFace classes. brand: Font [ FontFace [ src = "brand-400.woff2" ], FontFace [ src = "brand-700.woff2", weight = bold ] ] ui: Font [ family = "Helvetica Neue" ] fontFamily = { [app.brand, "sans-serif"] } `font Name [ … ]` is not a top-level declaration — a font is an object in the tree. A font name where a family goes is not a family — name the object in a `{ }`. A FontFace weight is a keyword, a whole number 1–1000, or range(lo, hi) with lo < hi. A FontFace lives inside a Font, and a Font holds FontFace children only.

entries.title: style
entries.text: style style block named style reusable style style bundle span class styled run A named record of text attributes — the style of a run of text that has no view of its own. inside HTMLText or Markdown wears it, and a drawing's d.fillText / d.strokeText and measureText take it. Its name is a value in any { }, typed by the fields it sets (Keyword.textColor). Like a theme record, a bundle holds literal values only: it has no place in the tree, so nothing in it can depend on where it is used. A look that should follow something — the theme, dark mode — is written where it is used: a textStyles = { … } map on the rich text, or a spread in a drawing, { ...Keyword, textColor: provided("theme").accent }. Top-level declared names are capitalized by convention. For whole views there is no bundle: reuse a look by subclassing (class Tile [ … ], or class Tile extends Card [ … ]), and provide values downward with theme and the face attributes. style Keyword [ textColor = #C678DD, fontWeight = bold ] HTMLText [ html = "class" ] // a run wears the bundle by name d.fillText("class", 0, 20, Keyword) // so does a drawn run A bundle sets text attributes; a name `Text` does not declare is refused. A bundle holds attribute sets only — no children, methods, or declarations. A bundle's fields are literal values — a `{ }` field is written where it is used instead. Its name shares one namespace with classes, themes, and fonts.

entries.title: theme
entries.text: theme tokens design tokens theming skin reskin dark mode preset token record A theme is a named record of tokens — colours, sizes, decorations — declared at the top level like a class or a schema. Token names are free; values are plain literals, value constructors, or lists of them. The library ships presets in scope by name (SanFrancisco, Cupertino, MountainView, Redmond, each with a …Dark companion), and theme Brand [ … ] declares your own. Providing and reading are the two halves of provided values. theme = Brand on the App provides the record to the whole tree — a plain set, no keyword. provided("theme").accent reads a token from the nearest provider; the standard library reads it for you (a Button styles off provided("theme") inside Control), so an app that only sets theme never writes the read. Because theme is an ordinary reactive value, dark mode is one expression — theme = { app.systemDark ? BrandDark : Brand } — and a subtree re-skins partially by providing a spread copy lower down. The library reads specific token names, so build a theme from a preset rather than an empty record. theme Brand [ accent = #CC3333, surface = #FFF7F5 ] // a named token record App [ theme = Brand ] // PROVIDE it — a plain set, no keyword fill = { provided("theme").surface } // READ a token anywhere below theme = { { ...provided("theme"), accent: 0xCC3333 } } // a descendant provides a modified one A theme named at a use site must be a preset or one the program declares. A token record holds tokens only — no children, methods, or declarations. A token is a plain value, a value constructor, or a list of them — never a datapath. Its name shares one namespace with classes, styles, and fonts.

entries.title: provided("name")
entries.text: provided provided value provided values provide provision context inherited value ancestor value cascade The one explicit up-the-tree read: provided("name") is the value the nearest ancestor makes available under that name — bare in [ ] like gradient(…), or a call in { }. Providing is just holding a value: declare a typed attribute on an ancestor (density: number = 2) and every descendant may read it; the built-in provided names — the text face, theme, iconSize, the rich-text attributes — need no declaration at all, so fontSize = 13 on a container provides it to every Text beneath. A value set locally always outranks a provided one. It is explicit on purpose: the read reaches past this node, and a non-local dependency is worth showing. You rarely write it — Text and the library widgets read the face and theme values for you; you write it where your own code wants a value from above. A read that finds no provider falls to its default, else fails at boot naming the value. provided("name") // the nearest ancestor's value under name provided("name", default) // … or the default when no ancestor provides one density: number = 2 // PROVIDE: declare a typed value on an ancestor fontSize = 13 // a built-in provided name is set bare on any container A read with no provider and no default fails at boot, naming the value. A provision is a value or a { }, never a datapath. A provided value of your own is introduced with a type; a bare unknown name is a typo, not a provision.

entries.title: schema
entries.text: schema declare a schema data shape typed data record type schema declaration A named data shape, declared at the top level like a class, and a type in the one type system: use the name in any type position — a declared attribute, a parameter, a return, a field of another schema — and declare a dataset's document with it. The dataset's .value is then typed, so a misspelled field dies at compile time; the runtime enforces the same declaration at every boundary — arrival, the literal body, and the mutation verbs — so malformed data yields .failed rather than undefined three steps downstream. Field markers: [] for an array, ? for optional. Field types are string, number, boolean, any, a literal union of strings or numbers, another schema's name, or a nested [ … ]. Extra keys always pass — a schema declares what the program relies on, not everything the document carries. schema Task [ id: string, done: boolean, status: "open" | "closed", note?: string ] d: DataSource [ url = "tasks.json", schema = [ tasks[]: Task ] ] sel: Task? = null // the name in any type position A field's type is one of the shape vocabulary; an unknown name is refused with the list. One schema per name. A field carries a type after its markers.
